GRANDMOTHER BROWN. Dear Grandmother Brown Lived in Cranberrytown, And a kindly old woman was she: There was no one so bad, Either lassie or lad, But some good in the same could she see. One June afternoon Mistress Polly Muldoon Ran in for that moment that ends In an hour or more, And did naught but talk o'er The shortcomings of neighbours and friends. But in vain did she scold About young folks and old: Only patient excuses she heard, Till at last she cried out, "You would speak. I've no doubt, For old Satan himself a good word." Then said Grandmother Brown, Of Cranberrytown, "Well, whatever his 'Winn may be, I don't think we could find Many people who mind Their own business as closely as he:" 4.—Harper's Monthly. MARGARET ETTINGE. WOODHOUSELEE. Woodhouselee was a cheery place When Bothwellhaugh brought home his bride ; The folk blessed either comely face, As he and she rode side by side: They welcomed both with song and shout, AS Roslin bells rang gaily out; Was never thought of dread or doubt At merry Woodhouselee. Woodhouselee was a dreary place When traitor Murray's minion came; No thought of pity nor of grace, But all the house was one light flame; They drove her forth, and bade her go Barefooted through the blinding snow, With babe at breast, they mocked her woe In cruel Woodhouselee. Woodhouselee is an eerie place When night upon the woodland falls, For then a form is seen to pace Beside the mere beneath the walls: A dame in white, who weeps and wrings, And now she shrieks and now she sings, Until a ghostly shot there rings Round haunted Woodhouselee. B. MONTGOMERIE RANKING. —Belgravia Holiday Number.

Pennsylvania has an editor 91 years old. He attributes I his long life and excellent health to the fact that he never expected to please everybody, and never tried to. Hotel.keeper, on being interrogated about a landscape painter who was his guest—" He's a penter ; but he's no I wan o' the kind that pents horses—he pents parks." "My wife," said a printer, " is very clever with a com- posing stick. When I get home late she uses the broom handle in a way that composes my spirits at once." An Irish gentleman, who had been spending the evening r with a few friends, looked at his watch just after midnight, and said, "It is to.neorrow morning; I must bid you good I night, gentlemen." " Darling." said a loyeastricken typo to his sweetheart, "do you know why I am like the letter q?" "No," she answered. "Because I am useless without u," answered he, , as he gently placed his arm around her waist. A train stopped at a station on a Texas railroad, where a gang of workmen were digging a trench. A lady passenger,i stepping to the station platform, asked one of the labourers what he was digging for? "For a dollar and a q'arter a day, mum," said he. " Doctor," said the grateful patient, seizing the physician's hand, "I shall never forget that to you I owe my life ! " " You exaggerate," returned the doctor mildly; "you Owe me only for fifteen visits. That is the point which I hope you will not fail to remember. "You may call me irritable if you like, but it would take a good deal to make me cross just now," remarked an old lady who wanted to get from one side of the street to the other, when two railway vans, a fire-engine, five omnibuses, a dozen hansom cabs, and a drove of bullocks were coming along at fall speed. A Dakota editor is out in the picturesque wilds calling upon the hills and rocks to fall on him and hide him from the wrath to come. He wrote: " Mrs. Allen called yester- day and presented us with some of her jam, and we unhesi. tatingly say it beats the world." The printer made it read "jaw," and hence The King of Siam wants 25 American officers to reorgan- ise his army. As his Majesty has a pleasant way of reor- ganising the field and staff by executing every officer who is defeated, there is a shyness peculiarly. American displayed by the modest, bat thoroughly competent officers to whom these presents have come greeting. A reporter coming into court somewhat late, and finding his post occupied, looked round in despair. At last he said aloud, "What, will no one give me a place ?" The prisoner, who overheard him, replied, "Yes, you may change places with me if you like." A general titter ran through the court, and the prisoner appeared greatly to enjoy the appre- ciation of his bon-mot. Passenger: "How long have you been employed on the astreet cars?"—Driver: "Fifteen year—barrin' whin I was sick."—Passeneer : "You must be a great favourite with the company ?"—Driver ; "Ha! ha! ha! D'ye see that owld gray mare I'm dhrivin'? Well, we both fell sick together at wanst last winter. They sint for a doctor for the horse, an' they gim me my resignation." While engaged the other day in one of his innumerable pranks, our Boy Bill slipped and sprained himself badly. When out of the doctor's hands he was so badgered that he -turned sulky and refused to answer any more questions, but set up a reply to the oft repeated " Wot's the matter, Bill ?" in a line of caps, thus : BA C KAC HE.

It looked almost worse than ipecaeuanha, and it was a long time before it dawned on some of his mates that the awful looking thing was only a THE REAL NEM YEAR'S DAY.—The 25th of March used to be the first day of the year, and it had a real and not a merely arbitrary claim to the distinction. The old year had truly passed away, and a new one was being ushered in. Under our present classification there is an awkward inter- regnum. The old year dies in December, but the new year makes no sign till long after the let of January. That is why the spring is sad: it is a true Anniversary, reminding us with painful distinctness of duties unfulfilled, of work eintnished, of ambitions more or less modest ungratified. The 25th of March is the great annual Day of Reckoning, when we are called before the inner tribunal to render our account up to date. We speak to the way-side flowers of our love, and to the fading leaves of our ambition. So Mr. Ruskin says. For the russet leaves of autumn I would, for my part, be inclined to substitute the firstlings of the spring —the violet, the wood-sorrel, the anemone. Here is another year visibly dead and gone, and we are no farther on than we were at its birth. It is no wonder that a sort of hope- lessness should take possession of the man who feels at fifty that he can do no better than he has done, and that every new year now must diminish the vigour of mind and body. —Good Words for August. TOICKY WALKING " WID THE WIDDER."—The life of a minister is nbt so prosaic and uneventful as many imagine; on the contrary, he often has many pleasant, though not altogether pious experiences. A rising young minister of the Methodist Church relates the following as an actual experience which he had not long ago :—There was an Irishman, whose name:we will call Michael, who was very sick. The doctor had given up all hopes of his recovery, and the wife was informed of the sad end soon to come. She took it very philosophically, and in her conversations with Michael everything was arranged, even to the funeral service. It seems he had no coat suitable to be laid out in, and with his consent it was decided to have the tailor make him a garment at once. This was done. In a short time Michael died, and the funeral day arrived. The minister had come to speak of the good qualities of poor Michael, and to comfort the hearts of the sorrowful. Everything was ready, but there was a delay, evidently caused by the non-appearance of some important mourner. Finally the man who had general charge of the funeral, getting impa- tient, called up the stairs, "Tommy I Tommy! come down. They're waitin' fur ye." The person addressed thrust his bushy head past the door, and concealed the rest of his per- son. Tommy's face was full of anxiety as he replied to the inquiry, and said," I can't—l can't." "But ye must come down," said the man at the foot of the stairs; "the funeral is waitin', and ye mast walk wid the widder." "But I can't," shouted Tommy, more earnestly than before. "I can't; the corpse has got me coat on." " Geh ! man, what do ye mean?" said the man. "Ye must come down any- how and walk wid the widder. Put on the corpse's coat, and come down." In a few moments Tommy appeared with the corpse's coat on. It was too long, and too large in every way. The sleeves extended over his skinny hands and as he slowly descended the stairs he was occupied in trying to roll them up. It gave him a most ridiculous ap- pearance, and as Tommy took his place beside the widow a suppressed smile was visible on every countenance. The minister could hardly restrain himself 'from laughter. The service, however, proceeded, and the coffin was soon carried out and placed in the hearse, followed by the minister' Tommy with the widow, and the friends. The procession was on the point of starting, .when suddenly Tommy began fiumping up and down, and, with his arms flying, shouted, me "Shtop! shtop ! the corpse has got me money and spec. tacles in me coat. Give me the money and the. spectacles." All the money Tommy had was locked up with the corpse. It would not do for him to lose it, and make this unneces- sary sacrifice. Nothing would do nov7 but to restore the personal effects to Tommy. The coffin was carried back into the house, and the corpse removed. The coat was taken cif and given to Tommy, who immediately took off the one belonging to the corpse, and put on his own with a degree of alacrity that was delightful to behold. Tommy found his money and his spectacles all 'right, and seemed quite contented. The coat made by the tailor was put on the corpse, which was then replaced in the coffin and the hearse. The humour of the situation was fully appreciated, and no less by the widow than the minister; for when she let down her veil and looked up her face was full of smiles as she said," I was just thinkin' what a tome time Michael i was havin' n Tommy's coat, wid his pockets filled cid money and a pair cf spectacles."

Small boy of seven to small boy of nine: "Now lernme smoke." Small boy of nine, shocked: " Why, you're too young to smoke ! " Lord Brougham once facetiously defined a lawer as "a learned gentleman who rescues your estate from your ene- mies and keeps it for himself." Visitor: Mercy me! What are those horrible sounds up- stairs P—Lady of the house: Oh, that is nothing but dear George! I suppose he has lost his collar-stud again. ANOTHER FACT ABOUT MARRIADE.—" Before marriage," she pouted, "you used to speak of my beautiful auburn locks; but now you call me red-headed." "My dear," re- plied the heartless man," marriage opens the eyes. Before that event, I was colour-blind!" Life is meant for work, and not for ease.—God gives poor souls time to recover their breath ere He strikes again.— Science moves forward swift and sure, under a higher guidance than one's own.—The true springs of all human action are generally those which fools will not see, which wise men will not mention.—The strange things which are done in the world. (which are some millions daily) are just what keep the world alive.—One thing . . . I have learnt, in .. my experiments on poor humanity; never to see a man do a wrong thing without feeling that I could do the same in his place.—Kingsley's " Two Years Ago" THE CHINESE CAEINET.—The "Nut Koh," or Cabinet, consists of four principal and two inferior members, half of them Manchus and half Chinese. According to the Im- perial statutes their duties are to "deliberate on the govern- ment of the empire, proclaim abroad the Imperial pleasure, regulate the canons of State, together with the whole ad- ministration of the great balance of power, thus aiding the Emperor in directing the affairs of State." Subordinate to the six "Chancellors" are six grades of officers, in all 200 persons, of whom more than half are Manchurian. The Chancellors have also ten assistanss. A remarkable feature in this "Cabinet" is, that as some of the six Chancellors and assistants are constantly absent in the provinces or colonies, their plates are then supplied by substitutes.— China and the Chinese. A FAST LINE.—We were going West on the Great Western Division of the Grand Trunk, and the night was chilly for the latter end of May. " Hi! porter," said the commercial man in the bunk overhead; "can't you give us another blanket P It's deuced cool to-night." " Aint got another blanket, boss." "Well, just see what you can do for a fellow," said the C. M., putting his hand out through the curtains with a quarter in it. " Danno, boss, but I'll do what I kin." There was scarcely a perceptible pause in the porter's measured tread as he passed our section fifteen minutes later, but the curtains parted and a blanket went through the opening as if it had been shot out of a cannon. "Thought I felt somebody carrying off part of my bed- clothes last night," said a passenger in the further end of the car, as he worked himself into his boots in the morning. "Dunno, boss; went mighty fas' las' night, making up -time; probably run from under 'ara."—Detroit Free Press. TWO STORIES OF CHEVIOT Doos —lt is related that when the late Principal Lee was preaching in a pastoral district he was surprised that none of his congregation rose when he pronounced the benediction. When he asked the reason be was informed that it was "tae cheat the dowgs ; for when we used to stan' they made sic a yaff-yaffin' at the thocht that they were to get oot that we never stan' noo, just to keep them quate." Another story is related of how an old minister in the Cheviots used, when excited in the pulpit, to raise his voice to a loud half whimper, half whine. One day a shepherd had brought with him a young collie, who I became so thrilled by the high note of the preacher that he I also broke out in a quaver so like the other that the minis- ter stopped short. "Put out that collie!' he said angrily. The shepherd, equally angry, seized the animal by the neck and, as he dragged him down the passage, sent back the growling retort at the pulpit, "It was yerseP begond (began) it."—Good Words for Avqust. THE KNIFE•GRINDER AND 1119 WORE.—The knife•grinder has, after all, a story to tell, and a very dismal one it is. He is environed by dangers as completely as he is saturated with the wet "swarff " (powdered stone), which dyes him a deep saffron colour from head to toe. He sits over a tool which at any moment may send him through the roof with all the suddenness and velocity of dynamite, and he works in an attitude and (especially it he be a " dry " grinder) inhales a dust which he knows will shorten his life by ten, twenty, or even thirty years, as constitution and fortune may serve him. The sharp crack of a breaking stone is an appalling sound to the occupants of a grinding-hull. A bang in a trough, a crash in the roof, and a piteous moan, and all is over. If the victim be alive he is hurried to the hospital; if dead, his crushed body is reverently carried away. No vigilance in the master, no care in the workman, seems able to avert these periodical catastrophes. The insi- dious water-rot, the hidden flaw, and the unequal grain do their fatal work in spite of all precautions.—The Eaglish Illustrated Magazine. August. Two SCOTCH Sroarns.—A respected minister, who is also a Peeblesshire laird, told me the following story illustrative of the matter-of-fact manner of the people. There was an old invalid man on Tweedside who was tended by a faithful Abigail. Like many frail persons he was always anticipat- ing his own speedy demise. • I'm thinkin', Nancy," he said one day, " that it canna be lang non. I feel as if this versa nicht the end wed earn." "Indeed, laird," said the atten- dant, "if it were the Lord's will it wad be real convenient, for the coo's glen to calve, and I dinna weel see hoo I am to tend on ye baith !" This, however, can be matched, lam bound to say, by another story lately told to me. the scene of which lay in the Perthshire Highlands. The minister had gone to see a dying parishioner, and when he reached the cottage be found the family bathed in tears. "Is he worse ?" he asked. "Oh, sir, he's just deein'," was the reply given in an agony of sorrow. Looking towards the "box-bed" where the sufferer lay, he was astonished to see two men bending over it. "What are they doing there ?" "Eh, sir, they're just shaving him !" " Shaving him !" said the minister in amazement, "can they not let the poor man die in peace ?" "It's far easier non !" was the strange answer which mingled with the sobbing.—Among the Peebles- shire Hills, in Good Words. AN EASTERN HOLIDAT.—In the East they dedicate a small portion of the year to avowed idleness, and nothing is then permitted to disturb the halcyon of utter leisure. The doors are shut even to friends. No one goes in or out. The inmates of the house are in their flimsiest tissues; they go unshod. The hawks sit nodding on their perches, the horses are idle in the stable. The fountain splashes in the scurries& and the turtle-doves among the pomegranate trees lull the garden to sleep with their sultry, slumberous cooing. The interval is sacred to the refreshment of the body. Gentle medicines are taken of a relaxing and blood- cooling kind. The hardest exertion of the day is the bath; Its chief employment the shampooing of the limbs with soft-scented oils. The ladies of the household recline with their cithars by their side of their master's conch, and the slave girl sits at his head with a fan, lest some pre- sumptuous fly should break the pions calm. The master of the house stretches himself at his ease and dozes all the day through, while the story-teller drones away in the corner like a bumble-bee in a scrape, and the either tinkles one of the thin, monotonous airs of the East. Now and again he stirs himself—a kite shrilling far up in the blue sky, a dog barking far off in the outer dust, has aroused him—and he solemnly cites Allah as a witness that the day is hot, and in the name of the Prophet calls for a sherbet of citrons. Such is the Afghan holiday. FEMMES FROLI THREE POINTS OF VIEIV.—We have all heard the saying of the man of Peebles, "I ha'e been to Paris, and I ken Peebles, and its Peebles for pleeshore!" This verdict is somewhat different from that of Lord Cock- burn, "As quiet as Peebles or the grave !" We agree with both conclusions. We can well understand the preference for Peebles over Paris entertained by the wearied soul on his return after an "--excursion" to the brilliant French city. How utterly confounded must he have felt when he found himself launched into the whirl of " doing" endless gal- leries, churches, boulevards, museums, within the prescribed three days! What a night-mare impression must he have carried back of gilded restaurants with their crowd of garcons with cropped hair, and unintelligible jabber; of cafe-ohantants, and of the ceaseless loss of money in an un- known coinage! And we can also understand Lord Cock- burn's sense of the stupidity of the slumberous little town, in whose daily annals the chasing of a cat by a dog used to form an event. But it is not of Peebles, but of the solitary Highlands of Teeblesshire that we mean to write; and we assert that for a nerve-bracing holiday, and for such enjoy- ment as springs from an abounding sense of renewee vigour in thew and sinew, there is nothing better than tin widelfreedom of such a pastoral region as is to be found there People in London can doubtless enjoy ex- quisite excursions into the umbrageous quiet of Kent, or have a bath in fresh sea-air or sea-water at Brighton c Hastings. But such changes are not to be compared to t 7 swift passage from the din of streets to those solitary she walks. Not only do you look out on the ancient peace of "nature undefiled," but you have also the advantage of getting among people who are living in a world whose interests are as different from yours as those of the dwellers in Shetland or the Faroe Islands.—D. Macleod, D.D.

"Good Words." ANYTHING SHE MIGHT NAME.—It is hardly credible that the 'United States' Supreme Court Justice Stanley Matthews, at the bidding of a prima donna, once turned a somersault in a parlour in the presence of ladies and a select company of gentlemen •, but still it goes down in history that the feat was performed. Some twenty-five years ago it 30 happened that there were at the same time assembled in a hotel at Columbus, Ohio, Justice Stanley Matthews and other dis- tinguished visitors. That winter Ole Bull, the renowned violinist, made a tour through the West, accompanied by Adelina Patti, who was a young girl of fifteen, and just then making her reputation as a songstress. One evening, after the entertainment at the Opera House was over, the whole party assembled in the parlours of the hotel, and of coarse Patti was asked to sing. This she consented to do, on con- dition that each one present would follow in a song orstory. All agreed to the proposition, and, as it was a brilliant party, Wit and merriment ran high. The young people were ex- tremely loath to disperse.as the fan had not been exhausted; and, that the sport might go on, one of the ladies kindly invited the party into her own private parlour. Scarcely had the" good time " been resumed, when Patti's mother , came with the unwelcome announcement, "It is time for I Adelina to go to bed." The dutiful daughter was about to 1 obey, when Stanley Matthews besought her to sing again, before she retired, his favourite "Home, Sweet Home," accompanying his request with the promise to do anything she might name if she complied. After some hesitation, she seated herself at the piano and, to the delight of all hearers, sang the song again. A. 1% soon as she uttered the last note, she turned on the stool, and, looking at Matthews, said, "Now, sir, turn a Somersault! " No sooner were the words uttered than the now dignified justice, without more ado, turned heels over head on the floor, much to the astonish- ment and amusement of the distinguisned party.

TENANTS' COMPENSWITON.—A highly important matter in connection with the Agricultural Holdings Act has re- c,ently been settled by the umpire appointed by the Govern- ment, Mr. J. Coleman, which should be noticed by every . . .
farmer and feeder of 'stock, for it shows at once he real
value of the Act. Mr. B. Holmes, on giving up possession of a farm in his occupation near Hull, claimed from Sir
Talbot Clifford Constlble, his landlord, compensation for cake, manure, and other feeding stuff consumed upon it, and

to which Ms agreement gave him no title. No satisfactory I arrangement could be arrived at between the parties as to I the amount to be paid, and the matter was therefore placed for settlement in the hands of the veferees. It was admitted on both sides that £596 us. 9d. had been expended upon cake, which had been consumed on the holding between April 8, 1882, and April 6, 1884, while the cost of the arti- ficial manure used was fixed at £4B 10s., and the amount to be allowed in respect of dilapidations to farm buildings at £l2 108. Mr. Stickney, the tenant's referee, chimed in respect of cake and manure £166 7s. 9d., and the referee of the landlord, Mr. Robert Wyse, offered £Bl 9s. 6d. This offer being refused, Mr. Coleman was requested tostate what he considered should be paid by Sir Talbot, and his award, dated June 28, directs that the tenant shall receive, after deducting the amount for dilapidations, £134 ss. 21, in addition to £l3 135., one half the costs of the ref,rence. COLT BREAKING.—The following is a very sensible method) which farmers may adopt for breakinga colt to work. When about two weeks old put a halter on it, and teach it to stand tied up in the stable. If it is necessary for it to go along when working a team, tie it in a careful manner to the side of its dam and in half a day or so it will have learned to lead. When fit for work harness it, and also a good quiet work-horse, mounting the latter and riding him rounlabout, the colt being led by its side. After this the two should be hitched to a waggon, the work-horse moJnted, and the coupling or hitching strap cf the colt taken in the right I hand, a line or rope being fastened to its bridle-bit and held by a person walking by its side. In a short time the check lines should be put on, and the young animal worked awhile thus, when it should be put on the nat side. In this way a colt will, more especially if it has a goo 1 temper, very soon be broken to work. To break one to the lead or single line when ploughing put the check lines on until the animal becomes accustomed to follow the farrow and turn at the corners of the land. Then put the headline on, walk by its side, and, in order to turn or guide it to the left, pull the line, making use at the same time of some appropriate epithet for its better guidance. To guile it to the right, jerk the line and make use of some other epithet. Pica STRIKE AT WATERFORD.—The Waterford pig buyers have induced the great body of the bacon merchants of that city to buy according to a certain uniform rate, to be fixed from time to time previous to each fair. No buyer was to exceed this fixed uniform price, so that if farmers refused one buyer he refused all, as no one else would buy from him. This would seem to be a very convenient rule for the buyers, but it is questionable whether it would be so , advantageous to the farmers. One Waterford firm of bacon merchants—we believe only one—Messrs. Richardson, dis- sented from this arrangement, and thus, we understand, in- curred the hostility of the buyers who promut d the scheme. An effort was made at Carlow fair to induce them to submit to the terms, but they declined, and pursued their former coarse of buying—every one making their own bargain. At Enniscorthy a large number of Waterford buyers attended, but we believe none, with the exception of the Messrs. Richardson's buyers, did any business. At about one o'clock a public meeting was called at the railway station, at which Mr. John Whitford (chairman of the Town Commissioners) took the chair. The object of the meeting was to lay this subject before the public. Mr. T. A. Byrne, Glentaigue, 'county Wicklow, who represented Messrs. Richardson, ad- dressed the meeting, and explained the situation in a forcible speech. We understand that the result was that the Messrs. Richardson bought all the pigs in the fair. Tann/mares Snowraorce CIRCULAR —The number for January, February, and March, 1884, has jest appeared. It tells of activity on behalf of at least one European Govern- ment to improve the country breed of cattle. Nearly 30 shorthorn bulls have in these three months been purchased In England for the Belgian Government. No strain of blood seems to have been preferred; the AO animals were selected from a very wide area, ranging from the Prince of Wales's home farm at Sandringham to the Duke of Northumber- land's at Alnwick, and again to Mr. B. H. Allen's in Here- fordshire. The returns from the Scotch herds are unusually folly made, showing that the good business they have been doing of late with America leads them to appreciate the value of a well-kept register as this is. The only pity is that the periodical is not issued under the auspices, of the Shorthorn Society. Of one Scotch ball, Athabasca, a white bull, it is shown that 30 calves were born to him in three months (three in one day), and that of these only two fol- lowed the sire's colour, whilst at least three times two were whole reds. To show that high forcing does not necessarily spoil fecundity, it may be pointed out that Mr. Willis's Vice-Admiral, which in 1879, 1880, 1831 was in every lead. ing showyard, has begotten several calves born in that quarter, and Mr.Foljambe's Bright Helm has been credited with one. Lord Fitxhardinge's Doke of Connaught, long famous as the highest-priced ball, promises to be one of the longest lived. In his eleventh year he can claim three calves already. A deputation appointed to visit butter and cheese facto- ries in England has reported at Perth to a meeting of the committee appointed to promote a factory in the Carse of Gowry. Mr. Smith presided, and read letters from Lord Binnaird, Sir James Stewart Richardson, Bart., of Pitfour, and Mr. W. E. Baxter, M.P., in which they all expressed themselves as highly favourable to the movement.

They would not have excessive expenditure and high rents to encounter; with superior cultivation and winter feeding greater quantities of milk and a steadier supply could be produced than in the south, and in all likelihood they would have a better demand for the separated and buttermilk. In all the circumstances he thought they would be able to pay , a fair price to farmers for milk, and a fair percentage on the capital invested, for it it paid the English farrcer with his backward and slovenly state of farming, it would pay them far better with their more improved system of hus- bandry and heavier crops. Mr. Anderson was awarded a vote of thanks for his piper. It was agreed to take immediate steps to confer with the proprietors in the district, and to endeavour to bring the matter to a practical issue.

THE TECHNICAL COMMISSIONERS' REPORT. NOTES IN LANCASHIRE. We have already given in a general outline the con- tents of the first volume of the Royal Commisiioners' Report. There are, however, several paragraphs in the portions referring to what was seen at home which it will be locally interesting to quote more frilly. Several high authorities are cited to show the advantagt s to em- ployers of the technical training of apprentices, and the Commissioners add :—" Without more particularly referring to the valuable work in the past, accomplished by the numerous Mechanics' Institutes spread over the country, many of them of long standing, we may point out that they are now largely remodelling their constitutions in order to bring up their teaching to the level of modern require- ments, as regards technical instruction. The Manchester Mechanics' Institute may be studied in this connection. Moreover, as evidencing the desire of the artisans them- selves to obtain facilities for instruction both in s3ience and art, we must not omit to mention the classes estab- lished and maintained by some of the leading co-operative societies. The Equitable Pioneers' Society of Rochdale has led the way ih this, as in:so many other social movements. It is much to be wished that the various trades unions would, also, consider whether it is not incumbent oe them to promote the technical education of their is embers." Speaking of Barrow-in-Furness, the Commissioners sketch the rapid rise of the town, and credit the School Boa et with energy and zeal. They mention that the School of A, t, which was erected at the sole expense of Sir James Ramsden, has 250 students, that all the girls in the elementary schools are to attend the cookery and domestic training school started in 1880, and the University Extension leccu ers are I engaged daring the winter months. The report proceeds :- 1 " The Commissioners visited the great industrial works of the town, and conferred with the proprietors on the sub- ject of the Commission. All the gentlemen with whom we conversed concurred in the opinion that, in the means for the higher scientific and artistic training of artisans,Barrow is seriously deficient. The population of the town has quite outgrown the educational provision for youths and appren tices, but we understood that the education question, par- ticularly in its bearing upon the local industries is receiv- ing most careful consideration at the hands of those public- spirited and enterprising promoters of the town to whom all classes of the population are already so much indebted." Twenty pages of the Rep ort are occupied with notes made in Manchester. Regarding Messrs. Blathers and Platte' Workshop School, the Report states : "This is a private technical evening school, established and supported by the firm for the benefit of their appren- tices. Under the guidance of Mr. Mather, we inspected the schoolroom and examined specimens of the students' draw- ings. Mr. Mather stated that there are 68 scholars in the school, which is designed to provide science teaching for the apprentices employed in the works. No strangers are ad- mitted for instruction. The drawings are of work actually in progress in the works. The teacher lectures upon them, I and explains and makes calculations, and the boys the next day at the works see the very thing they have heard about I here. They are allowed to go through the shop in all direc- tions with the teacher from time to time. Everything re- quired (patterns and models) is brought here fall size. The great feature is that in the workshop they have the actual things being made under their own observation, which have to be sold. The parts upon which they are working here in detail they afterwards see made up as a whole. In Mr. Mather's opinion you must bring the school to the workshop; you cannot bring the workshop to the school. Bringing the school to the workshop is simple and inexpen- sive. The teachers here are draughtsmen in the works, and by this teaching they add to their ordinary income. The teacher explained that the boys are not allowed to copy drawings; everything is drawn to a different scale from the flat copy, or the pupils have to draw from actual patterns or pieces of machinery used in the shops. Mr. Mather pointed out that the advantage of the teachers being per- sons employed in the works and being trained in this school, rather than in science classes, is, that he knows what each person is working at every day, and has the opportunity of pointing out something connected with the work he is doing. The teaching has an actual bearing on his every- day work. . The students are rewarded not only for profi- ciency in drawing, but for regular attendance and actual proficiency in their manual work. It is also a condition of employment that they should be regular in their attendance here. In reply to the question as to the advantage which the works have derived from the establishment of these schools, Mr. Mather replied An incalculable advantage. We desire to send oat abroad yearly one, two, or more thoroughly competent men, who shall not be simply me- chanics in the ordinary sense of the word, but who shall be able to turn their attention to anything coming under their notice, whether they have done the thing before or not (they are sent out simply as mechanics). We had the greatest difficulty in finding such men until we began to take them from this school, and since the school has been established we have been able to send boys at 20 and _ _ .

COTTAGE GARDENING Farm GATHERING. Much fruit is annually wasted through being badly gathered or gathered at the wrong time. It is of the greatest importance that all fruit in- tended for preserving should be picked in a dry state, or the labour in making it and the expense of sugar will be so much loss. Raspberries and other bush fruit dry in a short time after rain has ceased, but strawberries are very decep- tive, and take mach longer. The leaves may be dry enough, but not the fruit which is shaded by them. It is much bet- ter to wait until the fruit is dry than to pursue a course which will end in disappointment and loss. Ism MAKING.—It may appear beyond our functions to give directions for making jam in this column. Neverthe- less we are convinced of its necessity. It is as much to the interest of the cottager to know how to preserve his fruit as how to grow it. Old jam makers are aware that it requires equal weight of sugar and fruit to make good jam, and in- structions are usually given that the two mast be boiled for half-an-hour. Strict adhesion to this rule has spoiled much jam. Out of curiosity we asked an experienced jam maker, "How long do you boil your fruit ?" and received the curt reply, "As long as it wants it." The answer was correct enough, but conveyed very little information. Boiling must be continued till the mixture reaches a certain consis- tency, which is ascertained by raising a spoonful and allow- ing it to drop back into the pan. At first it will leave the spoon instantly, and as clean as if it were water, but towards the end of the first half-hoar much more slowly. When it adheres so as to form a continuous rope from the spoon to the pan it may be considered sufficiently boiled. If at any time it is found that the jam does not set after having been poured into the pots a few hours, it is a sure indica- tion that it has not been sufficiently boiled, and it should receive another boiling. For gooseberries and plums the sugar is first converted into a syrup by adding half a pint of water to a pound of sugar, which should be afterwards added to the fruit and boiled as directed. These fruits are not so juicy as some of the others, hence the advantage of the syrup. All mixtures for jam must be well stirred whilst boiling. A wooden spoon is considered better for this pur- pose than an iron one, and a copper pan is preferable to an iron saucepan._

..Cannaok.--We have made a small sowing of these for next spring, on a rich friable piece of ground, and have pro- tected them with a net without waiting for them to came up. We shall make our general sowing later on, because the earliest sown are too forward when the winter sets in early and severe; and in unusually mild ones they are apt to " bolt" or run to seed early in spring instead of forming heads. This was the case in many gardens last spring, and where there was no second lot to take their place the cab- bage bed was very defective. The kinds we usually sow are Early York, Cattell's Reliance, and a good selection of Nonpareil.

THE FRONT GartnEN.—The weather is now most favour- able for pricking out small batches of Columbines, Wall- flowers, Sweet Williams, and Canterbury Bells. Where there is accommodation, they will be best in the back garden until some of the summer tenants of the front garden are cleared, or until the early part of the year. The Grass Plot should be frequently mown, so as to have a close vel- vety surface. We have previously pointed oat the mischief wrought by allowing the grass to get too long, therefore we need not dwell upon it here. The surface should be kept firm by beating with the back of the spade; if this is prac- tised footprints will not appear so readily. PlNRS.—Cattings of these may be placed in a shady corner, or. what is much better, under an old hand-glass or frame. We have only just put a portion of ours in at pre- sent. The cuttings or pipings are made three inches long, and are severed at a joint. If the pipings as they are stripped are of the desired length, they require nothing more than stripping the lower leaves off with a sharp knife, as if they are left they decay before roots are formed, and convey decomposition to the stem. When sand is plentiful, we like to spread an inch on the surface of the soil. This descends to the soil with each cutting as it is inserted, and chiefly fills the vacant space round it. As it is free from vegetable matter, it is an active agent in preventing decay within, as well as protection from without.

THE Wurnow,---Pelargoniums that have cpmpleted flowering, or have only a few left, should be turned out of doors to receive sun and air to ripen their wood. Without this they cannot be expected to do well another year, and they will have a melancholy appearance during the whole season as compared with plants which are properly treated. During wet weather the plants must be turned on their side, with the bottom of the pot to the south, so that the sun may shine on the shoots more effectually. It is not necessary to place them upright till they are quite dry for the purpose of watering. When laid down again the oppo- site side should be placed upwards. The object is to allow sun and air to play on all parts of the plant till the wood is as hard as that of a lead pencil before the plants are cut down. Careful watering will be an additional means of bringing this about. The plants require to be kept dry rather than wet after the wood commences to colour brown, and the quantity of water reduced till maturity is reached. All kinds of plants intended for exhibition are best indoors for two or three weeks before the date of the show, as sun and rain are frequently most destructive to the flowers.

THE MANAGEREN'T OF POULTRY. THE DORKEV3I- FOWL': Amongst our oldest breeds of English domestic poultry must be placed the Dorking, which rivals the game in this respect. Those who are, or desire, to be old-fashioned in poultry, declare that these two are the only real English breeds. The others, they say, are all foreign or manufac- tured breeds, and though this is perfectly true, we all can confess that there is a place and plenty of room for every breed of fowls we possess. Still the newer breeds, valuable . _

does remarkably well, and there IfJ no difficulty in breeding I and keeping the variety. In-breeding also must be avoided, and, from the heavy body and the not.proportionately heavy legs, old birds are very subject to a disease known as " bu m- ble foot," an inflammation and enlargement of the ball of the foot. But in favourable places, where table fowls are wanted first of all, Dorkings can be recommended, as the birds grow very rapidly and to a great size, and the white feet, as well as the beautiful flesh, make it a universal fa- vourite. In the London markets it commands the highest prices always. Farmers, above all others, should take the advantage offered them of getting their birds out on to the fields, when the crops are being taken off. If there are no movable houses at hand, there will be some lumber at least which can be utilised in the making of a few, and a day spent in this way by a handy man would be enough to supply a reasonable-sized farm. The birds will be fed for nothing, as they will eat the grain that would otherwise be wasted; they will clear the land, manuring it at the same time; so that the advantage will be a treble one. If even we have mentioned this before, it is worth doing so again, because of the great waste resulting from the neglect of an opportunity like this. Whilst the birds are out in this way the per- manent houses can be lime washed inside, and painted or tarred outside, and the runs will get a much-needed rest.

We learn from the Atheneum that Mr. P. G. Hamerton is engaged upon an illustrated work dealing with "Landscape." The new German orthography, which tries to omit all mute letters, is to be made official next year in the Grand Duchy of Oldenburg. Waterproof paper and pasteboard as strong as parchment are now made by treating the sheets with a solution of oxide of copper in ammonia' so as to partially dissolve a thin film of the paper, which is then dried. The Atheneum says that an explanation of the phenome- non of "The White Lady of Hohenzollern " whose sup. posed reappearance in Berlin at the time Of the German Emperor's recent illness caused such alarm, is to be given by Mr. Karl Blind in the August number of Cassell's Magazine. New South Wales, it is said, can boast the possession of one of the richest silver producing districts in the world. It is situated in what are designated the Barrier Ranges, near where the colony joins South Australia, but it is at present extremely difficult to reach in consequence of the absence of ordinary travelling accommodation, though the road is described as being much better than the average Aus- tralian bush track. POISONOUS Ds.—The danger wearing next the skin articles of clothing dyed with% substances obtained from benzol and other products of coal tar has been declared many times by medical men, who have given instances of the ill effects caused through the absorption through the 1 skin of these irritating and poisonous compounds. Their warnings are repeated and illustrated in a case of exhibits sent to the Health Exhibition by an authority on skin diseases, Mr. James Startin, M.R.C.S. In this case, which will be found in the dress section in the east quadrant, near the entrance from the conservatory, are specimens of some of the beautiful aniline colours, rosaniline, magenta, violet red, methyl violet, Bismarck violet, &c., and gloves and stockings dyed with the substances by which these hues are obtained that, in cases coming under the treatment of the exhibitor, had produced eruptions on the skin of women and children, in some instances of a very severe character. Below are shown many vegetable dye stuffs and gloves, stockings, and other portions of dress dyed with them, from which no danger of the kind need be apprehended. THOMPSON'S PERFECT-COMBUSTION STOVE.—A domestic stove which it is reasonably claimed offers a satisfactory solution of the smoke difficulty has been invented by Mr. Henry Thompson, of 29, Marqaess-road, Canonbnry. Ex- ternally it resembles the ordinary register stove, but in its internal construction it widely differs from it. A recess at the back of the Thompson stove is filled with coal at start- ing, and behind the coal is a vertical hinged plate which is so arranged as always to exert a gentle pressure on the coal and the body of the fire, tending to push both forward to- ward the bars. A slight stirring of the fire causes it to be loosened, and the fuel to be pressed forward to the front to replenish the fire. When the coal has been consumed the vertical plate is pushed back and a fresh charge of coal in- serted. It will thus be seen that the coal at the back is undergoing a process of coking before being pushed forward. The gases evolved from it, instead of passing up the chim- ney and into the air in the form of solid carbon, are carried downwards by the draught produced by an ingenious but simple arrangement at the back of the stove, and are de- livered beneath the grate. At this point they are drawn upwards through the incandescent fire in which every par- tide of smoke is consumed. The waste products of com- bustion pass up the chimney in the usual way, but without the usual attendant results of smoke and soot. EATING AT NlGHT.—Popularly eating at night is thought Injurious, but unless dinner or sapper have been late, or the stomach disordered, it is harmless and beneficial—i.e., if one be hungry. Four or five hours having elapsed since the last meal, invalids and the delicate should always eat at bed- time. This seems heretical, but it is not. Food of simple kind will induce sleep. Animals after eating instinctively sleep. Human beings become drowsy after a full meal. Why? Because blood is solicited towards the stomach to supply the juices needed in digestion. Hence the brain receives less blood than during fasting, becomes pale, and the powers become dormant. Sleep therefore ensues. This is physiological. The sinking sensation in sleeplessness is a call for food. Wakefulness of ten is merely a symptom of hunger. Gratify the desire and you fall asleep,. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4-15. r, TILE CONFERENCE —ln answer to Lord Salisbury, Lord wwativireez slid the Conference met to-day, when an impor- tant point arose which requires reference to the powers. We Meet again to-morrow in the hope of the Plenipotentiaries haying received their instructions. This, however, is not certain. We are snaking every effort in the Conference to eeeno time. Attlee' RETIREMENT—EarI Powes called attention to What he called "The New Warrant," suspending voluntary retirements for captains and majors of the line, and moved for returns .—The Earl of MORLEY declared that no new Warrant had been issued, but only a regulation, and that no ren.eaurrge had taken place in connection with voluntary retire- 'nents. He had no objection to the production of the et rt.—After a few words from the Earl of Longford, the Motion was agreed to. ''RE HYDE PARK PROCESSION—Lord STRITHEDEN and ;Omani, asked the Government on what ground the dif- rerent routes to Parliament were blocked lID or prohibited on lion-lay, the 21st inst.—The Earl of DALHOUSIE stated that e Government had not arranged the route of the proces- :l°ll, and did not see that they had any reason to apologise 2: what bad happened.—The Earl of REDESDALE asked 1,713' was the procession allowed to come round by the ;eases of Parliament P—The Earl of DALHOUSIE answered that that was a question which ought Lather to be addressed to the leaders of the procession than 'Sr Majesty's Government. (Hear, hear.) It was no part I:1 the duty of the Government to tell the procession what ronte to take. YORKSHIRE REGISTRIES BILL—In Committee Of the Lorkshire Registries Bill, on the motion of Lord WENLOCK O n amendment was agreed to to the effect that the expres- aian o mortgage " which includes any charge on any land !or securing money or money's worth should include also 'AcY transfer of a mortgage."—The bill was then passed through Committee. WESTMINSTER HALL —Lord SUDELEY, in reply to Lord ee.oortee, stated that it was proposed to restore Westminster Oat' to the condition in which it was during the reign of Richard 11. by constructing a cloister along the west front. ?Mrscgua,NEors.—The Naval and Greenwich Hospital eneion Bill and the Teachers' Residences (Ireland) Bill Were read a third time. The Scotch Sheriff Houses Bill was read a third time. The Trusts (Scotland) Bill was read a See, ond time. The Oyster Cultivation (Ireland) Bill was 'Sad a third time and passed. Their Lordships adjourned at 6-40. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 4-0. A number of petitions were presented in favour of the kanchester Ship Canal Bill. AI7STRALIA AND FRENCH CONVICTS—Mr. ERRINGTON .asked whether steps were being taken to remonstrate with ;he French Government against the deliberate importation rth! our Australian colonies of a class of criminals whom elr own country will not receive —Mr. ASHLEY : The %svernment have been in communication with the French evernment, and believed that their representations were teceiving attention. It was hoped that it would be unneces- -BaerY to make it penal for captains of vessels to land released •eurninals in the colonies. HE AFGHAN BOUNDARIES.—Mr. J. K. CROSS, replying to Onslow, said Major-General Sir Peter I umsden had appointed British representative to examine and report ,Pon the Afghan boundaries in association with the Russian r.oePresentative, and it was hoped the Commission would coin- "e work in October next. Le'sletE SOUDAN.—Mr. CAMPBELL BANNERMAN, answering a "ru B. Churchill, said a gratuity on the same basis as that :larded for the operations in 1882, would shortly be ply- ° to the l and marine forces employed this year in the Sondan7ava LORDS AND IRISH BILLS. Mr. PARNELL asked f " Gladstone whether his attention had been called to the set that floe bills relating exclusively to Ireland had been rOected daring the present Parliament by the House of ; that during the same period only one bill relating e:sotesivaly to Great Britain was rejected under similar igeurnstances ; and whether, in view of these facts, he will re'roduce the Poor-Law Guardian Bill as a Government f:eaaure during the autumn session, or send it back to the olds by tacking it to the Appropriation Bill this session. O'Donnell supplemented the question by drawing at- s.'dore to the fact that 20 Irish measures had been rejec- eid b Y Government majorities In the House of Commons j;e Parliament; and two this session ; and that a "ed Purchase Bill was withdrawn by the Government ....luerely to add some political scenic effect." (Laughter.) lo!4,1'. GLADSTONE said the hon. gentleman who put the question put it for the sake of "scenic effect" (Load , Zeghter ) In answer to Mr. Parnell, he said he regretted tbE) loss of the bill to which he referred ; but tacking on to aAnDropriation Bill was contrary to Parliamentary usage, CO" if it were not another bill would take preference. Neither bli the Government entertain the proposition that the cro should be introduced in the autumn session. If the a„verninent was to go beyond the one bill for' which the io'tlßl session is to be held they would find great difficulty io,atoPping at that measure. The Government would take 4,0 careful consideration whether they could make the bill lai,evernment bill. A point ouconsiderable importance arose in the course of the dis- tosaion upon which the plenipotentiaries found it necessary th refer home. (Opposition cries of "Oh.") They all of 00211 uudertook to press for an immediate reply, and I Old how) that most or all of them will obtain it even by "Morrow. Trl bee E PEERS AND THE FRANCHISE BILL.—Mr. WILLIS: I (is leave to give notice that on the earliest opportunity— ,' laughtar)—l shall move the following resalution : 'That it is necessary to declare that the House of Lords tejecting the Representation of the People Bill for the Itatleoee of forcing the Ministers of the Crown to dissolve tberliament have abused their authority, encroached upon rbiti Prerogative of the Crown, and assailed the indepen- twee of this House, and that the House of Lords in re- te,,ng its assent to the second reading of the said bill, in o;7l3,principles of which it concured—(hear, hear),—be- rZa the said bill was net combined with provisions for the tlabution of electoral power, has violated the funda- wi'lutal right and privilege ef this House to determine in tb:t order it shell redress the grievances that happen within tperir3ealrn." The votes of £1,420,000 for teoensions, .C 105,000 for superannuation allowances. and Nl' 00 for retired allowances to officers of the military, artOariry, and volunteer officers were, after brief discussion, tboeed to.—The Navy Estimates were next considered, and I.4oreotaining votes passed, and progress was reported at Ihe Chartered Companies Bill was read a second time. 1:4,411 IRISH BILL: MORE Onsrunonerse—Mr. COURTNEY lar;'l,R moved the second reading of the Magistrates (Ire- tea) Salaries Bill, Mr. HEALY opposed it, and was inter- -1" by an ineffectual "count." The hon. member prorated that if the Government persisted with this bill the ele:r.gation could not take place by Saturday week.—Mr. reteNEY assured Mr. Healy that whether Mr. C. Lloyd bier "Id to Ireland or not he would not be paid uncler the ten;s-Colonel NOLAN followed.—Another unsuccessful at- Was made to count out the House.—Mr. WARTON fol- te otl4-Mr. HARRINGTON also opposed the bill as an attempt Or fel 010 strife and discord in Ireland —Another unsuccess- folleo-eTPt was mule to count out the House.—Mr. KENNY tee,:eu,-.Mr. GRAY also opposed the bill.—Another un- Fierie`aeful attempt was made to count out the House.—Mr. dleda't Moved the adjournment of the debate.—The House teed—For the motion, 11; against, 38.—Mr. MOLLOY ned the feeling of retaliation the Irish members felt er,lnst this bill.—Mr. COURTNEY moved the adjournment Ue debate, which was agreed to. (NroreoßtreaNnous.--,The Metropolitan Board of Works hoeneY) Bill was read a third time and passed.—The loePtenee Court of Judicature Amendment Bill was read a tine—The Public Works Loan Bill was read a third p`u.e and passed.—The Military Pensions and Yeomanry OS' Bill went through Committee and was read a third 6415.—The Prosecution of Offences Bill passed through t:nlmittee ; and the Expiring ',ewe Continuance Bill was road a second time.—The Building Societies Acts Amend- tittt. Bill passed through Committee, and was read a third 'the House adjourned at 5-15. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TunsnAv. 'ohe Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4-15. BE CONFERENCE.—The Marquis of SALISBURY inquired ko".uer the Foreign Secretary had any information to come teeil'cate with regard to the Conference.—Earl GRANTIf.LE teVed that none of the Plenipotentiaries had yet had time te ieheeive answer to the communications they had addressed ke Powers they represented. bkr.P.TOING ORDERS '--011 the motion of the Earl of Runs- Nlla new Standing Order was adopted for the classifies- 81/47„ „"t local bills; and at the instance of the Marquis of Deo,;!nnrur a Standing Order was passed requiring that when ce,r;'rtY Occupied by the labouring classes was taken by a teritrnY under compulsory powers the promoters should be teed r,ed within a limited time to provide sufficient accom- lerVon for the persons displaced. eento SUEZ CANAL—Lord LYMINGTON drew attention to the Itton of the Suez Canal. which he described as the foul- kai:e.aaPOol in the world.—Earl GRANVILLE said Her %eol'Te's Government had received no complaint, the Suez Bland Company had received no complaint, and the corn- of Her Majesty's ships passing through the canal 'ikele,,a,Gle no complaint. At the same time he thought it roi "Qat a narrow piece of water like the Suez Canal had ot be free from some of the charges the noble lord ?lopmetight against it. A technical commission was em- ,larkiW na considering plans for doubling, or very much en- 'abeorl the canal, and he hoped that the result of their 4444 0i would be known at the end of this year or the begin- ill _neat year. nom% adjourned at 5-0. The HOUSE OF COMMONS—TUESDAY. V,ke'rleaker took the chair shortly before 4-0. 44.4, entsTrow.—ln reply to Mr. Hopwood, Mr. G. Bps- hard4sid the functions of the public vaccinator were all by' rules sufficient to afford protection against a h hut .e den, minimum risk of injury, and more could not (ItleCanded from him than the due observance of those "44A.—In reply to Sir W. Lawson, Lord FITRIAAII-

RICE referred to the 3rd article of the treaty with the King of Abyssinia which, he explained, contemplated the giving of facilities by King John for the passage of Egyptians through Abyssinian territory. A reference to the papers would show Admiral Hewitt's belief that King John did intend to take possession of Kassala and Amedib on the retirement of the Egyptian garrisons, but that was not a matter of treaty. Fool, Arrn MOUTH DISEASE.—In reply to Col. King Har- man, Mr. DODSON said it was hoped an outbreak of this disease in Ireland had been stamped out. Gonnow.—ln reply to Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett, Lord E. FITZBIACRICE said that in a message alleged to have been received from General Gordon through the Mudir of Don- gola there was no statement to the effect that he would on no account desert those whom be went out to rescue. THE SUEZ CANAL —ln reply to Sir R. Peel, Mr. GLAD- STONE said that in pursuance of the articles of agreement entered into between M. de Lesseps and the representatives of the British shipowners, a commission, consisting of en- gineers and shipowners, had been appointed to examine and report on the best mode of improving the Suez Canal. That commission had appointed a sub-commission, which was to visit, and he believed had visited, the isthmus, and would prepare a report on the subject for the consideration of the commission. The agreement between the Suez Canal Com- pany and the shipowners provided for a large reduction of the canal dues besides other advantages in favour of trade and shipping. THE LORDS AND THE FRANCHISE BILL—In reply to Mr. Labouchere, Mr. GLADSTONE Said that he believed it was correct to say that the Franchise Bill had not been thrown out by the House of Lords, although he found in the report of a speech attributed to Lord Salisbury the fol- lowing passage :—" The House of Lords has a right to say, We do not approve of the measures you bring forward. If yen like to accept their rejection, well and good ; if you object to their rejection, your remedy is to go to the coun- try." He was, as he said, under the impression that the bill had not been, strictly speaking, rejected, but had been I laid on the shelf by two motions, made one after the other, 1 by not inconsiderable majorities, although the second was somewhat less than the former. As at present advised, the Government did not mean to make any further motion with respect to the bill, and their reason was that it would merely, without gaining any important advantage, give trouble to the House of Lords, which should not have trouble given to it. (Laughter.) It would merely result in the production of some third by-motion. If they could have a direct issue taken on the bill, he was of opinion that this would be very desirable • but it was not in the power of the Government to secure this.

..... „-- LUNACY LAWS.—In reply to Mr. Molloy, Mr. GLADSTONE said that although due attention would be given to the de- licate and difficult matter of the lunacy laws, as illustrated by the case of Weldon v. Semple, he was not prepared to say that the Government would introduce any measure on the subject. SUPPLY: A BANKRUPT CROWN SOLICITOR.—In Com- mittee Of Supply, Mr. COURTNEY proposed to withdraw for the present the vote for law charges and criminal prosecu- tions in Ireland.—Mr. HEALY asked whether it was in order to put off the vote and take the estimates out of the sequence in which they appeared on the estimates. It was notorious that the vote was to be postponed because it con- tained the salary of Mr. George Bolton, whom the Irish members had charged with being a bankrupt, a fraudulent trustee, and as having acted dishonestly in other ways A libel trial was now proceeding at Belfast in which Mr. Balton was plaintiff, and if he got a verdict the Treasury would come down to the House and triumphantly propose the vote with his salary in it. But whether Mr. Bolton got a verdict or not, the Government ought to dismiss him.—Mr. Sexton and Lord R. Churdhill objected to the course proposed by the Government, and Mr. TREVELYAN stated that as the proposal did not seem to meet the approval of hon members opposite, it would not be pressed.—The vote, which was to complete £99,031 for law charges and criminal prosecutions in Ireland, was then proceeeled with—Mr • SEXTON objected to the vote as highly extravagant. —Mr. TREVEL fAN de- fended the vote against the charge of extravagance. With regard to Mr. Bolton he deprecated any such conclusion as Mr. Sexton seemed inclined to draw from the information received from Belfast that day.—Mr. A. ARNOLD was of opinion that when a public servant presented a petition in bankruptcy be ought to be suspended from his office.— The debate was continued by Mr. T. P. O'Connor, Mr. Labouchere, Mr, Gregory, Mr. Illingworth, Mr. Gibson, Mr. Cowen, and Mr. Sullivan.—Mr. GLADSTONE said it was the duty of the Government to ascertain the legal con- struction of the rule as to officers of the Crown who became bankrupt. This would be done, and the report of the vote would not be taken until this point was settled—Mr. SEX- TON urged that Mr Bolton ought to be suspended at once.— After some remarks from Mr Healy, Mr Dawson, Mr Har- rington, and others, Mr PARNELL, on behalf of Mr Sexton, withdrew the amendment—Mr PARNELL then called atten- tion to the case of the Tubercurry prisoners, and to demand of the Government that they should b 3 released on bail or at once b- brought to trial.—Mr Harrington and Mr Sexton supported Mr Parnell's demand.—The SOLICITOR-GENERAL for IRELAND stated that there had been no more delay in the Tubercurry cases than was absolutely essential. Too pri- soners would be brought to trial in October.—Mr W Red- mond, Mr J McCarthy, Mr J H McCarthy, Mr Sullivan, and Mr Gregory continued the debate.—Shortly afterwards, Sir H Maxwell moved to report progress, and expressed dissatis- faction at the "attempt of the Government to liberate them- selves from the engagement" made by the Prime Minister. —Mr. GLADSTONE; resented the accusation, which he sail few men in the House on either site would have made, anA s id he had just su,rgested to the Chief Secretary for Ireland that it was time to renort progress. He adopted the motion to report progress.—Progress was then reported, and the House resumed.
BURGH POLICE AND HEALTH (SCOTLAND) BlLL.—This Bill was then proceeded with. The House continued sitting till a late hour.
HOUSE OF COMMONS -WEDNESDA.Y.
The Speaker took the chair at taw minutes after twelve o'clock. _ _ _
The Hull and Barnsley Railway and Docks (Money) Bill was read a third time by 82 votes to 31.

THE STATE OF ZULTTLAND.—in Committee of Supply an important discussion was raised on the state of affairs in Zululand.—Mr Guy DAWNAY proposed a reduction of the vote for charges connected with the Orange River territory, the Transvaal. and Zululand, and urged that a general con- flagration in Zululand was the natural result of the policy of the Government. The only two alternatives, he thought, were to appoint a Commissioner to reside on the Transvaal border and preveat Boer aggression, leaving the Boers to ex- terminate themselves: or to extend the R,serve territory, which was the policy he recommended.—Sir H IIomAND strongly condemned the restoration of Cetewayo, and COR- tended that it had been the cause of all the recent troubles. The Government ought to firmly insist upon the Boers ful- filling the requirements of the Convention.—Mr E ASHLEY said the policy of the virtual annexation of Zululand which had aeen recommended by Mr Dawnay was a policy which not only the present but the late Government refused to adopt. He admitted that the restor- ation of Cetewayo had been a comparative failure, but that was in no way the fault of the Government. Matters now wore a far more peaceful aspect than they did some time ago. Mr. Forster argued that to leave matters as they were could only mean withdrawal from South Africa. He held it to be the duty of the Government to try to stop the inter- necine warfare going on among the natives. Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN thought it would be unwise to undertake new respon- sibilities in connection with which so little advan- tage was to be gained, and he maintained that the Govern- ment ought not to undertake fresh and tremendous respon- sibilities by extending British rule in South Africa indefi- nitely and without reference to the demands which had been made upon the Treasury and resources of this country. Sir S. NORTHCOTE considered that we had a responsi- bility of which we could not get rid in regard to protecting the Reserve territory, and said it be- came a serious question bow the duties arising out of that responsibility were to be fulfilled. The policy of the government was one which had never been likely to succeed, and the present discussion had been raised with the object of obtaining some more satisfactory statement as to the policy which the Government intended to pursue.—The PRIME MINISTER declared that the Government accepted the restoration of Cetewayo, not as a measure certain to suc- ceed, but as the most hopeful remedy they were able to apply. He agreed that they ought to discharge all the responsibilities they had undertaken, although their respon- sibilities ought not to be exaggerated; but above all new responsibilities ought not to be assumed in a hurry without sufficient consideration. In the Reserve British authority would be maintained, but with regard to the country beyond that the Government saw no reason for interference, and they declined to extend British authority over that region.— Upon a division the proposed reduction was rejected by 155 against 99, and the vote was agreed to. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Metropolitan Asylums Board Bill, the Superannuation Bill, and the Expiring Law Continu- ance Bill were read a third time. The Public Health (Ire- land) Bill passed through committee. The Waterworks Rating Bill, the Municipal Corporations (Borough Funds) Bill, the Public Health Acts Amendment Bill, and the High Court of Justice (Provincial Sittings) Bill were withdrawn The House adjourned at six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—.THIIRSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. MrscaLLANEOtra.—Earl GRANVILLE made an announce- ment in the House of Lords of the determination to further adjourn the sitting of the Conference until Saturday.—Ths Marquis of SALIEBIIRY complained of the Prime Minister's criticism on the speech made by the noble Marquis at the Cannon-street Hotel meeting last week, which Mr. Gladstone had been "pleased to misunderstand," and Earl GRANVILLE explained the present position of the negotiations with Spain, Turkey, and Japan for fresh commercial agreement. The noble Earl gave an opinion that both with regard to agricul- tural depression and the depression in prices amongst the industrial population, we are not in a worse but a better posi- tion than any other country in the world.—The Canal Boats Act Amendment Bill passed through committee, the York- shire Registries Bill was read a third time and passed, and the Municipal Elections (Corrupt and Illegal Practices) Bill was read a second time.
Their Lordships adjourned at twenty minutes to seven o'clock.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIIIIBSDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIIIIBSDAY.
The Speaker took the chair a few minutes before four o'clock.

QUESTIONS. &c.—. The Chancellor of the Exchequer was asked if any compensation could be made for losses and suf- ferings resulting from the dynamite explosions. His reply was that many persons suffered from crimes of violence but the State neTer made compensation, and the Government
TH-141 EXAMINER. SkTUR,DAY ATIGITST 2. IRR4.

The total value of the imports into the port of Liverpool in 1883 was £114,625,829. Messrs. Leeming and Learning, of Halifax, have been re- commended by the judges of the competitive designs as the architects for the new Admiralty and War Offices. The London and North-Western fast train from Birming- ham to Wolverhampton had a narrow escape on Monday night, a large stone having been placed on the rails. Fortu- nately it was pushed aside by the engine guard. Mas. WELDON has scored another and a very substantial victory in the law courts. The trial of the action brought by her against Dr. Semple for trespass and libel resulted on Monday in a verdict in her favour, with £l,OOO damages. A gas explosion occurred at the Vine Tree Inn, Monmouth, on Tuesday night. The housekeeper and a gentleman un- wittingly entered a room filled with gas from a pipe left open by careless workmen. An explosion ensued, and both were badly burnt. PROPOSED Irma SIIIP CANAL —Plans have been prepared for the construction of a ship canal 127 miles long from Dublin to Galway. at a cost of £8,000,030 for ships of 1.500 tens; of £12,000,000 for ships of 2500 tons; and of £20,000,000 for ships of 5,000 tons and upwards. THE NEW MASTER OF ETox.7At_a_meeting of the . .
governing. body, on Tuesday, the .Rev E Warr, Mi, who has

for some Time Officiated as- assistant master of the upper school, was appointed head master of Eton College, in the place of Dr Hornby, who vacated the office upon his admis- sion to the Provostship. From a parliamentary paper published on Wednesday, it appears that the number of agrarian outrages committed in Ireland for the quarter ending Tune 30 numbered 186. There wera no cases of murder or manslaughter. Intimidations by threatening letters and notices numbered 93, and incendiary fires 27.

ANOTHER ATTEMPT TO SWIM THE CHANNEL.—MSS Beck- with, the well known exponent of natation, will make an attempt to swim from Dover to the shore on the other side of the Channel early in August. Arrangements are being made at Dover. She will be accompanied by Toms, the pilot, who went with Captain Webb. THE CHARGE AGAINST AN IRISH SOLICITOR.—At Wick-

low Assizes, en Wednesday, the charge against Toomey, solicitor, of assaulting Mrs Gyll was proceeded with. Several witnesses for the defence were cAlled to prove that they heard no cry nor struggle at the time of the alleged assault in Toomey's office. The jury, after an hour's consultation, said they were unable to agree, but finally returned a verdict of not guilty. LOVE TRAGEDY Ix IRELAND—Thomas Parry, described as a rteward, is is custody at Gal way, charged with wilful murder. On Tuesday he entered the Royal Hotel, at. Gal- way', belonging to Mr Mack, and fired five shots from a revolver at Miss Byrne, his stepdaughter, who died within a few minutes. Prisoner afterwards fired at himself, but in- effectually. He said Miss Byrne was his sweetheart, and that he had come 112 miles to shoot her. _ .

DESPERATE DUEL IN TEXAS —A duel with pistols was fought on the 14th at Dallas, Texas, between W. H. Beale and a man named Bowie, in a room en the third floor of the National Hotel. The shots were heard and the r.om was broken into. Both men were found lying dead, the pistol of each by his side. Both were shot through the heart and head. Shortly prior to the duel the men were devoted friends. A few minutes before the tragedy they had a quar- rel, and they retired to the room. TETE BRITISH MEDICAL ASSOCIATION —At a meeting of the British Medical Association at Belfast, on Thursday, Dr. Cameron, M.P., read an exhaustive paper on the Cholera Microbe and how to meet it. In anticipation of an invasion of the epidemic he recommended the daily disinfecting of public sewers and stricter attention to the character of public water supplies. India was the breeding-place of cholera, so far as England was concerned, and if we could remove causes of disease there, much would have been done to free the world from cholera poison. MURDER AND MYSTERY:A remarkable incident has oc- curred at Stoke-on-Trent. In December, 1877, a mysterious murder was committed there, and a bottle has just been found containing what purports to be the confession of a man named Capewell, who added that he intended drowning himself at Stone, near which town the body of the man in a decomposed state was lately discovered. The boots of the deceased have been identified by Mrs. Capewell, whose hus- band recently disappeared. The circumstances are being investigated. THE DANGERS or PRIVATE ASYLIIMS.—in the Court of Appeal. on Tuesday, the Master of the Rolls, in dismissing Dr F Xinslow's appeal against the order granting a new trial in the case Weldon v. Winslow, said nothing more danger- ous than such a combination of professions as were found in Dr. Winslow could be conceived. Dr. Winslow was the last person in England who ought to have given any advice as to whether a person was a lunatic or not, that per- , son being ens who, if found insane, was to be confined in his own asylum. IMPERIAL FEDERATION.—Mr W E Forster, M.P., presi- ding at a Conference to promote Imperial Federation at Westminster Palace Hotel, on Tuesday, said something should be done to make separation from our colonies impos- sible. Our present ties were not strong enough to bear strain- ing. Federation should be based on perfect equality. Mr, W H Smith said unless the colonies had a voice in colonial affairs disintegration must ensue. Lord Rosebery suggested the appointment of a Royal Commission to consider the question. Resolutions favouring federation were passed.

WHO IS THE CONSERVATIVE LEADER 7—The relations of the Conservative leaders with the National Union of Con- servative Associations have (says the Daily News) taken a new and almost surprising turn. As we stated last week, Lord Salisbury's friends, whilst claiming a majority amongst the members of the council, have resolved not to oppose the re-election of Lord Randolph Churchill as chairman. Lord Randolph, not to be outdone in generosity, has determined to retire in favour of one of his " leaders " on the front bench. He will accordingly propose Sir Michael Hicks- Beach as chairman, and the right hon. gentleman will, we understand, be unanimously elected. HEAVY SENTENCE ON A WIGAN STOCKBROKER—Seven years' penal servitude was, on Tuesday, awarded John Yates Mawson. at the Liv3rpool Assizes, for forgery and frauds on the Wigan Provident Permanent Building Society and the Miners Permanent Relief Society. The prisoner was a stockbroker of Wigan, and for some time a town coun- cillor, and his respectability secured the confidence which he abiged. His total defalcations were stated at £12,000, about two-thirds of which belonged to the building society. The only defence was that he speculated freely and indis- creetly. In passing sentence, Mr. Justice Day said that poor people were sent unhesitatingly to long terms of im- prisonment and penal servitude for offences which were trifling compared with those established against Mawson, whose position was certainly no mitigation of his offences. THE SOUTHPORT AND -WEST LANCASHIRE BANK —A petition for the winding up of this bank was Presented to the Chancellor of the Duchy on the 23rd hist by Mr. Wm. Newsham, a shareholder, residing at Ornskirk. The petition is directed to be heard by the Vice-Chancellor at the sit- tings of the Court to be held at Liverpool on the sth inst. On the 30th June a meeting of shareholders was held in Southport to consider certain arrangements which had been recommended by the directors, by which the property would be transferred to the Manchester and Liverpool District Banking Company. In consequence of it being then an- nounced that if such a step was not taken the bank might have to close before the end of the week, the agreement was unanimously endorsed. The circular convening that meet- ing stated that a call of 303 per share would be made to pay off the debts of the bank, and this has caused some conster- nation amongst the shareholders. THE DUBLIN SCANDALS.—From Dublin it is reported that a medical officer of the Grenadier Guards has been arrested in London in connection with the charges of felony now be- ing investigated in Dublin. A detective officer has left Dub- lin to take the prisoner to Ireland. This is the seventh ar- rest in connection with what are now known as the Dublin scandals; and it is stated that the police have warrants for the apprehension of other army officers. Two men, named Robert Fowler, Daniel Considine (blind), were arrested at Dublin on Tuesday, in connection with the recent scan- dale. A large draper, on being informed that he would be arrested, escaped over the house top.—On Wednesplay the inquiry before the Dublin magistrates into the charges against Cornwall and others was proceeded with, and eventually Cornwall was committed for trial on four charges. DORMANT FUNDS ne CHANCERY—in addition to the cases published recently where funds are lying unclaimed in the , Court of Chancery are the following relating to Lancashire —ln the matter of the trust of the bank for savings, lately carrying on business at St Helens. Account opened by an investment June 11th, 1861; no transactions since.—Ellen Threlfall, ex parte Ellen Threlfall, the widow, and Elizabe.h Threlfall, an infant, the surviving daughter and heiress-at- law of James Threlfall, late of Broughton, near Preston, farmer.
