div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.
EGYPF AND THE SOUDAN. ATTACK ON SUAKIM.-LETTER FROM GENERAL
GORDON.

Stamm, MONDAT.—The rebels are cmcentrated at Tamai and Handoub. Seventeen thousand women and children have been sent to the hills. There were niehtly attacks last week at a very short range. To-day an immense num- ber of the enemy appeared within two miles of the forts. They were repulsed by the Krupps. Our casualities during the week were one of the Royal Engineers and two Egyp- tians wounded. The rebels had ten killed and seven woun- ded. They attacked the friendly tribes near Agig, and it is reported that 500 were massacred. A SSOIIAN, MONDAY.— The inhabitants of Dongola have, through the Mudir's Vakbeel, telegraphed to the General in command at Assouan assurances of their loyalty. They say they have, through the firmness of the Mudir, been brought to see the error of their way. The fact of a telegram, couched in this strain, being sent from Dongola, is regarded as an additional proof that the Mandi's influence is declining. An Arab trader, who left Amarar on July 20th, has arrived here, and says Osman Digna is reported there to have been killed on July 18th by one of the Bishareen tribe, whose nephew had been stabbed by Osman because he declined to join his forces.

CAIRO, MONDAY.—A merchant has arrived from Kassala, who tells me that he read a letter to the Mudir from General Gordon, dated 11th June, ordering the Mudir to remain and protect Kassala. General Gordon adds that the rebels are surrounding him, but that he will destroy them at the rise of the Nile. The spirit of the soldiers was good. He was short of money, but issued bonds in some of from 20 to 2,000 piastres.—Daily News. CAIRO, MONDAY.—The 56th Regiment, 670 strong, will go up the Nile to Assouan on the 31st inst. Major Kitchener left Wadi Haifa yesterday with forty men for Dons°la on a visit of inspection, and his report will finally set at rest the vexed question of the loyalty of the Mudir. Further augmentation of the British fleet at Suakim has, it is reported, been decided on, and her Majesty's ship Tur- quois left Jeddah on Saturday to fulfil the order. Ar,Exernata, WEDNESDAY.—A telegram received from the Mudir of Dongola states that a report is current there that General Gordon has captured Berber. The Mudir adds that he has despatched an official to Debbah to ascertain the truth of the rumour.

_ Summr, WEDNESDAY.—The Turquoise. with Mason Bey on board, has left for' Massowah. General Freemantle ar- rived here yesterday and inspected the fortifications, with which he expressed himself satisfied. The steamers Camel and Engineer are discharging their cargoes of railway plant. DEFEAT OF A REBEL SHEIK BY TILE

div.head: MUDIR OF DONGOLA.
div.p: MUDIR OF DONGOLA.

The Times Alexandria correspondent telegraphing on Thursday, gives a translation of a telegram from amigola, dated July 25, stating that the rebel Sheik Ahmet Elhoda entrenched himself at Ehhatani, where the Mudir of Don- gola proceeded and attacked him, killing three hundred rebels. The Sheik Elhoda fled, but the Mudir pursued him to the pass of Elahmow. The telegram adds tht a letter had arrived from General Gordon by special messenger.

div.head: CHOLERA.
div.p: THE CHOLERA.

MARSEILLES, SATURDAY.—The official bulletin gives the number of deaths here during the last 24 hours as 89, of which 58 were from cholera.—Sundav : The number of deaths during tha oast 24 hours are 77, of which 36 were from cholera. The official bulletin gives the number of deaths during the last 24 hours as GO, of which 24 were from cholera.

TOULON, SATURDAY.—There were thirteen deaths here from cholera last night. The epidemic continues. 5-16 p.m.: There have been four deaths since this morning. Up to the present 593 deaths from cholera have occurred here. Through the flight of the inhabitants, combined with the large death rate, the population of the town has decreased by two-thirds. ARLES, Smqn.ay.—Twelvs deaths from cholera have oc- curred here during the list twentArfour hours.—Monday Six deaths from cholera have occurred here since yesterday evening. PARIS, MONDAY.—t. case of cholera was this morning taken to one of the hospitals; the patient's condition, how- ever, is not serious. ROME, SUNDAY —Three workmen, corning from Toulon, after having undergone quarantine at Ventinuglia, were taken ill at Rio Maggiore, near Spezzia, and one of their number has since died. It is believed that the disease with which they were attacked is cholera, but this has not been positively ascertained. The district has been surrounded by a military cordon, and completely isolated. MARSEILLES, TUESDAY—Nine deaths from cholera oc- curred here last night.—Noon : There have been two deaths from cholera since nine this morning. TOULON, TUESDAY MORNING —There were 21 deaths from cholera here yesterday. The sanitary condition of the city continues to improve.
MARSEILLES, WEDNESDAY, 9 P —An official bulletin issued this evening gives the number of deaths during the last twenty-four hours as 71, of wliich 24 were from chslera. _ _ .

ARLES, WEDNESDAY, 7 P.M.—Eight deaths from cholera have occurred here during the last 24 hours. MADRID, WEDNESDAY.—Seven days' quarantine is en- forced on arrivals from Newfoundland, owing to the fre- quency of their communications with France. FRANCE— HIE SENATE AND REVISION BILL. PARIS, SATURDAY —After a confused discussion, the Senate to-day adopted by 173 votes to 16 the clause of the Revision Bill, already approved by the Chamber, which proposes to expunge from the Constitution, the articles dealing with the election of Senates. The object of this provision is to enable the Government to remodel the system of Senatorial elections by a special bill to be intro- (laced later. The Right abstained from voting upon this paragraph. PARIS' SUNDAY—The Temps of this evening publishes a despatch from Moussey, in the Department of the Vosges, stating that an epidemic, supposed to be purple typhus, is raging there. Ten persons have succumbed, and 30 others are said to have been attacked. _ . _

- PARIS, MONDAY—It is reported that the Government have, in pursuance of an arrangement with the majority in the Chamber, decided to abandon the revision of the bud- getary powers of the Senate, in order that an agreement may be effected in that House regarding the revision of the other parts of the Constitution mentioned in the Ministerial Bill. The Senate to•day adopted the Sugar Duty Bill as passed by the Chamber of Deputies' including the raising of the surtax on raw sugar invorted from Europe from 3f. to 7f. THE FRANCO-CHINESE DIFFICULTY.

PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—The Premier gave audience this morning to Li Fong Pao, the Chinese Minister, who is un- derstood to have requested an extension of the respite granted to the Chinese Government for complying with the French demands. This request is stated to have been re- fused. The delay expires on August 1. Negotiations con- thane at Shanghai between M. Patenotre and the Viceroy of Nankin. SHANGRAI, TELIIRSDAY.—It is reported that the difference between France and China has been arranged, the amount of indemnity being fixed at 5,200,000 taels. No official confirmation of this intelligence has, however, vet been received. COLLISION ON LAKE SUPERIOR _ • _

The steamer Alberta, of the Canadian Pacific Railway Line' on Sunday night, collided with the steamer Osborne on Lake Superior. The Alberta was badly damaged, while the Osborne sank. eight men being drowned. RISING IN ARABIA.—CAPTURE OF TOWNS AND VILLAGES BY THE INSURGENTS. VARNA, WEDNESDAY.—& serious rising has taken place in the province of Yemen. The insurgents who have declared in favour of the Mandi, have captured several villages and towns, including Sane, the capital. Ten thousand troops have been ordered front Jedda and elsewhere to put down the rising.—Daily News IMPERIAL MEETING. Crtecow, SATURDAY.—The Czas announces that a meeting of the Emperor of Austria and the Czar will take place at Granica,in Poland. Thence their Imperial Majesties will proceed together via Warsaw to Alexandroff, where they will be joined by the Emperor of Germany. • A STEAMER CAPSIZED ON THE VOLGA.—TWENTY _ _a_
LIVES LOST. S. PETERSBURG, SUNDAY.-The passenger steamer Anionta capsized on the 24th inst., during a storm on the Volga, near the village of Badning. Twenty persons were drowned.

TURREY.—TOWN BURNT. CONSTANTINOPLE, MONDLY.—A most destructive fire has occurred at the town of Mara* Asia Minor. A thousand shops, two hundred how/es) four hotels, three mosques, and the municipal palace have been burned to the ground.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

The number of visitors to the Health Exhibition for the week ending July 28, was 155,655. Total since the opening 1,493,607. At Tramore, county Waterford, steeplechases, on Tuesday, a horse fell and broke its neck. The jockey, named Cahill, received such serious injuries that he expired on Wednesday morniag. The Sligo Corporation on Wednesday unanimously adopted a petition in favour of commuting the death sentence passed on ex-Constable Muldeuney for the murder of Peter Doherty at Craughwell. MINERS' WAGES.—Over 500 men and boys are on strike at the Shipley collieries, near Derby, against a proposed re- duction of 3d per ton; and 1,100 colliers Rear Leigh have struck work against a 10" per cent. reduction. THE MURDER OF A FAMILY AT SHEFFIELD.—At Shef- field, on Monday, Joseph Laycock, a hawker, was commit- ted for trial on a charge of wilful murder. On the 4th inst. the prisoner killed his wife and his four children by cutting their throats with a table knife, and then tried to destroy himself. His throat was still bandaged, and he appeared to be very ill. MURDER IN IRELAND.—A. magisterial inquiry was held on Wednesday into the circumstances attending the death of Miss Alice Byrne, who was on Tuesday shot by Thomas Perry, at Mack's Hotel, Galway. The sister of the deceased who saw the shot tired, and several other witnesses, having been examined, the prisoner was committed for trial on the charge of wilful murder. CONSERVATISM IN SHEFFIELD.—ID increasing distress at their fruitless search for a candidate, the Sheffield Tories have been trying to keep alive their hopes by spreading the rumour that Mr. E. Clarke, M.P. for Plymouth, would came forward to help them out of their difficulty. The rumour has reached Plymouth, and Mr. Clarke, feeling his present seat endangered, has telegraphed to say he will not contest Sheffield, but stand by Plymouth. REMARKABLE CRICKET MATCH.-1 cricket match has been played during the recent Donegal Assizes in the ,grounds of the Carnus Rectory, near Strabane, when eleven ladies chal- lenged the earae number of gentlemen to a match, the former using bats and the latter broomsticks. The ladies were cap- tained by Miss Claudine Humphreys, and the game resulted in a victory for the ladies by one wicket. An Irish Queen's counsel, with his broomstick, scored 93. EMBEZZLEMENT BY A STARR•BOWKETT SOCIETY SECRE- TARY.—A, secretary of two Starr-Bowket Societies, named Pratt, was on Saturday, at Devonshire Assizes, sentenced to five years' penal servitude for embezzlement. The prisoner wore a blue ribbon, and in defence sought to throw blame on members of the societies, whilst he pleaded his education in mitigation of his punishment. Mr. Justice Field thought his education an aggravation of the offence, and characterised as cowardly the attempt made by the prisoner to throw blame on those who bad trusted him. He thought, too, that find- ing himself in the dock, the prisoner might have removed the blue ribben from hie coat, and so have avoided bringing the badge of temperance into disgrace. THE WIMBLEDON MEETING was brought to a close on Saturday. Cons'elering the state of the weather the shoot' ing has been quite up to the average, but the number of visi- tors to the camp has naturally been much smaller than usual. In the absence of the Countese Spencer, the prizes were de- livered by the Duchess of Abercorn. drie of the most inter- esting presentations was that of the Elcho Challenge Shield to the Irish team, headed by the Duke of Abercora. Hearty cheers weref given for the Canadian team who carried off the Kolopore Cup; the Com nons team, will), headed by the Speaker, received the Vizianagran Cup; the Bluejackets from H.M.S. Excellent, who took away the Army and Navy Challenge Cup; and Osborne, of Birmingham, Taylor, of Glasgow, and Gallant, of Middlesex, who received the St. George's Vase, the Queen's Silver, and the Qeeen's Gold Prize respectively. THE MAORI KING AT WlNDSOR.—Tawhiao (the chief of chiefs of the Maories), and four other Maori chiefs, accom- panied by Mr. Fuller, of the Colonial Office, and the Rev. F. H. Spencer (who acted as interpreter), left Paddington on Monday by the 11 a.m. train for Windsor, where they arrived at noon. After partaking of luncheon, his Majesty and suite visited the Castle. the Albart Mamorial Chapel, the Royal Mausoleum at Frogmore, Virginia Water, and other places of note and interest in the neighbourhood. The King and his party having expressed themselves much pleased and delighted with their reception. returned to town in the evening. While at the Castle the King left for pre- sentation to the Queen a Maori chieftain cloak and wand of office. The Maori King and chiefs attended the anniversary demenstration of the Uxbridge Gospel Temperance Mission on Wednesday evening. The visit created great interest in the district, and crowds of people lined the route. THE PARCEL POST.—The 30,11 report of the Postmaster General, Mr. Fawcett says the parcel post was brought into operation without causing the slightest delay in the delivery of letters. It was estimated that the number of parcels would be about 27.000,000 a year. In the first weeks of the Parcel Post the number carried was at the rate of 15,000,000 a year. Gradually the number has increased to the rate of between 21,000,000 and 22,000,000. Without venturing to predict whether the parcel business of the Post-office will be large or small, Mr. Fawcett is confident that the working expenses can be adjusted to the number of parcels carried, thus securing the revenue against loss. The most effectual way of securing economy in the pucel post working, it has been found, is to amalgamate with the general postal service of the country. So far from supplanting pri- vate enterprise. the railway companies and other carriers have been stimulated to introduce a cheaper and better par- cele service.

INTERESTING DISCOVERY.—SOMEI Old newspapers have been found at Eccles bearing date 1791 Amongst the pub- lic announcements is one from the Poor Relief Committee, ordering that at certain days of the week potatoes shall be sold at 41b5. id. at the Market Hall, Manchester. Amother notice advises the reduction of wheat flour at least one- third of the ordinary quantity consumed. In the deaths column is a rather unique announcement having reference to the death of Mr. J.Shaw, master of the Punch House in this town, so well known for the singular custom of com- pany never staying in beyond eight o'clock in the evening." He kept it 58 years. The death of the chaplain to the Duke of Bridgewater, the Rev. S. Lord, is announced as having taken place on January 18th. Further on we are told that at Exeter the people, by way of protesting against the price of butter, is. 4d. per lb., called a public meeting, when it wee unanimously decided to eat bry bread only for a week. The following week the butter merchants sold their butter at the reduced price of Ild, per p.und, thus showing that " boycotting " was not unknown even in those days. THE COLLISION OFF FINISTERRE.—On Saturday, Messrs. R. Harrowing and Co.; of Whitby, managing owners of the screw steamer Laxham, which foundered after collision with the Spanish steamer Gijon, off Cape Finisterre, received a telegram informing him that thirteen men had been landed at Gravesend that morning by a French steamer. Those landed were four of the Laxham's crew, viz., Wm. Sample, Whitly, chief officer ; George Ogden, second officer ; John Milton, chief engineer ; and George Hart, second engineer ; also the third officer and eight of the crew of the Spanish mail steamer Gijon, which likewise foundered immediately after the collision. According to the narrative of one of the crew of the Laxham, the vessel carried twenty hands. There were also on board two passengers and the captain's wife and child. Both vessels must have sunk within twenty minutes after the collision. The Gijon carried a crew of 78, and had 113 passengers, and, so far as it could be ascertained, only three of her boats were lowered. The survivors fear that most of those on board must have gone down with her. The survivors pulled about some time, but failed to pick up anybody, and then proceeded in company. They soon, however, lost sight of each other in the dense fog, and the gig, after pulling all night through a heavy sea, was fallen in with early on the following morning by the Ville de Valence. The latest estimate places the num- ber lost at over 100.

DISAPPOINTED LOVE AND SUICIDE.—The West Kent coroner, on Monday, held an inquest, at Ladywell, on the body of John Avery, aged 23, a gentleman residing at Blythe-vale, Catford.—Al fred Avery, a student, said the de- ceased had been depressed in spirits through his having broken off his engagement with his young lady about three weeks ago. He had no other troubles with the exception of his mother's illness, which had also affected him, his nature being very sensitive to trouble. Witness last saw him alive on Friday night, when after kissing his mother, he went out. The letter produced, dated July 19th, was in the de- ceased's handwriting. It was as follows:—" Dear Thomas and Fred. and Kate,—l know you will blame me for doing this bloody deed, but then you don't know what trouble is until it comes upon you. It is all very well for one to say that lam a fool for doing this. Only wait till trouble visits him, and he will see. I leave you, Fred., my watch and chain, and I trust you will not break the sad news to mother until compelled to. Take my advice, and never have any- thing to do with girls, or else you will lay yourself open to have four heart broken, like mine, Fred. I hope that you, Tom, and Kate will forgive me for what I have done, and that mother will recover. I shall die in peace, but it's hard lines.—Your loving brother, JACK"—Thomas Avery, resid- ing with his mother and brothers, stated that he went out into the fields to look for his brother, who remained out all Friday night. A dog found the body in a field near the house. His brother was lying on his back, quite dead, with his left hand, in which was a revolver, across his breast.— The jury returned a verdict "That the deceased departed this life by shooting himself in the mouth, at the same time labouring under temporary mental, derangement."

' The European Conference on Egyptian finance met on Thursday at the Foreign Office, all the representatives of the Powers being present. The Rev. Mark Pattison, 8.D., rector of Lincoln College. Oxford, died at Harrogate on Wednesday. The deceased, who was in his 7lst year, was well known in literary circles.

Anurrcrtorr.—At the Liverpool Assizes, on Wednesday, Thomas Reed, a bricklayer, was found guilty of abducting a girl of sixteen from her parents' house at Bootle. The prisoner, falsely representing himself as unmarried, per- suaded the girl to leave her home and they afterwards lived together in Liverpool and Manchester. A sentence of two years' imprisonment was imposed, THE CLERICAL IMPOSTER.—John Lindsay, the person who under numerous aliases succeeded recently in deceiving a number of clergymen and in passing himself off as having taken holy orders, was tried on Wednesday at the Leeds Assizes before Mr. Justice Mathew. The prisoner's ex-

periences have been already fully detailed in our columns. He was now indicted for having falsely pretended to be in orders, and for solemnising matrimony on several occasions. The jury fouhd him guilty, and a sentence of 14 years' penal servitude was pasvd. BREACH OF PROMISE Can.—At the Staffordshire Assizes on Thursday, before Baron Pollock, Eli Bowers, a farmer's son, was sued for breach of promise by Annie Blakeman, daughter of a farmer at Stone. The parties had been ac- quainted from childhood, and defendant obtainod permission of the plaintiff's father to marry her. Subsequently ha underwent an operation in the hospital, and now pleaded physical incapacity. The defendant recently obtained a life interest in £60,000 from his uncle, and had other - petty. The jury found a verdict for plaintiff, with dar £2,000.

MWESLEYAN CONFERENCE.—The Wesleyan Conference did not meet on Thursday morning in consequence of the or- dination services which were held at Charles-street Chapel, Hanley, and at Brunswick Chapel, Macclesfield. The admis- sion was by ticktet, and both places of worship were filled to overflowing. Thirty-nine junior ministers were ordained, the president and leading conference officials taking part in the services. At Hanley the ex-president delivered the or- dination charge, and at Macclesfield the Rev. Dr. Pope. THE BOOTLE MURDER—At Live pool Assizes on Thurs- day Petty Cassidy, tinman, 54, was indicted for murdering his wife Mary, at Bootle. The woman had been away for more than a week, and when she returned Cassidy told her to clean the place oat. She went upstairs, and the people lodging in the house heard a fall. It was then discovered that the prisoner bad attacked his wife with a butcher's cleaver, and inflicted terrible wounds on the head, which caused death. The prisoner was found guilty and sentenced to death.

SHOCKING CHARGE AGAINST A CLERGYMAN AT BORN- ' LEY.—At the Burnley Police Court, ,on Thursday, the Rev James Laing, a clergyman of the Church of England, was placed in the dock on a charge of indecently assaulting two little girls, five years of age, who live with their parents at , Rosegrove. The prisoner, who' is at present curate of a church at Thornton-in-Craven, formerly held a curacy in Salford and another in Ancoats. About three month ago, being then out of a situation, he went to live at Rosegrove, and a month ago was appointed to the curacy be at present dsolds, but continued to live at Rosegrove. Evidence was given in support of the charge, and the prisoner, who reserved his defence, was committed for trial. THE CASE OF BOLTON V._O'I3RIEN —This case was con-

tinned before Lord Justice Barry at Belfast, on Wednesday. Further evidence for the defence having been given, the plaintiff was put into the box. He stated that since 1852 he had been in the service of the Crown in Ireland. When he met Mrs. Bolton he was worth £3,000 a year, and enjoyed a good social position. He was worth £20,000 in State securities, and other extensive property, and it was arranged that £52,000, or two-thirds, should be put in settlement. It was not true that he had broken up.a tin box and stolen the securities. In cross-examination, the plaiwiff said he was 66, and his wife 20 years older. He knew that as husband he had a first life interest in her estate, or he would not have married her. The daughter of the plaintiff gave evidence, and counsel then addressed the jury for the defendant —The case was not concluded when the court rose —On Thursday afternoon, the jury, after nearly three hours' deliberation, returned a verdict for the plaintiff, and on the first issue awarded £3,000 damages, and on the second £5O. SALE By ALErION OF WOMBWELL'S MENAGERIE —OR Tuesday the whole of the live stock of Wombwell's Menagerie was offered for sale by public auction in Lon- don. This menagerie was founded by the late Mr. George Wombwell in the year 1805, and has been successfully managed and owned for the:last 50 years by his niece, Mrs. Edmonds, who is now retiring from business. Mr. George Nichols, of Bristol, acted as auctioneer, and there were many circus and menagerie proprietors present, each of whom bid freely for the animals as they were offered for sale. The male African elephant "Emperor," a splendid specimen, 18 years of age and standing eleven feet high, was sold for 100 guineas to Mr. George Sanger, who was the principal purchaser. A cage of performing lvons was sold for £370. The famous lion " Wallace " was purchased for £200; and a cage of performing leopards, four in number, fetched £210; and a sum of £l2O was paid by Mr. Bostock for a very fine Bengal tigress. A case of boa constrictors was knocked down for £2l. Altogether, the sales amounted to over £3,C00.

div.head: TEE MANCHESTER SIIIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: TEE MANCHESTER SIIIP CANAL BILL.

The Select Committee on this Bill sat on Monday for the 16th time, Mr. Sclater-Booth presiding. The case for the Mersey Dock and Harbour Board, which has occupied the attention of the Committee for six days, was again procee- ded with.—Rear-Admiral Grant, C. 8., stated that the navi- gation of the channel in the estuary would be dangerous, and that he did not see how the loose walls could withstand the rush of water.—Mr. Barry was of opinion that the walls, whether high or low, would, however, lead to the silting up of the lower estuary, because they would put an end to the eroding process which now kept open the bar. Mr. T. H. Jackson, the chairman of the Liverpool Steamship Owners' Association, said that the view of that body was that it was far better to leave the bar to the operaion of natural causes than to maintain it by any process of dredging or improve- ment works —Mr. Hornby, chairman of the Dock Board, re- sented the imputation that the Board had been guilty of dis- graceful neglect.—Mr. Bidder, in summing up for the Dock Board, said if the execution of these works were succeeded ' by a reduction of the tidal capacity of the upper estuary, all the injurious consequences apprehended would follow. —The learned counsel had not finished his address when the Committee adjourned. On Tuesday, Mr. Bidder' Q.O , resuming his address on behalf of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board against the Bill, said there had always been a tendency to silt up in the upper estuary of the Mersey, and the tendency would here- after be increased if the proposed works were constructed.— Mr. Crimes at this point asked to he allowed to intervene to read a letter which the promoters received from the agents to the Mersey Conservators late on Saturday night. The letter was as follows :—" Manchester Ship Canal. Dear Sirs,—We have been requested by our clients, the Mersey Commissioners, to send you the following amendment, which they require to be inserted after the word dock,' line 15 of page 41 of the Bill, namely :—' Or if accretion resulting from the works cause injury to the navigation.' We will thank you to send us an undertaking that these words shall be inserted in Committee in the event of the preamble being Droved.— Yours faithfully, WYATT, Flosecexs, and Mr Bidder: I am waiting to hear whether the promoters assented to the insertion of these words.—Mr Crisp: We are prepared to assent to them, and we have given the under- taking for which the Conservators ask.—Mr Bidder, con- tinuing, said that even if the Committee inserted a clause ordering the absolute demolition of the works in case they proved to be injurious to the estuary, that could not be done except at a large expenditure of money, as much, at least, as the works themselves would cost—£l,soo,ooo or £2,ooo,ooo—there would be no security thatsuch demolition would be carrieel out.—Mr Dugdale, Q.C., said he had only onewitness to call onbehalf of the Shropshire Union Railway and Canal Company, and he would then address a few ob- servations to the Committee in support of his case.—Mr George Robert Jebb, the engineer to the Shropshire Union Railway and Canal Company, was examined as to the re- sults which the opponents of the Bill allege will follow the works, especially as far as Ellesmere Port was concerned.— Mr Dugdele, in his address to the Committee, said if the Bill were passed his clients would be left entirely at the mercy of the promoters, as it was doubtful whether the proposed subsidiary channel to Ellesmere Port would be satisfactory. Ile therefore hoped, in case the Bill were Passed, that the promoters would be placed under an obliga- tion to maintain a satisfactory channel to Ellesmere Port.— Mr Aspinall informed the Committee that Sir W Forwood would be the only witness on behalf of the Liverpool Cor- poration, end he might call one witness from the Birkenhead Corporation, and one from Miss Watt.—Mr Pope added that the railway case would conclude the opposition. On Wednesday the opposition evidence of the Liverpool Corporation was continued. Sir W. Forwood made an offer that if the promoters would be content this year with their canal down to Runcorn, and would next year produce a scheme for carrying the low water channel along either the north or south bank of the estuary, no opposition would be ' offered by Liverpool. He "solemnly protested " against the scheme as at present putforward, apprehending, as he did, deadly injury to the navigation. The Committee inti- mated that they did not now think it necessary to call Ad- miral Spratt, the acting conservator, whose evidence had previously been considered desirable. The case for the Lon- don and North-Western Railway, the last of the petitioners, was opened, Mr. Findlay, general manager, being ex- amined. On Thursday the Chairman said the Committee recog- nised the importance of the North-Western objections to the commercial case, but at the same time they must not forest that the great issue before them was the engineering quo. tion. They trusted therefore that the commercial part of the case would not be protracted.—Mr. Pope promised not to enter upon the commercial question at any lengtb.—The examination of Mr. Findlay, general manager of the North- Western Railway was resumed. Examining Mr. Adameen's estimates of the quantities of coal, alkali, and salt which would pass over the canal, be said they were excessive. He did not see the slightest reason to expect as a result of the canal, anything but a local trade at Manchester.

VOLUNTEER SUPPER AT WARRINGTON.

On Monday evening the committee and members of the 9th L.R.V. Wimbledon Subscription Club held their first annual supper at the Pelican Vaults. The chair was Occu- pied by Colour-serg(ant Daniels, and amongst those present were Colour-sergeants Daniels, T. Watmough and Hewitt; Sergeants Cliffe, Potter, Wood, G. Watmough and Painter; Corporals Ince, Kidd, Hampson, and Heaton; Privates J. Ince, Griffiths, Bennett, Yardley, and Pioneer Moores, dm. After supper was concluded, the Clienteles proposed the "Health of the Queen," and of the "Prince and Princess of \Vales and the rest of the Royal Family," which sentiments were honoured in a most loyal manner—Sergeant T. Weir- MOUGH Proposed the health of Lieut.-Colonel Greenall and officers of the 9th L.R.V, which was duly honoured —The Cwsineres gave "Prosperity to the Wimbledon Subscription Club," and coupled with the toast the names of three of the members of the club who had greatly distinguished them- selves at Wimbledon during the late prize meeting, viz., Sergeant G. Watmough, Pioneer Moores, and Sergeant Dolan (Newton Company). He thought it very creditable that out of ten members sent from the 9th L.R.V such a good proportion obtained prizes. Sergeant U. Watmough and Pioneer Moores had competed amongst 2,500 other volunteers, and both obtained positions in the first 560 in the Queen's prize, thereby bringing home money prizes. And Sergeant Dolan had been successful in three competi- -1 times. viz, the Alexandra, the Alfred, and the Windmill prizes. He felt that after finding such markmanehip dis- played, they need not despair of some day bringing the Queen's prize to Warrington. (Applause.)—Pioneer MOORES- responded in a neat manner on behalf of the three successful competitors—Sergeant POTTER proposed the health of the treasurer, Mr. J. Allen, wire, in responding, said he was greatly pleased to know that the club had turned out so successfully.—The CHAIRMAN then stated he had a most pleasing duty to perform, which was to present to their esteemed Secretary (Corporal Kidd) a silver pencil case, as a slight recognition of the trouble and labour he had gone through on their behalf during the past twelve months. A more energetic secretary he thought it would be impos- sible to find. Upon the pencil case was engraved the fol- lowing inscription :—" Presented to Corporal Kidd. for ser- vices rendered as secretary of Wimbledon Club, 9th L.R.V.. Warrington, 1884."—In acceping the present, Cor- poral KIDD said it would give him great pleasure to con- tinue to act as their secretary; for he found that the other officers of the committee rendered such valuable assistance that there was, comparatively speaking, no labour arising from the office. Corporal Kidd proposed the health-of the Trustees, Sergeants Potter, Wood, and Mr. John Allen, together with the remainder of the committee.—Sergeant POTTER suitably responded.—The CHAIRMAN stated that it was their intention to hold the first meeting for 1885 on Monday next, at the Drill Hall, and he hoped to see a good number prepared to join the club again —The health of the Chairman was proposed and drunk with musical honours The healths of Corporal Kidd and the Staff of the 9th L.R.V. were also drunk, and votes of thanks to the Chair- man and hest brought the proceedings to a close.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

BOWLING Cum.—On Tuesday afternoon the return match with Leyland was played on the Golborne ground. Taking both matches together the visitors proved victorious by 19 points. At the conclusion of the game au adjournment was made to the Legh Arms Hotel, where a sumptuous repast was enjoyed. Toasts and songs followed, and a pleasant evening was spent. THE Gottroarix MINERS.—A disagreement having ariseta between the manager of Messrs. Richard Evans and Com- pany's colliery, Golborne, and the check-weightnan, whose duty it is to protect the interests of the men, the firm last week decided to stop the check-weighman from resu Aug his customary duties. This action created considerable dis- satisfaction amongst the men, who ultimately appointed a new check-weighman. As showing the eonfidence the men had in their late check-weighman they have voted him £8 out of the check-weighman's fund towards paying his ex- penses to America, he having expressed a desire to go there rather than contend with the difficulty of obtaining another public situation.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

STONE THROWING AT HAYDOCK.—ii the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, Francis Hughes, John Marsh, and Robert Hazlehurst, (lads), pleaded guilty be throwing stones on the highway at Haydock on the 13th ult.—Superinten- dent Weir remarked that there had been many complaints about the stone-throwing nuisance at flaydock. Indeed, he could hardly describe it; it looked more like a yard where there had been a lot of houses pulled down owing to the quantity of brickbats and stones —The Bench imposed a tine of 2s 6d and costs on each defendant, and stated that they would have to pat a stop to stoue•throwing, which was becoming a regular nuisance.

• HAYDOCE WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE SOCIETY.—The an- nual demonstration and gala in connection with the Hay. dock Wesleyan Band of Hope Society was fixed for Satur- day last, but the incessant heavy downpour of rain in the afternoon considerably marred and interrupted the proceed- ings. It had been arranged that the members and friends of the society should gather at the school, march through the village in processional order, headed by the Havdock brass band, and afterwards indulge in various sports and amusements in a field near the Heyes, which bad been kindly lent by Mrs. Evans, but this part of the programme had to be abandoned on account of the wet weather. It is needless to add that much disappointment was expressed by the juveniles at the loss of their afternoon's enjoyment. Nei- withstanding the unfavourable weather, however, about 300 persons gathered at the school-room, and there the proceed- ings were made as pleasant and enjoyable as they could be under the circumstances. Mr. Jacob Billings presided, and brief addresses were given by one or two friends. There le some talk of the demonstration and gala being held on a future day, when the weather, it is to be hoped, will be more favourable.

div.head: LOCAL BOARD MEETING.
div.p: LOCAL BOARD MEETING.

The monthly meeting of the Haydock Local Board was held at the Local Board Offices on Monday afternoon, when there were present Messrs. Charles Pilkington J.P., (in the chair), Thomas Jackson, W Alker, W Bal harry, and Thomas Turnbull (clerk.) The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed.
Acoontrrs.—Accounts amounting to £165 14 lid were examined and passed for payment._

• - WATER SUPPLY TO THE GIB COTTAGES.—The CHAIR- MAN remarked that with reference to the resolution of the Board that they should supply water to the Gib cottages through one-inch pipes, it would require a long length of piping and would be some expense. Messrs. Richard Evans and Company were putting down pipes as far as the boilers on the line, and it was thought that if a stand-pipe was erected the people residing at the Gib cottages could fetch their own water from the stand-pipe. It would save a lot of piping, and the Local Board would be paid for the water passing through Messrs. Evan's meter. Messrs. Evans would afterwards make arrangements with the people of the Gib cottages themselves.—Mr BALHARRY : Have you re- plied to the Newton Commissioners P—Mr TURNBULL : have told them that we decided to give them a supply of water.—The CaAramAN remarked that his suggestion seemed to be the cheapest way of doing it, So that the Local Board would have nothing to do in the matter.—The CLERK observed that if the suggestion was carried out the former proposition would want rescinding.—Mr THOMAS JACKSON did not see why the township should not supply the water to the Gib cottages if the people were willing to pay for it. It would be a long way for them to carry their water in winter if the Chairman's suggestion was adopted.—Mr BALITARRY asked if the Newton Commissioners would be satisfied with the people carrying the water such a distance.—Mr JACK- SON: I don't know. They wrote to ask if we would supply water to the cottages and we consented.—The CHAIRMAN remarked that if the Board did that it would cost between .£4O and £5O, and he thought as it was solely for the benefit of the Newton township, the Newton Commissioners ought to pay the whole of the expense of petting the pipes down. —Mr JACKSON moved that the water question in relation to the Gib cottages be left over until the next meetirg, and that the Clerk write to the Commissioners to see if they would bear any portion of the cost of laying down the pipes. —Mr BALHARRY seconded the motion which was passed. THE Foon AND DRUGS ACT.—Oa the motion of Mr JACKSON, seconded by Mr BALHARRY, the Nuisance Inspec- tor was empowered to take samples of any article fur ana!y. sic under the Food and Drugs Act. A SUBSIDENCE.—[he SURVEYOR reported upon a subs- dance in the road near Mrs Cawley's farm, and on the m.- tion of Mr JACKSON, seconded by Mr BALHARRY, the Sur- veyor was ordered to examine and repair the subsidence in the road.—This was the only business of interest.

A meeting of the leading Conserva- tives was held in London on Thursday, the Marquis of Salisbury presiding. The proceedings were private. Mns. WELDON'S ACTION.—IO the Appeal Court, on Thursday, Dr. Forbes Winslow's appeal against the decision of the Divisional Court, granting a new trial of the action brcught by Mrs. Weldon against him for libel was finally dismissed, their lordships deciding not to call upon Mrs. Weldon for a reply on the legal question raised as to her power to carry on litigation under the Married Women's Property Act apart from her husband. STATE OF THE COTTON TRADE. The Primrose Mill at Clitheroe, containing 17,000 spindles, which has been run for a great many years by Messrs. Mercer and Hodgson, has ceased operations. The spinning depart- ment at the Holmes Mill, comprising 16,000 spindles, and belonging to the same firm, will also be stopped this week, and about 160 hands will be thrown out of employment. The stoppages are caused by the desire of the firm to retire from business. Biliousness. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, AUGUST 2, 18S4.

THE Reform Demonstration in Manchester, on Saturday, was worthy of the city and worthy of the occasion. The people were not to be damped even by an incessant down- pour of rain, and the result was that the Palace at Pomona was crowded to its utmost capacity by an audience of 15,000 persons, whilst other 15,000 attended the overflow meetings in the Agricultural Hall. Steam is up, and the engine needs only to be well directed to ensure that the great and pre- cious cargo shall be carried swiftly and safely to the journey's end. It is an augury of success that the Demonstration was held in the same place, with many of the same speakers, and with the same or heightened

enthusiasm as that which characterised the memorable gathering of 1879, which did so much in bracing Lancashire Liberals for the conflict which terminated in the Tories being hurled from power in 1880. Lord HARTING- ToN made a powerful speech, and his strength as usual lay in the justice and moderation of his statements. The enthusiastic reception which was accorded to his reference to the unconstitutional action of the House of Lords in seeking, as "The Tory Caucus," Ito force a dissolution to serve party purposes was an indication of the high pitch of feeling against the Upper House—an indication which was confirmed by the adoption, later on, of a resolution in favour of abolishing the s ilegislative veto of the Peers. Lord HAR- TINGToN, as a member of the Government, 1, would seem to be afraid of a diversion in the direction of demanding a reform of the House of Lords at the hands of the present Parliament. He looks back to the pledges given and to the work which has yet to be done, and thinks it as much as can be expected if the Government manage to pass the Franchise Bill, and overtake other im- portant arrears. He is unquestionably right in urging that it would be unwise to atternPr, to deal with the Constitution of the House 01 Lords until the Reform Bill proper has become the law of the land ; but on the other hand he underrates the strength and the determination of the nation if he sup- poses that it is not equal to the task o' agitating at one and the same time for the re- form of the Upper as of the Lower House' Granted that the duty that lies nearest to us is getting the Franchise Bill passed, it would be accomplished at too great a sacrifice if were attained by the deliberate withdrawaL of all agitation against the House of Lords. I There is room for and there is need of both agitations. It may be that the feelinz acrainsl the Lords is an unexpected by-product, but it is a by-product which we are under obligation to utilise, and which is likly to become as I valuable as the original material. With the Liberals everywhere demanding, and the Tories everywhere professing to approve an extension of the Franchise, it goes WithOUt saying that that reform cannot be long delayed. The tug of war will finally come on the question of the revision of the constitu- tion of the House of Lords, unless, as is much to be feared, their lordships surrender during the autumn session. In that case 3 too-indulgent people may give them another lease of life, though the signs of the times suggest that the ruthless hand of Fate is upon, them. "Though the mills of God grin' slowly, yet they grind exceeding small." The, eeers are now in the mill, and If they are no‘ on this occasion ground as they have so often ground others, we cannot but say, whatever Lord HARTINGToti may think; that a golden opportunity has been neglected. So far as the leaders of the Tory party are concerned, it is obvious that they mean 01, fight. This is a matter of course with Lot° the SALISBURY. When he is on the scene sound of battle hurtles in the air ;" but It would seem, too, that Sir STAFFORD NoRTS" COTE has buckled on his armour for the fray. He is quite touched with the expres- sions of opinion from Tory clubs which ate pouring in upon him—expressions which, 01 the words of Lord SALISBURY, may be taken as "produced to order," seeing that they are the outcome, in this district as elsewhere, 01 the circular issued the other day by th "Conservative central office at Westminster. He knows all about it of course, and prac- tically admitted his knowledge of the situa" tion when, speaking to the Tory delegates at the London Conference on Monday, he said—" Don't fall into the error of sitting still; go out and fight the battle." There, that is something like an "order ;" no skulk" ing behind billiard tables when defiant reso- lutions are being passed—" go out and fight the battle." It will be interesting to note the response in this part of the country t° this trumpet call. Men who are nol to a " SALISBURY " in stating a case may manage to put a good face on it whilst trying to show that the Lords have thrown out the Reform Bill because of their love of Reform; but, if we are not wholly in error, it will be found that even Toryism in the North is is too honest to attempt to make much of such a sham. They would Seem to be less particular in the South, for they did not check Lord SALISBURY when he again sought to make it appear that Mr. BRIGIiT was the advocate of the rejection of any Fran- chise Bill which did not include Redistribu- tion, notwithstanding the fact that Mr• BRIGHT had within forty-eight hours shown that he was quoted by Lord RUSSELL as an authority for doing what the present Govern- ment are doing—dealing separately with these separate questions—and that he gave the same advice to Mr. DISRAELI in 1867 r when Lord SALISBURY and he were memberS of the same Government. It must have been a bitter pill for his lordship to be reminded that Mr. DISRAELI had been in consultation with Mr. BRIGHT as to the Reform Bill of this period—a bill which finally so roused the ire of Lord SALISBURY, because of the wide extension that it gave to the borough fon" chise, that he left the Government and de- nounced Mr. DISRAELI as "a political ad" venture." And yet he would have people believe that he has undergone some sort of conversion 'on the franchise question, whilst offering as proof Of it that but for him, and him alone as Tory leader in the House of Lords, the present Franchise Bill would by this have received, the royal assent ! Let him follow the bent of his craze, for it is indeed true that " Whom the gods would destroy they first make mad."

THE Miners of St. Helens and district I were to be applauded for the firmness they displayed in resisting in the first instance the proposal of the employers to reduce wages by x o per cent. ; but when they were outvoted in the Conference at Wigan they were setting themselves a task beyond their powers in re- solving to fight the battle single-handed. Looking at all the circumstances of the case, we could not perceive that they had any rea- , sonable chance of success in fighting as it were both their brethren and their employers, and hence the counsel we gave that they should accept the inevitable. There might have been something of the heroic in it, but still it would have been a sorry sight, if, aS Mr. CROSS suggested, they had let thenr selves be reduced to starvation point before giving in. Indeed such a course would have been fool-hardy in view of the confirmed decision of the Conference; and we are glad, therefore, to know that better counsels pre" 1 vailed on Monday, and that it was resolved to resume work. The immediate cause of this, favourable turn in events is the decision 01 the delegates of the Lancashire and Cheshire Miners' Federation, which met at Man- chester, on Monday, that it was best that the Miners throughout the entire district 0.1 West Lancashire should resume work. is much better than continuing in a hopeless struggle. The Miners should now set them- selves to the task of preparing for a conflict, if need be, for the return of the jo per cent When conditions are favourable to their win- ning the battle. To this end they should adopt the advice which the most far-sighted amongst their number have again and again tendered, and that is become members of the Union, so that they may always be pre- pared with the sinews of war. So long as the bulk of miners are non-unionists, so long Will they be subject to irregular conflicts on the wages question. It is to the interests alike of employers and employed that strikes Should be avoided, and it is a matter of com- mon observation that there are fewest strikes Where there are the strongest organisations. As a rule, it is the unionist who has to do the fieitinz, and it sometimes happens that he is victimized for his pains. Non-unionists ought really to feel ashamed that such things Should be, especially when it is in their power to protect themselves and their leaders by Proper organisation. The lesson they have just had is, we grant, a bitter one, but they will have themselves to blame if they do not Profit by it.

EGYPT is again to be the theme of debate in the House of Commons before Parliament rises, but, charmingly as Lord SALISBURY said matters were going on there—from the Opposition point of view—we do not see that the Tories are likely to do anything better With their opportunity than they have done in the past. Their chance all along has lain in mischance; but, although the most ter- rible things have been predicted as the cer- tain result of "the blundering of the present incapable Government," the seers have hitherto Droved like those we hear of in the land of the Pharoahs—so many " false prophets." General GORDON ought by this to have been hanged, or drowned, or shot and cut up into mincemeat; but he keeps living on, and holding his own, as if to spite the Tories. Accounts which come down to the middle of lune represent him as har. rassing the rebels. and threatening to des- stroy them on the rising of the Nile. The Nile is rising, and the latest rumour is that he has captured Berber. If this be so, it is obvious that he is in no need of an expedition to relieve him. But whether or not, it is certain that he is able to take care of himself, and that, if he thinks fit, he will soon be in a position to return to Cairo. Our OW n fear is that General GORDON will take an early opportunity of resuming offensive Operations, and, in this way, bring us trouble With the natives. He wants to " smash up the MARDI," and, if he gets a chance, will keep his word by striking a blow in that direction before finally leaving Khartoum. It is evident, at any r4te/ tlnt therf:i ,9 Pith Pressing need of an apedition to effect WI; rescue as the Opposition attempted to make PIA P, few weeks ago. If the Tories had had their way, we should, by this, have been in the thick of a useless undertaking, involving the loss of millions of money and hundreds, If not thousands. of lives. It is true it might in some degree have diverted the attention of the country from the Franchise Bill. The little game was well played, but it failed— utterly failed; and at the fag-end of the Session there is less likelihood than ever, we trust, of its proving successful.

The Manchester Ship Canal Bill has again Miscarried. •Last evening the Select Corn- 1 Mittee of the House of Commons decided that the premable of the Bill had not been proved, which is equivalent to its rejection. There is naturally a strong feeling of disap- pointment in Manchester, and similar feel- ing was shown last night in Warrington, Run- corn, and other places. The result is wholly unexpected, for after the Bill had passed the Lords' Committee it was taken as a matter of course that there would be little difficulty with the Commons. especially when it was remem- bered that on a previous occasion it was the committee of the Upper House that had been the stumbling-block in the way of its accept- ance. It would seem after all that the Lords in scme things can show- themselves liberal, Whilst conservatism reveals itself in the Com- mons. It has become an axiom that "It is the unexpected that happen," but when it happens in an affair of such magnitude it Comes as a staggering blow. With a . view to shorten the case, so that the Bill might be got through before Parliament rose, the promoters have refrained from laying full evidence before the Committee, and it will now be felt that the project has suffered in consequence. But what was to be done? To have prolonged the hearing and examina- tion of witnesses would inevitably have re- sulted in the Bill falling through for lack of time. The Bill had to wait on Parliament, not Parliament on the Bill. Mr. SCIATER- Boom, the Chairman of the Committee, in giving the decision, stated that Mr. PEMBER, Who appeared for the promoters, had lost nothing by forbearing to pursue the commer- cial side of the case ; and the inference is that the Committee have rejected the project because of the risk which they think it Would involve to the port of Liverpool. It can hardly be that there was any question , as to financial difficulties, after the guarantee to provide Ls,ooo' 000 before the work was commenced. If there was, it seems to us that there must have been a serious error of judg- ment. If people think fit to embark in such an undertaking in the belief that that it will ultimately prove a sound investment, we do not see how that can be a matter of moment to a House of Commons Committee It is hard for the promoters that, after two years' labour and enormous expense, they should have the cup which was being raised to their lips dashed ruthlessly to the ground. But the" Men of Manchester" are not easily beaten; and, if we are not mistaken, they will try again, having faith in the homely saying that "the third time pays for all."
