C.E,T S., WIDNES.—Tto weekly meeting of this society W 8 held at the National Schools on Thursday evening, when the Rev J Wright Williams, vicar, the Revs A P Hamilton Wilson, and C Ramat, curates. and Messrs Foley, Cane, Wilkinson, and Dodd offered up prayers entreating the blessing of God upon the work of the society. The Rev A P Hamilton Wilson also delivered a short address.

THE ALLEGED BURGLARIES AT WIDNES —At the Liver- pool ASSiZeg on Wednesday, Walter Bushell (28) and Peter Connolly (50), both labourers, were acquitted on an indict- ment charging them with having committed burglary, at Widnes, on the 13th inst. SCHOOL TREAT AT FARNWORTH.—The Scholars attending the Farnworth Parish Church Sunday Schools had their annual treat on Friday afternoon last week ; when about 500 children and teachers assembled in a field placed at their disposal by the Vicar, and spent a pleasant afternoon in a variety of ways. The Widnes Star of Temperance Brass Band was present. SWINE FEVER AT Rmecoas —On Monday, a pig be- longing to John Jones, of 16, Vine-street, Runcora, was certified by Mr, Hugh Ferguson, veterinary surgeon, of Warrington, to be suffering from swine fever, and the animal was destroyed. Inspector Atherton was the means of discovering this case, which makes the second which has occurred in the locality within a short time. RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANdE —From our advertising columns it will be seen that the members of this order will bold their annual demonstration to-morrow (Sunday), and on Monday. To-morrow the Rev W Vause will preach to the members in Bethesda chapel. On Monday the usual procession will take place on a greater scale than formerly, and if favoured with fine weather will be a success. • FATAL BATHING ACCIDENT.—TVIG boys, named Percy Lyle, aged 10, and Ernest Pethrill, 12, visiting Bude, were drowned on Thursday afternoon in attempting to swim across the harbour mouth. The Rev Mr Pethrill, of Man- chester, witnessed the death of his only sen. The other boy was the son of a London doctor. The deceased were warned by Buds school children not to venture into the stream. THE RUNCORN MANSLAUGHTER CASE —OR Wednesday, at the Chester Assizes, Michael . Murphy (48), master mariner, was indicted for having unlawfr lly and maliciously caused certain grievous bodily harm to William Stringer, at Runcorn, on the 17th May last, under circumstances already reported. The jury found the prisoner guilty, and the judge, in passing sentence of two months' imprisonment, said that be did not think there was any intention on the Part of the prisoner to injure Stringer in such a manner as he did. Rmeconar PARISH CHURCH TRIP —The annual trip in connection with Runcorn Parish Church took place on Monday, Blackpool, " the Brighton of the North," being again the favoured locality. About 450 persons travelled with the trip, which started from Runcorn about seven o'clock, and arrived at its destination shortly after ten; the Revs. R. Edwards and T. Edwards, Messrs. W. Whittaker, P. Briscoe, and Crosby were among the excursionists. Arrangements had been made by which those accompany- ing the excursion were admitted into the Winter Gardens, Haikes Hall, the Aquarium, and Pier at reduced rates, and despite a few hours rain in the afternoon a thoroughly en- joyable day was spent, the return journey being safely ac- complished in good time. A RELIGIOUS MANIAC AT WIDNES.—Mary Davies, wife of a workman at Messrs. Gossage and Sons works, Widnes, and living in Oahland-street, was on Wednesday conveyed to Rainhill Asylum on the authority of air. E. Gibbon, JP., suffering from religious mania. It appears that lately the woman, who is repeatable and of middle age, has been at- tending Evangelistic meetings held in connection with the I Welsh Calvanistic Methodists in Widnes. Since that Hine 1 she has been in a depressed state of mind, and expressed deep despair at the fact that her sins were not forgiven. She has also declared that she was sinking into hell and other- wise acteti strangely. Dr. Cooper certified as to the woman's I condition. and Mr. Scannell obtained the necessary order for I I

her removal to the asylum. RUNCORN Y.M.C.A. Prextc.—The annual picnic in con• nection with the Runcorn Young Men's Christian Associa- tion took place on Saturday. For several years past Weaverham Wood has been the destination of the members, bat on this occasion Hatchmere on the borders of Delamere Forest, had been chosen for the afternoon's pleasure, and about two o'clock, the party numbering about 20 person., started from High-street in a large waggonette belonging to Mr. Peck. Unfortunately, the atmospheric conditions were very unfavourable, rain descending in a steady downpour durirg most of the afternoon, but the party nevertheless I continued to extract amusement and pleasure from tbeir sur- roundinge. At half-past four tea, provided by Mr. W. Shri YoS orteftig, of in a farm house, and the weather shortly aftereraftil bflailialink the wonders of the forest ' were to some extent explf'tedt rr-lurn journey was safely accomplished by nine o'clock. RUNCORN NATIONAL Scnoon.—The annual Setneali tfl aid of these schools were preached in the Parish Church oa Sunday by the Rev. Thomas Edwards, rector of Llaptibangel- y-Pennant. The musical part of the service both morning and evening had been specially arranged. In the afternoon a children's flower service was held, and there was a large attendance. Most of those present gave bouquets of flowers at the conclusion of the service. The sermon was preached by the Rev. T. M. Armson. In the evening a flower service was again held, the members of the congregation to a great extent bearing offerings of flowers in their hands. The Rev. Thomas Edwards preached from the words "Bring them up in the nature and admonition," delivering a discourse on the training and education of the young. At the close of the service the congregation laid the offerings of flowers within the communion rails, and they were on Monday distributed amongst the sick homes in Runcorn. and forwarded to the hospitals of Widnes, Liverpool. and Chester. The collections for the day amounted to AN 12s sd. LIVERPOOL Assns.—The following gentleinen were among those who served on the grand jury at the Liverpool Assizes this week, viz :—Mr John Dun, Warrington •, Mr A McCorquodale, Newton-le-Willows, Mr Thomas Pilking- ton, Prescot ; and Mr HRD Willie, Prescot. Mr Justice Day, in charging the Grand Jury, on Monday, expressed a hope that no inconvenience had resulted from the postpone- ment of business which had been rendered necessary by the pressuee of work at Manchester. His Lordship added that he was one of a number of judges who had resolved to clear off the business of each circuit before proceeding to the next assize centre, so that suitors should not be dis- appointed and distressed. Mr. Justice Day waa induced to remark that nowhere but in Lancashire were there so many cases of cutting and wounding and using knives, but he considered that many of those assaults were committed by strangers in the county.—James Mitchell, labourer, pleaded guilty to having feloniously entered the house of John Bond, at Southport, on May 20th, and stolen six cigars and other articles. He was sentenced to six months' impri- sonment.

SUDDEN DEATH OE A RUNCORN MAN: PAINFUL AFFAIR —A man named Joseph Brown, who has for the last ten years been employed at the Co-operitive Stores, Sankey- streec, Warrington, has died suddenly node very painful circumstances. It appears that the deceased, who was married, lived in lodgings at 3. Golborne•street, his wife re- siding with an aged uncle at Runcorn, where Brown is well known and respected. It was his habit to go home to Runcorn on Saturday evenings, bat he had recently decide to live at a house of his own, situate in wakefield-street. Early on Friday morning he went to this house, which was empty, on some business connected with the papering and painting of the place. He did not make his appearance at the usual time at business, and he was accordingly sent for. At his lodgings, however, nothing was known of his whereabouts, and as he failed to appear all the morning, it was supposed that he had gone home to Runcorn. It was not till seven o'clock in the evening that he was found, and then he was discovered lying on the floor of the empty house above- mentioned, in a state of unconsciousness. Dr. Joseph was immediately sent for, and attended to the deceased, who, it was discovered, was suffering from an apoplectic lit. It was conjectured that he must have been in a fit many hours, and though alive when found, the doctor said had he re- mained undiscovered two hours longer he would have been dead. Notwithstanding the medical attendance, however, there appeared to be no hopes of his recovery, and he ex- pired at twelve o'clock the same night. This was not the first time the deceased had suffered from apoplexy. Just before his ntarriage he had a similar fit, though in other res- pects hie health was fairly good. The doctor's certificate is to the effect that the deceased died from apoplexy, and hence no inquest was necessary. It had been intended to bury the deceased in Warrington; but ultimately Mrs. Brown decided that the funeral should take place at Run- corn. Accordingly the remains were conveyed to Runcorn, where they were interred. The deceased leaves no chil- dren. He was 51 years of age and had been married about eight years. FLOWER SERVICE AT BETHESDA CHAPEL, BUIVCORN.— On Sunday evening the annual flower service was held at Bethesda Congregational Chapel. The sacred edifice had been charmingly decorated for the occasion, and the floral adornments, whilst pleasing to the eye, filled the air with a rich fragrance. On a raised platform near the pulpit plants were gracefully disposed, and the front of the gallery was also adorned with flowers and shrubs. Depending from the pulpit were baskets filled with bright flowers, and a handsome bouquet occupied each gas globe. The commu- nion appeared one mass of bright blooming plants and foli- age. The Rev J D and Mrs Thomas had had charge of the decorations, and they had received assistance from Mrs T Handley, Mrs J D Jones, Miss Rhodes, Miss Ainscow, Miss Amelia Chadwick, Miss Annie Chadwick, Miss Maggie Beck, Miss Littler, Mr F Fairhurst, Mr John Chadwick, Mr Harold Chadwick, Mr J David Jones, .irc. Plants were lent by Mr P Speakman, Mr Thomas Booth, Mr Thomas Andrews, Mr W H Chadwick, Mr F Fairhurst, and Mrs Rhodes. Mr C Wigg, 0 Halton Lodge, gave a quantity of flowers. There was a large congregation, and hymns ap- propriate to the occasion were rendered. The Rev J D Thames preached from Isaiah xxxv, 1 2; and in the course of his sermon the rev gentleman compared the state of Christendom to a beautiful garden which had been invaded by swine and other animals. The enemies that had made the invasion were four :—Love of strong drink, the greed of filthy lucre, the animal passions, and unbelief. Haying alluded to the extent and character of the transformation, the speaker said that in this connection he wished to call atten- tion to a lesson taught by the flowers. When they entered a garden and were struck with the beauty of the place, they did not suppose that it was the full blown scarlet rose that contributed all the beauty. Nay, the lesser flowers although they were not so striking, all had something to do with the pleasant impression. It might be that if one were taken away it would not be missed, but still each flower was a contribution to the beauty of the whole scene; and in like manner every Christian man, however lowly his positbn or humble his attainments, was a contributor to the beauty and grandeur of the scene which Christendom in its highest phases presented. As long as they were alive and endea- voured to walk near to Christ they helped to create an im- pression favourable to Christianity. At the close of the service the flowers brought by the congregation were col- lected. and on Monday were sent to the homes were there were sickness in Runcorn.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, AUGUST 2. 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, AUGUST 2. 1884.

TRESPASSERS AT WIDNXS.-/k.t Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr E Gibbon, John 1 Walsh arid John Hockleton, young men, were summoned for having on the Ch July wilfully damaged the grass on a field belong- ing to Mr William Longton, of Appleton.—P.C. Almond proved that the defendants trespassed upon the ground, which Mr Longton said was sown with oats and grass. He had fixed a fence and notice boards, but people would persist in trespassing upon the land.—Luke Burns was summoned for trespassing upon the land on the nod June. P.C. Almond proved the case.—Each defendant was fined 81 and costs 7s Al. THE EXTRAORDINARY ASSAULT IN RUNCORN CEMETRY FIELDS.-At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday Robert Moores appeared to answer an adjourned summons charging him with assaulting John Dimelow, of 0. Union-street, on the sth July. The circumstances of the assault have been reported in the Examiner, and evidence of identification having been given to the satisfaction of the. Bench, Mr. Bankes characterised the assault as of a most gross and brutal character, and altogether unwirrantable. Simply because the complainant had prevented him from committing a most disgraceful act he must grossly assault him. As the defend- ant had been 19 times previously convicted, he was sen- tenced to a month's hard labour without the option of a

fine. A DESERTER FROM WARRINGTON BARRAcKs.—At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, Joseph Moran, a private in the 2nd Battalion of the 82nd Regiment of Foot, stationed at Warrington, was charged with being a deserter.—P.C. Cum- mings stated that at a quarter past seven on Sunday night he met the prisoner in Waterloo.road, Widnes, and asked him if he was on leave. The prisoner replied in the affirma- tive, and proceeded to feel in his pockets as though in search of his pass. Being unable to find the requisite document be said he must have mislaid it. Inquiries had been made at the Warrington depot, the commanding officer of which wrote to the effect that the prisoner was absent without leave.—The prisoner was accordingly remanded to Walton gaol to await an escort. POACHING AT ROCK SAVAGE—A young man named George Darlington was summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday charged with searching for game, and for hav- ing in his possession certain nets and pegs used for the pur- pose of taking game.—P.C. Finney said he was going down a footpath towards Rock Savage about half-past one on the morning of the 24th lust, when he met the defendant and five or six other men. They all ran away. The defendant was carrying a bag which he dropped in a field. Afterwards the defendant came back into the road, and the pegs and stone produced were found upon him. The net and bag produced were subsequen ly found by P.C. Egerton.—The Bench imposed the lenient nenalty of lOs and costs, as it was the defendant's first offence, and ordered the nets to be

destreyea. BOY DROWNED AT WESTiN.—An inquest was held yes- terday week, at the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, by Mr. T. J. Ridgway, coroner, touching the death of Jas. Mather, 12 years of ago, wno was drowned in the Old Basin, en Thursday morning. The deceased was last seen on board the tug Regulator about eleven o'clock. Shortly afterwards he was vnisse I, and his cap was seen floating in the dock. It was surmised that the boy had fallen into the water, and grappling irons were procured, and a search resulted in the finding of the bedy at the bottom of the dock.-The jury re- turned a verdict of "Found drowned." The deceased was interred at Runcorn Cemetery on Sunday afternoon. He had been for some years a scholar at the Newtown Missioe Sunday School, and about three weeks ago passed the sixth standard at the National Schools. The teachers of the Sun- day School and a number of scholars were present at the funeral, and the scene in the cemetery was very impres- sive. The funeral service was conducted by the Rev. J. J. Bryant. M.A , incumbent of the Church, Weston Point. The scholars at the close oang in a very striking manner the hymn commencing "When our heads are bow'd with woe," to the tune of Redhead. Trte FoRTHCOMING FRANCHISE DEHONSTRATION AT WIDNES.—The arrangements for this demonstration are fully completed, and provided the atmospheric conditions are favourable there will doubtless be an imposing muster both of the electors and non-electors. It is needless to say that the unenfranchised in Widnes far outnumber those who are within the pale of citizenship, and it has been estimated that had the Bill as introduced by Mr Gladstone passed the Lords, the electorate would have been increased by about 4,000 names. In this fact alone the speakers at to-day's demonstration will have a text by which they can rouse the enthusiasm of the assembly. The meeting will take place on the gronnd near the Market HalI; and the ktidience Will arrive In four de- tachmentel The first predession, headed :by the Star of Temperance Band, will leave the promenade West Bank at 2 p.m., and proceed through Mersey and Victoria roads to the place of meeting. Marshals in charge,MrW Whitley and Mr I Jackson. The second procession, headed by Ditton band,will leave Ditton at 2 p m , and proceed by Farnworth, and Peel- ! house-lane to the place of meeting. Marshals in charge, Mr. Warne and Mr. Gardiner. The third procession, headed by the Catholic Young Men's Bend, will leave Moss Bank at the same hour and proceed through Lugsdale and New- town, marshalled by Mr. P. Teflon and Mr. Heaney. The Irish National Foresters' Band will head the fourth proces- sion, which will start from Halton View, and proceed , through Mill Brow and Simms' Cross. Mr. J. W. Carlile ! and Mr. D. Wright will act as marshal% BALE WAILES...-Uale was quite festive eh Monday, when the annual wakes commenced, the eharming village having been to some extent taken possession of by owners of swing- ing boats, flying boxes, hobby horses, shooting galleries, and the thousand and one frivolities of a fair. The young Hodges and the Lancashire witches and other pleasure seekers enjoyed themselves in a hearty manner, additional bustle being lent to the festivities by the arrival of several school trips. About 300 children and teachers connected with St. Augustine's School, Shaw-street, Liverpool, entered the village about ten in the morning, accompanied by the curate, the Rev. J. W. Morton, and took up their quarters in a field near the Wellington Hotel, where dinner and tea was served. The choir and members of St. Athanasius Church, Kirkdale, Liverpool, in all about 120, also spent the day at Hale, and were privileged to enter Colonel Blackburne's park. In the morning the members of the Loyal Ireland Blackburne Lodge of Independent Order of Oddfellows (Hale district) celebrated the anniversary of their establish- ment by parading the lanes of the village attired in their regalia, and attended by the Roughdale Fire Clay Co.'s band. They concluded their peregrinations at the Parish Church, where the Rev. S. B. Steward, the vicar, preached an appropriate sermon to them. Dinner was afterwards partaken of in a tent erected en the grounds of the Cock and Trumpet, followed by a meeting. The loyal and patriotic and other toasts were given. The annual report showed that during the year £143 103 had been paid by the lodge to sick members. There was a balance in hand on the 11th Decem- ber of £3,260 10s Bcl.—The festivities of the afternoon were marred by heavy rains. THE El-FEMALE SEARCHER AT RUNCORN FlNED.—Be- fore Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. James Handley at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Sarah Withington, a married woman, ex-female searcher at the police station, was sum- moned to answer a charge of using obscene and profane language in St. John-street on the 19th inst. Defendant pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Wallace said about eleven o'clock on the night of the date mentioned he saw a crowd opposite the house of Richard Hedgecock in St. John-street. Amongst the crowd he saw the defendant, who had her sleeves rolled up, and she was challenging Hedgecock to fight. She used very abominable language and called Hedgecock foul names. She was very excited and in drink but not drunk.—The defendant stated that she always wore her sleeves stripped up as she could not bear them down to her wrists. She alleged that her sister and Hedgecock were fighting and that she had nothing to do with the disturbance The case was brought as a piece of spite. The constable bad not let her alone since Mr. Williamson died, and Mr. Wallace had told his landlady that he had it in for her. (Laughter.) She did not wish the young man any harm as he would not hurt a hair of his bead—(laughter)--but she could say , something if she would. She had always done her best, and she had been at the police station 14 years and was not in the habit of coming out with those kind of speeches. (Laughter.)—Defendant called John McLashlan, 18, St. John-street, who, however, stated that be did not see any- thing that occurred in the street, and Mrs. Ann Rogerson, sister to the defendant, admitted in reply to Superintendent Leah that the defendant came to take her part when Hedge- cock struck hen—The defendant acknowledged that this statement was correct, but denied using the language com- plained of, and appealed to Mr. Handley, who had known her 22 years.—The Bench had no doubt of the defendant's guilt, and fined her 10s and costs. POACHING AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. E. Gibbon at Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Robert Edwards and James Hoyle, young men, were brought up on a charge having on the 20th ult trespassed on land near Birch- field-road belonging to John Ingbam.—George Scott, gamekeeper to Mr. Sydney Young and Frederick ' Wilson, of Wavertree, said about eight o'clock on the Sun- day morning in question he was walking on his beat at,Birch- field-road when he saw the defendants about 40 yards ahead of him. They had a fully grown greyhound with them and also a pup similar to the one Edwards now held in his arms. Knowing that Edwards was an old offender, be (witness) jumped over the hedge and followed them. He saw Hoyle scale the fence and enter Ingham's field, followed by the greyhound, and Edwards followed. He saw the dog run into the beat as if in pursuit of game, and Boyle went in after it. When the men got back into the road he (witness) went up to them and charged them with running a hare. They said nothing, but afterwards Edwards asked him not to summon them.—Mr. Knowles, who appeared for the defend- ants, cross-examined the witness at great length to show that the greyhound did notbeleng to the defendants, and that the defendant Edwards was merely training a dog for another person.—Thomas Scott, son of last witness, corroborated.— Mr. Knowles pointed out that the gamekeeper had stated that the right of shooting had not been conveyed to his employers by deed, and contended that they could not pro- secute in that court unless they had a deed conveying or leasing to them the right of sporting.—Mr. Gibbon said he never knew a case either in England or Scotland where there was a deed ; and he intimated that he was against Mr. Knowles on the law in this matter.—Mr. Knowles then en- tered into the circumstances of the case. He said the young men were employed in Widnes and had families to main- tain. On Sunday morning they accidentally met, and went a walk, accompanied by a pup, along Chester or Cheshvre's- lane, where Hoyle went into afield, but not for the purpose of pursuing gams, Edwards never left the roadway, and the greyhound which the gamekeeper had seen belonged to three men who were concealed behind the fence.—The defendants were each called as witnesses.—Mr. Gibbon said be had no doubt of the defendants' guilt, and fined them each 103 and e costs, 14s 6d.

THE RUNCORN MANSLAUGHTER CASE. At Liverpool Assizes, on Wedeesday, Michael Murphy, aged 48, master mariner, Runcorn, was indicted for the manslaughter of William Stringer, a dock labourer, who ' lived at 29, Falkner-street, Runcorn. Mr. Burke Wood said the prisoner commanded a sailing vessel which plied between Runcorn and America. On the morning of the 17th May he went into a public-house kept by a man named Bradburn. At half-past two the deceased (Win. Stringer) called at the same house, and there were a number of other men present. As Stringer was in the lobby, about to leave for home, the prisoner put his hand on his sheulders, put his bead against his chest, himself fell on his back (still re- taining his hold of the deceised), and with his feet threw the deceased right over his head and against the wall. F-om that moment the deceased never used his limbs; he did not lose consciousness, but he coulel not move. The prisoner was asked to send for some brandy, but he replied, "No, he is only foxing ; I will not send; if anything happens to him we'll have a good spree over it." The deceased was taken home in a wheelbarrow, and was placed under the treatment of Dr. Bagnall. He, however, became gradually worse, and his depositions were taken, and in two months he died from the injuries caused by the fall. In his depositions the accused stated that he had no words with the prisoner, and did not know what he threw , him for.—Mr. Marshall, for the defence, urged that all the witnesses for the prosecution were unanimous in stating that there was a total absence of animosity between the prisoner and the deceased. As to the throwing, it was a favourite , exercise of the prisoner's, who frequently practised it, and , invariably with success, the persons operated on alighting , on their feet. He contended that the deceased himself , agreed with the prisoner to hive the experiment tried.—The jury found the prisoner guilty, and he was sentenced to two ronths' hard labour. His Lordship, addressing the pri- i soner, said he did not think he meant to kill the man, but that he had chosen to perform a very reelless trick. He

ODDFELLOWS AT HALTON.—The members of the Rising Sun Lodge of Odafellows celebrated the anniversary of their eltaalishment at Halton on Monday by a procession, in which the Runcorn Volunteer Band took part, and a dinner at the Castle Hotel. ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.— The scholars had their annual treat on Tuesday. Mr Jos. Booth, of Halton, supplied the committee with four tarries, 1 and the children were conveyed on them to Overton, where they spent a pleasant day. Runcorn was reached about 0 o'clock at night. THE ROBBERY OF ROPE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday; Jas. Gray and John Taylor, boat- men, were charged upon remand with stealing from the 2at William, at Widnes, 100 yards' of rope, value £l. the pro- perty of Messrs. Paris and Co., shipowners' of Liverpool. The prisoners were remanded to Woolton till Friday.—Yes- terday the men were brought up at Wootton Petty Sessions, and were each committed to gaol for a month. A DESERTER AT WIDNE.s.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Patrick Starkey. a young man, was charged with being absent from the 3rd Battalion of the King's Militia without leave. P.S. Strickland deposed that on the previous afternoon he met the prisoner in Ann-street West, and asaed him for his pass. He then admitted that he was absent from his regiment without leave, and was taken into custody. He was now committed to gaol to await an escort. BOWLING MATCH AT RUNCORN.—For the second time this season the Runcorn Bowling Club met the members of the Widnes Bowling Club on Thursday. The match took place at the green attached to the Bridae Hotel, Ashridge- street, and resulted in an easy victory for the Runcorn team by 67 points. Sohn Redmond, 20 years of age, who was A.B. on board the ' i close of schooner Alfred, of Chester, was found drowned at the tidal wicks' basin, bottom locks. It appears that on Thursday evening, I Sat' the 24th July, Redmond and Thomas Lloyd, sailor on the 18. schooner Alice Latbana, went to the circus which was in the ' I i town, and at the conclusion of the performance proceeded to ! a public-house at Top Locks, where they became to some latent intoxicated On leaving this place Redmond obtained a quart of ale in a bottle, and together the seamen walked to the docks, and got on board the Alice Latham. Next morn- ' ing Lloyd discovered that while Redmond's hat and coat and the quart of ale were 9n the ship he was nowhere to be teen, and the dock was dragged several times without result. On Thursday the body floated, and it was recovered by Joseph Cook, the dock constable, and conveyed to the mor- tuary.—Yesterday afternoon Mr. T. J. Ridgway, the coroner I for the honour and fee of Halton, held an inquest on the body of the deceased at the Burial Board Office. Evidence was given by George Brunt, of Widnes, cook on board the Alfred, of Chester; Thomas Griffiths, of Connah's Quay, seaman on the Win. PRESENTATION TO A. SEAMAN AT RUNCORN. In accordance with thespecial reqnestof the Board of Trade, Mr. R.Shaw, the chairman of the Board of Commissioners, on Monday evening presented A.lbertPahner,seaman on board the vessel Viola, with a silver medal and diploma which had been forwarded by the president of the French Republic for presentation, in recognition of the courage displayed by Pal- mer in rescuing the crew of the Frenct fishing smack LA Gustave, wrecked in Cherburg Roads, November 17th, 1883. The presentation took place in the Commissioners board- room, Town Hall, there being present besides Mr. Shaw, Messrs. James Pritchard, John Pritchard, William Farrell, W. Brooks, and a number of seamen. In handing the medal , and diploma to Palmer, Mr. Shaw said he could assure him ' that it afforded him great pleasure to meet with one of our brave sailors who devoted their lives to a calling fraught with danger and peril at all times. But Palmer had given lustre to his calling by his bravo and noble conduct in yol- ! untarily taking upon himself to risk hit own life in rescuing I those who but for his timely help mast have perished, and thereby caused many a jayous home to be turned into a place of inmrning. The remembrance of that fact would be a source of pleasure to Palmer, and he thought he might be, permitted to sly that as a nation we had reason to be proud ! of him, and such as him whose noble deeds played such an I important part in uniting in closer ties of friendship the peoples of Great Britain and France. He sincerely hoped that Palmer would be long spared to wear the medal. He was convinced he would prize very highly this token of i gratitude on the part of the French Republic.—Palmer, who is a young man, briefly thanked Mr. Shaw on receiving the medal, which bears the following inscription :-" A Albert Pal- mer, Mann Anglais, courage at devonement. 1883." On the motion of Mr. John Pritchard, seconded by Mr. Farrell, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Shaw and the proceed- ings concluded.

OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THIMISDLY. Last week I ventured to call attention to the rapict advan- ces which public opinion is making upon the issue wantonly raised by Lord Saliabery. Before the Franchise Bill went up b the Lords, and in anticipation of its being rejected, there was a good deal of writing and speaking to the effect that the bill must be passed. There was at that time no question mooted as to the constitution of the House of Lords. On Monday week when the great demonstration took place in London there was, officially at least the same reticence. An attempt made to introduce into the programme for the I day a resolution calling for the reform of the House of Lords was after earnest discussion unanimously rejected. It was said the business the people had in hand was to pass the I Franchise Bill, and it was well to keep strictly to that. What I pointed out last week was the significant manner in which, whilst the official prog-aiame was strictly adhered to, the people themselves, the two hundred thousand collected in Hyde Park, took the course of regarding the Franchise Bill as an already accomplished fact, and marched straightfor- ward to the next work, that of reforming, or as some ardent spirits would have it, abolishing the House of Lords. Ten days have passed, and the public mind has moved forward with accelerated pace to the inevitable goal—the dealing once for all, in some manner hereafter to be deter- mined, with the House of Lords. The strength and rapidity of the movement can be tested by consideration Of the ques- tion whether it would be possible, supposing the London demonstration were fixed for Monday next, to withhold from the list of resolutions one directly denouncing the Lords, and demanding that the power so disastrously used by them shall be withdrawn. Everyone knows it would be utterly impossible to do so. At the Conference of Liberal Delegates held in St. James's Hall yesterday, a body retire: sentativeof National Liberal politics, it will be found that the question of passing the Franchise Bill was not discussed. Ills settled, and what business men have now directly turned their minds to is as to measures to be taken in order to prevent a repetition of the public inconvenience occa- sioned by the action of a body of hereditary legislators. The very first resolution submitted to the meeting yesterday condemned the action of the House of Lords as factions and nopatriotic," and this was moved, not by an advanced I Radical like Mr Jesse Collings or Mr Labouchere, but by Sir John Lubbock, one of the staidest and least adventurous Liberals in the House. If these things are done in the green tree what shall be done in the dry? If we get so far in a , fortnight, where shall we be by November, more particularly I if the Lords reject the Bill a second time as Lord Salisbury osteringly declares they will? Lord Randolph Churchill is the " Sim Crow " of English politics. He is always "jumping about and turning about" so that no one knows from day to day where they shall find I him on the morrow. Certainly his latest feat exceeds all expectation or imagination. The last place in the world Iwhere anyone would a week ago have expected to find him is that where he is dining to-night at No 20, Arlington- street. Neither Lord Randolph nor Lord Salisbury is defi- cient in self-confidence and self-possession. But ills im- possible to conceive them meeting to night as guest and host without betraying some slight evidence of shame-faced- nesa. It is three weeks to-morrow since Lord Randolph in the Hones of Commons declared he "viewed with appre- hension the coming conflict" upon which Lord Salisbury had just led his peers, and with a solemnity and gravity unusual with him he besought Mr. Gladstone to open the door once more for compromise and declared that a grave responsibility would rest upon anyone who refused to enter. Now he has formed an alliance offensive and defensive with Lord Salisbury and is bound to assist him in bearing and enlarging responsibility, the gravity of which he in a sober moment perceived. It is said, I believe with truth, that this ill•assorted union will not last very long. Bat whether long or short it sounds the funeral knell of Lord Randolph's praspects as a statesman. One of the first regmsites in inch a character is that a man is to be trusted. But who can trust one who plays fast and loose with the gravest public affairs in the manner of Lord Randolph Churchill ? It would be interesting to hear Sir Stafford Northcots's private ! views on the episode. • ••

Icaptain tells me that similar proposals have been made from America to take effect upon the return of the Philaciek- Warts. The Australians are tempted by the promise of a series of profitable matches all over the States, but at present the offer has not been accepted. The French Australiaz Packet Company offer to take the team back to Australia at merely nominal fares, whereas if they go to New York they will have to pay full fare besides railway journeys across the States. Still cricketing is a very lucrative profession, and would stand these expenses if the Australians cared to extend their tour.

Mr. (lye has abandoned his intention, conditionally formed, of conducting the Opera House at New York. He has been led to this conclusion by the diEculty met in matt- ing attractive engagements. Patti declined to go though he offered her the almost incredible sum of £BOO a night. This I offer had other effects beyond disappointing nim as to the imperious littleprima donna. Failing to get Patti he went to Nilsson and offered her £4OO a night, which she scorn- fully declined. "If Patti is worth £800," she said to the unhappy manager, "surely Christine Nilsson is worth £600." Mr. (lye did not think so, and the business came to an end. Nilsson is now in Germany, having just fulfilled an engage- ment to sing two nights at Carlsbad. She is expected 'back in London to-day or to-morrow, and means to take a months rest. As for Patti, she is singing better than ever, if that were possible. I beard her in "Traviata" the other night, and whilst listening it was quite possible to believe that she was worth the £BOO, though it is a pretty stiff sum for an evening's work. .

• -- - - - The London police have received a commmunication Leone the authorities of New York making inquiries as to a person calling himself Lord Abercrombie, who has excited some attention in that part of the .world. He appeared there in the autumn of last year, giving his name as Walter Adams Mayhew. He seemed to have money. He certainly bought, of all things in the world, the good will, • fixtures, and stock-in-trade of a fur store its Broadway. A little after this he coyly confessed that his real name was Lord Aber- crombie, under which name he received letters. Circum- stances subsequently happened which drew increased atten- tion to him, and upon reference to Barke's Peerage it was discovered that there is no Lord Abercrombie spelling his name as the mysterious Englishman does. There is a Baron Abercrombv. But he is a reputable person married to one of her Majesty's bedchamber women. Moreover, he is 46 years of age, whereas the American " peer " is de- scribed as a young man. The conclusion that the whole matter is a hoax would be easily art iced at but for one cir- cumstance. Lord Mandeville is at present in New York, and has been much in the society of the claimant. He, being questioned, vouches for him, declaring that he re- members him at school, and is prepared to swear to his bon a fides. Still that does not get over the difficulty that there is no Abercrombie with an "ie" in the Peerage, and that Lord Abercromby with a " y " is now in London. Lord Mandeville, whose declaration adds so much to the mystery a the situation, is a man of whom there should be no mistake in America. He it the son and heir of the Dike of Manchester, and is married to a daughter of a Caban gentleman who has an estate in Louisiana. Lori Mandeville is Conservative member for Huntingdonshire, which he haB represented for seventeen years. He is one of the silent members. As lex-as I know he has not yet made his maiden speech. div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE:
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE:

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. Paffrigniv—Before Alderman Olandley and Mr Fairolough. IMPUDENT THEFT ET A FEMALE.—Emma Howard, described as a seamstress, of Hoyle-street. was charged with stealing a vest, value 2s. from the shop of Mr. E. V. Morton, on the pre vim. day, when she was noticed in the prosecutor s front shoo in Winwick street. and shortly afterwards was seen in .the back part of the premises, offering a wale . coat in pledge. The vest was discovered by those in attendance to belong to a sot of clothes that had been ritsced in the front shop, and the pri- snner was In consequence given into custoy. Two previous convictions were recorded against her, and she was sent to prison for two months. MoNDAY—Before Mr John Pairelough and Alderman Holmes.' THE DRUNKER LIST.--The following persons were dealt with for drunkenness, viz. :—Cath-rine Paley, fined is and costs or seven days; Patrick Macdonald, fined 10s and ens.s or fourteen days; Michael Cain:ran, 9th appearance. fined 105 and costs or fourteen days; Emily Richardson and Margaret Baldwin, young girls, fined is and ousts or seven days; George Eephton and Richard Weaver, fired is and costs or seven days; Mary Lee. fined ss, including costs; Alice Dawson, dismissed; Louis Twyberg. fined 10s and costs or fourteen days. Evros THROWlNG.—Catherine Ball, a middle-aged woman, was charged with throwing stones in Marsh House-lane. She took occasion to complain strongly of the conduct of her hus- band, who was present and expressed his willingness to give her an allowance in order to be rid of her, as they could not live happily together. She agreed to receive that amount. The Bench dismissed the charge of stone throwing. THEFT or Trasszn.—,John Birmingham. a boy, son of Mi- chael Birmingham, Friars'-green. was charged with stealing from the Conservative Club now in course of erection in Bankey-street. on the previous day, two pieces of timber, valua Ts, the property of William Porter, builder. It appeared that as P.O. Shaw. who was dressed in plain clothes, was passing the building in question when his attention was attracted by a noise and on making a search he discovered the prisoner in the act of taking a Diem of timber frond the building into the adjoining field. There were there two younger boys who were in company with the prisoner. On the constable taking Blr- minghim into custody the latter admitted having taken the wood and alsohaving taken w od on previous occasions.—Pri- s mar was ordered to go to prison for a month, to be followed by rive years in a Reformatory. GIVING Him A. CHANCE.—William Fernley, fustian cutter, was summoned by his wife for assaulting her. The wile ex- pressed herself willing to give him another chance. He had promised to keep from the beer, and when he did so he was all right.—The Bench ad] purneti the case for a month to see if he would fulfil his promise. PROVOKING LANGUAGE.—Sarab Williamson was charged , with using provoking language to Ann Bennett on the 23rd July. She was ordered to be bound over in one surety to keep the peace for six menthe. UNREGISTERED LOCGING-HOUSES.—The followin r were sum- moned at the instance of Inspector orman for keeping lodgers without having their houses registered. viz. :—John Kelly, Smith-street, dismissed on payment of costs; Daniel Allen, Smith-street, fined 20s and costs; Alice Urey, Smith-street, dismissed on payment cf costs. TU/nDAY—There were no cases down for hearing. THURSDAY.—Before Captain Litton. DRUNICENNESS —Elizabeth Glover, a young woman belong- ing to St. Helens, was charged with being drunk and disor- derly in James-street on the prevtous evening.—She pleader.' for leniency, and the magistrate dismissed her on the promise that she would leave the town. SLEEPING OUT,—George Jerrold, for sleeping in the Market- place, was sent to gaol for 14 days. FRlDAY.—Before Messrs. C. Broadbent and John White, ALLEGED ASSATT.T.—John Hickey, a labourer, of 12, Owen- street, was charged with having assaulted Michael Duffy, an elderly man, on the 29th July.—Oomplainant did not wish to press the case, but the Chief Constable said the defendant was a most worthless fellow.—Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six months, or in default of sureties one month's imprisonment NEGLECT OF ORDERS —William Longshaw, a labourer em- ployed by the Corporation, was ordered to contribute 3s per week towards the snaport of his mother and towards the pay- ing off of arrears amounting to £1 17s tild on an order of the Bench.—Jobn Lawton was ordered to pay a similar amount per week, on a like order.

Ihe case against Thomas Hughes was dismissed; and Alfred Hughes, who had been several tins previously convicted, was bound over to keep the peace for six months —James Coreoron and Thomas McLoughlin, young men. obarged with fighting in Market-street. Eariestown, on the previous Sunday afternoon were also bound over for a like perloi.

TEMPOS LIM AuTnoniTT. —Ralph Atherton Wag granted temporary authority ti sell at the Waterman's Arms, under the license lately held by Henry Armson. MISCELLANEOI79.—John Collins. for being drunk and dis- orderly in Eibaw-street on the 19'h inst., was on the evidence of PC. Bryan fined lOs and goats 9 6d.—Ann Woodcock was bound over to keep the peace for six months, herself in £lO and one surety of £lO. for using abusive and defamatory language toward.s Martha Griffiths. of the George Inn, Pool- lane.

WEEK END TIPPLERS —The follossing persons were each -fined 5s and costs for being drunk on the 26th or 27th instants: John Tiernan. Patrick Griffin, James Richard Wind, Henry McFarlane, Michael Costello, John Brear. Martha Rrear, Michael Tobin, Memel Carney, Michael Carr, and George IDanni ngham. eLEEPING °Tn.—Timothy Boris was committed to gaol for seven days' hard lab :nr for sleeping on the Widnsa Alkali Ga.'s chemical works on Sunday morning. BEndt.sa..—James Williams was, on the evidence of P.O. McGuinness. convicted oi begging in Eleanor-street on Sianday and he was sentenced to neves: days' hard labour. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. E Olden. DRUNKENNESS. William Shaw, Ellen Mulvey. Alfred 'Waller, John Wail, Mary F x. Henry Dickinson, Maly Daly. and Margaret Reynolds were each fined 5s and costs for being drunk.—For being drunk and riotous at the Stonemasons' Arms kept by Wm. Ince, Thomas Dunne, who was an old of- fender, was fined 15s and costs. BIM.= OF THE PEACE.—Thomas Burns was bound over to keep the pence for three months. himself in £lO and two sureties of £5, for riotous conduct in Lugsdale-road.
