div.p: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
TIIESDAY.—Befara Messrs. Plernoint; W. Long. and James Marson.

DEUTNXENNESS —The following persons were charged with having been drunk and disorderly, and were dealt with as fol- lows :—Edward Atherton. at Appleton, on the 21st ult., 5s and costs ; John Hunt, at Moor, on the 21st Jane, 5s and costs; Charles Clifford, on the 12'h inst., at Appleton. be and costs; and John Norman, at Little Leigh, on the 21st ult., 5s and costs. Alf MA17210178 BICXCLIS2.—WaIter Greenhouse, a young Man. was charged with having unlawfully ridden his bicycle on the foolpath at Appleton on the 2nd ult.. at 6-30 p,m. The defendant pleaded gniity.—The clerk (Mr. Nicholson), said this was the first case of that kind that 'bat bench had had be- fore ik—Defendant was ordered to pay costs of the summons, 4s 6d. CHARGE AGAINST A PITIILICAN.—Mary Ann Cowap, the land- lady of the Horns Inn. Little Leigh. was charged with having unlawfully kept open her house for the sale of intoxicating liquor at 10.15 pm. on the lot silt; she was also charged with unlawful y permitting drunkenness on her premises on the same day. James Haddock and Thomas Withinshaw, young men, were charged with being on the above-named premises during prohibited hours; and Charles Lightfoot, another young man, was charged with haying been drunk on the said premises.—Mr. R. Davies defended.—P.O. D sley stated that at the time named on the day in question be visited Mrs. Cowap's premises and found Haddock and Withinshaw In the kitchm in company with Mrs. Cowap's daughter and a woman whorn he believed to be a charwoman. In the tap-room wit- ness found Lightfoot asleep and drunk. There were, however, no signs of drink about —ln defence it was stated that /awl dock was a servant of Mrs, Cowap's. and lived In the house; that Lightfoot bad been mowing hay for Mrs. Cowan during the day, and intended to stay In the house all night, and besides had not been served with any drink in the house; and finally that Withinshaw. who is a travelling tailor, had hired a bed for the might. —The Beach said it was their opinion that the policeman had acted in every way that was right in the mat- ter, but the evidence was not sufficient to convict.—Ali the Cases were therefore dismissed, DISEISTE DILTWEEN MASTER AND SERvANT.—Albert Johnson. S young man, claimed from John Swinton, farmer. Moor, th sum of £2 16s 9d the balance due of wages under contract and in lieu of one month's notice.—Mr. A. Brovrne appeared for the Plaintiff, and Mr. Moore for the defendant.—lt appeared that the plaintiff had been hired at the usual year.lve. htring for the annual payment of £lO and keep. On the 24.nJuno p'alntiff asked the defendant to allow him a half holiday to play in a cricket match but defendant would not agree. and some alter- cation took place which ended, according to the plaintiff, in the defendant telling him to leave. The defendant would not. however, pay him t e balance of wages due to him.—ln de- fence it was stated that plaintiff left his work of his own ac- cord —& verdict of 12 for the plaintiff wi.h costs was given. B/D LANGUAGE.—Sarah Wilkinson was charged with having used defamatory language coneernisg Enoch Jackson at Par- tinaton on the 7th July, and was bound over to keep the peace for six months. • ST. HELENS POLICE COURT. l'illDAT.—liefore Mr Thos Pllkington and Mr A Sinclair. DRUNNENNESS AND ASSAULTS. ThOttlaS Moore for being drunk in Pt.ytloish-street ou Tuesday night, was fined Se and 7s 6d clots or seven days, and for assaulting Police-constable Peters l'Os and costs or fourteen days; and Thomas Poster, for assaulting Police-constable Peters was fined its and costs or

fourteen days. —Alfred Eloulton. a bottle-hand from Warring- ton. was fined 16s and costs for assaulting John 0 Wright, a railway detective. by striking him in the face at the St Helens passenger station. on Thursday.—Edward Leonard of Ashcrof t- street. was fined 103 and costs for assaulting Mary Iltelary, of Baxter-street. Parr. It was alleged that he went to her house and struck her two heavy blows in the face.—Elizabeth Dolan was fined 10, and 6s 6d costs for having, at Gerard's Bridg... broken open the door of the dwelling-Irmse of Mar- garet Bowes sod struck her in the face with the lock. THE ALLEGED THEFT OF A SOVEREIGN —Mary J Wolsten- groft, under remand charged with stealing a sovereign from the person of David Simms. cf Parr Stocks, with whom she had been drinking at the Globe and Crescent Hotels, was die' charged, the magistrates stating that they were disposed to believe prisoner's statement teat prosecutor had given her the money. SATURDAY.—Before Aldermen J. Harrison and Mr. A.

Sinclair. BEGGING.—SamueI Smith, of Rainford, wal fined Is and costs for beg4ing on the previous day, and Peter limghley and Patrick. both of Windle. were committed for seven days for begging early that morning. MONDAY %torn Mr. W. Blinklywn and Alde•man Cook, ASSAULT.—Oharles Knowles, of Sutt..n. was fined 5s and costs for &multi .g Ellen Garnet on the 24th ult. ALLEGED THEFT Or NEAT PIES —John Andrews, of Eccles- ton. was brought up on a charge of stealing three meat pos. the property of Mary Hill Makin on the 26th ult.—The case was dismissed. TUESDAY.—Befnre Alderman Cook and Alderman Meßryde. A VIOLENT FEMALE —A middle-aged tema'e named Mary Pinder, residing at Parr. was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Ratcliffe s.court on the previous evening. and also with breaking a window in a cottage belonging the London and North-Western Railway Company The prisoner was fined lOs and cogs or seven days' imprisonment, and for smashing the window she was further fined 5s and costs, ordered to pay Is as damage, or in default of paymen;, a further period of seven days' imprisonmsnt. ThuusnAY—Tief ore Alderman Harrison.

BLEEPING AT a BOTTLE WOKS.—Patrick Feigh and John McCaoly, young men, were charged with sleeping in a " cave" at the glass-bottle works of Messrs Mooney, Winds early that morning.—Peigh, who had been several times previously con- victed, was committed to prison for 14 days, and klcOooly, who was brought up for the first time, was sentenced to 7 days' imprisonment. ItawKiNg WITHOUT A LICENSE.—A young Ilan named James Kearns was brought up for hawking without a licsnse at Windle on the previous afterno-n —P O. Mitchell stated that prisoner and another man were hawking from door to door. and on seeing him they ran away. He followed and coughs the prisoner, who, it was ascertained, was without license.— The prisoner was remanded.

div.head: REFORM AGITATION.
div.p: THE REFORM AGITATION.
GREAT LIBERAL DESIONSTRA.TION AT MAN- CHESTER.

The demonstration in support of the Franchise Bill, held at Pomona Gardena, Manchester. on Saturday had been pro- moted by the Manchester and Salford Liberal Association and the Liberals of Mid and East Cheshire and North-East and South-East Lancashire, and tickets of admission were allotted in certain proportions to those towns and districts. There were altogether three meetings. The priecipal one was that in the palace, where Mr Bright took the chair; and the other two—one of which would have been held in the open air had the weather been fine—took place in the Agri- cultural Hall, a vast building, capable of holding 50,000 people. It is estimated that from 15,000 to 20,000 people were present at the palace meeting, and that a similar num- ber attended the other two gatherings. The proceedings were of a most enthusiastic character. The palace was fil- led in every part. The platform had been reserved for mem- b;rs of Parliament, Liberal candidates and other invited guests, and they were loudly cheered as they entered the building. Amongst those present were Sir Henry James (Attorney-General), Mr J K Cross, M.P, Mr R Leake, M.P., Mr.W Agnew, M.P., Mr Hugh Mason, M.P., Mr Peter Ry- lands, M.P., Mr E L Stanley, M.P., Mr B Armitage, M.P., Mr Henry Lee, M.P., Mr F W Grafton, M.P., Mr WE Briggs, M.P., Mr R Fort, M.P, Mr W Summers, M.P., Mr C H Hopwood, M.P., Mr F Pennington, M.P., Mr J G Mc Minutes, M.P., Mr J F Cueetham, M.P., Sir IT Kay-Shuttle- worth, Mr I S Leadam, Mr Thos Ashton, Mr T Rigby, Mr W Crosfield, Mr J Tomkinson, Mr David Duncan, Mr F &tett, Lord Lymingten, M.P., the Hon C R Spencer, M.P., Mr H Dunckley, Mr C Scott, Mr C Flower, M.P., Mr J A Bright. Mr G W Latham, Sir Arthur Hayter, Bart, M.P., Mr C Russell, Q.C., M.P., the Hon A D and Mr B J Broadfield.

Mr Bright and Lord Hartington had been the guests at lunch of Mr W Agnew, M.P., at Pendleton, whence they drove to Pomona. They arrived at the gardens shortly be- fore half.past four o'clock. Mr John Bright took the chair. Lord Hartiugton sat on his right, and Sir Henry James on his left

The Chairman, in introducing Mr. Thomas Ashton, J.P., ' to move the first resolution, said :—I believe Mr. Thomas Ashton. if he had been so inclined, would long ago have re- , paesented a division of this county in Parliament. (Hear, heir.) He is the son of a man whom I knew forty years ago—as it were the most venerable father of the cotton in- dustry of this county. The son, as you know, is one of our most eminent employers of labour, and one of our most eminent merchants, and we are glad to have him here,and many like him to give their support to the cause in which ws are engaged. (Cheers.) Mr. Ashton moved :—" That the country at the last elec- tion emphatically approved the extension of the county suffrage to householders; that the Franchise Bill introduced by Mr. Gladstone is just and moderate; that it has been carried by overwhelming majorities in the House of Com- mons; that in these circumstances this meeting protests against the refusal of the House of Lords to pass the Bill, and against the pretension of Lord Salisbury, by a dangerous assertion of the privileges of the Peers—tending to subvert the principles of representative government—to dictate a dissolution of Parliament; and that this meeting heartily supports the Franchise Bill as an act of justice to two mil- lions of capable citizens, and pledges itself to stand by her Majesty's Ministers in their determination to adhere firmly to the policy of passing the Franchise Bill, to be followed immediately by the Bill for redistribution." Sir U. J. Kay-Shattteworth, Bart., seconded the motion. Lord Hartington, no longer a new figures at Manchester meetings, was cheered again and again as he came to the front of the railed-in rostrum. His characteristic equanimity was disturbed by his hearty Lancashire welcome. He estab- lished sympathetic accord between himself and the multi- tude almost in his opening sentences. Begin with an apt joke, experienced orators say, and you keep the listeners waiting for the next. No joke could be more apt that the conversion of the uncongenial climatic circumstances attend- ing the meeting to a jest at the expense of Lord Salisbury's gibe at legislation by picnic. The people, many of them wet through, laughed at their own discomfort when they were reminded that they ware not precisely among picnic sur- roundings, and cheered the noble Lord again and again in tones that supplied on the instant proof of his remark that they were good.humoared as well as determined. Nor was there ' room for a doubt that the crisis had found Lord Harlington as resolved as they were. More of these !meetings and more he urged, until they had been held in 1 every town, in every district, and in every village in the country, to express confidence in the Government of Mr. Gladstone (whose name evoked another outburst of ap- plause), and to protest against the "unprecedented and un- constitutional " action of the House of Lords, the mention of which august assembly provoked some hearty but not ill- natured hoots and hisses The assemblage soon began to re- cognise that Lord Hartington had come to deliver a vigorous campaign speech, and as he went on, making great physical efforts to send his words flying to the further walls, every sentence almost was punctuated with responsive applause. How masterfully he exposed the hollow pretences of the Lords, that they are not really opposed to the extension of the franchise, but are only desirous of passing a "perfect measure "—how plainly, in the same spirit as Lord Gran- ville exhibited, he indicated his disbelief in Lord Salisbury's sincerity in making such professions—how he subjected Lord Randolph Churchill to merciless criticism, yet, as Isaac Walton would have woven the worm on his tioh-hook "lovingly," was patent to everyone. The people bad looked rather to Mr. Bright than Lord Hartington for epigrams, a story or two, or a poetical illustration. But Mr. Bright could not have introduced in a more telling manner J. P. Kemble's historic couplet, which the Franchise Bill might have addressed to its professing friends— Pernapi it was well to dissemble your love, But—why did you kick me down stairs? There was a significant emphasis in the injunction that if the issues between the people and the peers are to be made ,clear and decided "you of the North" must bear a con- siderable part in the struggle. There was a truth which was quickly appreciated in the statement that Lord Sails- bury'e flank attack on the Reform Bill pointed to the desire on his part to perform the work, and in the Tory interest, of "gerrymandering the constituencies." We have been, and are, and are likely to continue to be a majority in the cocntry, said Lord Harticgton amid cheers, renewed again and again. And, he went oa to point out, the peers know that, and want by devices of their own to prevent that ma- jority taking effect. All through the speech came the re- curring remark, always cheered, that the Lords have acted without precedent, and in defiance of the unwritten laws and contrary to the spirit of the constitution, of which re- sponsibility is the keynote. It was possible to discover a , difference in the note of sympathy when Lord Hartington proceeded in some passages, which had evidently been care- fully considered, to urge on the country not to jeopardise the Franchise Bill, or the other measures in the Government programme, or the great question of the reform of procedure in the House of Commons, bvimmediately raising the ques- tion as to what is to be done with the lords. But his perfect frankness and firmness, or, as we heard it called, his hitting Out from the shoulder, made a visible and immense impres- sion. It was " jannock " it was said, and in style and tone and matter one would say this genital fighting speech has, more than anything else since 1880, made Lord Har- tington a popular hero in the Liberal party. It had been arranged that Mr Bright should speak last. It says much for the good effect of Lord Hartington's speech that be was listened to with such close attention and eager in- terest for nearly an hour, and with the orator of the day to follow. How would Mr Bright speak, people were asking ; answered heard ali matr e unrcieg.h jst important with regard to its substance, but to the delivery only, was the question raised. The question may as well be wpaosrtathnet speeches of i ntcheosleB6wd that hohahvee was never heard in better voice or more effective style. There was an interval before the meeting had a chance of settling that question for itself. Some minutes passed before Mr. Bright could make himself heard. The cheering which had greeted him two hours before broke out in apparently greater force. Again and again the enthusiasm started anew, until there came the curious effect that the clapping of hands sounded like a tropical hail storm on the roof. And I then away in the distance a bold tenor voice started the i first line of " For he's a jolly good fellow." I There was no need for Mr. Ward or the band. The audieoce 1

"leaped at" the suggestion. The chorus was taken up all over the ball, the audience rising to their feet, Mr. Bright all the while standing at his little table, Lord Hartington looking oa with amused interest, and Sir Henry James sit- , ting on the other side beating time to the unpremeditated music with his foot. Almost before the echoes had ceased to reverberate one heard the clear notes of the well-known voice urging that the time had come when be ought to be a spectator rather than an actor in reform demonstrations. Thereat there was a unanimous protest. "I am not unac- customed," the voice went on in stronger tones, "to periods of crisis" There broke out a quick shout of ackaowledg- ment of a fact everyone present was glad to remember. Then Mr. Bright settled down in his old form to deliver him- self on the great question of the hour. There was much in it of the retrospect we look for now from the great Reformer ; but it bore throughout upon the question of the obstruction always offered by the peers to reform of every kind. There were many characteristic little hits, like the reference to the "grotesque costumes" of the Lords who pronounce that "Le Heine il vault;" or their prayer, "Give us this day our daily bread" while they were defending the corn law; or to the House as "The caucus of the Tory party." Epigrams fell now and then, such as that the people were " accustomed to conflict, but not less accustomed to conquer." There was no mincing of words in describing the rhetorical artifices of the Lords as •' gross misrepresentations," " persistent and dishonour- able," which Lord Salisbury, if he were not the Tory leader, would himself be shocked to hear another leader rise in the House and make. It was interesting to everybody to hear Mr. Bright recite for the first time in public the story of his talk and correspondence with Mr. Disraeli anent the ridiculous Reform Bill which would have created a number of "grotesque franchises," and only have affected 15 seats in, the redistribution. There was one of those happy illustrations which Mr. Bright has crystallised in political speech, as he did the "Cave of Adullam" and the "Skye terrier "alliance, in which you could not tell the head from the tail. "Bob, the grinder," in "Dombey and Son," was the nec3ssary complement of Lord Hartington's quotation. The pertinence of Rob's protest, "Can't you be fond of a cove without squeedging and throttling him ?" • to the action of the House of Peers towards the Franchise Bill, was recognised in a moment 'amid hearty laughter. There was no peroration particularly; but there was a note at once of cheer and warning sounded in the closing sentence that the view of the English people will be that, if their fore- fathers had the power to curb despotic monarchy, they had ' the power equally "to curb an arrogant and unpatriotic oligarchy." (Cheers.) After finishing his speech, Mr Bright put the resolution to the audience, saying "Those who approve of it say aye," and a terrific response awaited his invitation. Mr Roby next moved a resolution to the effect that the power of veto of the House of Lords was an intolerable anomaly, productive of much mischief and no good, lead to just irritation in the people, was a constant hindrance to good and necessary legislation, and ought to be abolished. (Loud cheers.) Mr G W Latham seconded the resolution.

Mr Bright called for a show of hands, and the number held up for the motion was so vast as to be indicative of practical unanimity. He said a friend near him thought there were probably twenty hands against the resolution. He supposed his own eyes were not clear, for he only noticed one. The resolution was carried by an enormous and over- whelming majority. (Loud cheers.) Sir H James, who occupied a special position as selected candidate for a Lancashire borough, was unfortunate in the noise caused by people leaving the hall. He evidently left much unsaid that he would have urged. This was to be deplored, as his speech made an excellent impression, and had been generally looked forward to. It being, however, now close upon seven o'clock, the remainder of the proceed- ings were hurried. The singular unanimity and enthusiasm were notwithstanding sustained to the end. The resolution of thanks to the chairman was carried amidst a repetition of the former demonstrations, and "God save the Queen" came as the last item of the progromme. Most of the gen- tlemen who had occupied the platform passed over through mud and rain to the overflow meetings, which broke up a little later.

LORD SALISBURY AND SIR S. NORTLICOTE. A conference was held in the hall of the Canon-street Hotel, London, on Monday night between the presidents, secretaries, and leading members of the Conservative Asso- ciations of the metropolis and neighbouring counties, "in support of the House of Lords." The hall was densely crowded. The Lord Mayor presided.—Lord SALISBURY said be could not help wondering why it was the truths (expressed in a number of Conservative 'resolutions which were read) which seemed so obvious had not made their im- pression upon the Government—why was it that they raised up gratuitous difficulty, and introduced the subject of re- form in the eccentric and abnormal manner in which they had? It was said to be in consequence of the extraordinary block in the House of Commons, but as the controversy went on candour increased, and he hoped before the discus- sion was concluded all false pretences and hollow pretexts would be discarded, and the cause which was right ulti- mately triumph. Mr. Gladstone had always followed up a victory with vigour. If he had his Franchise Bill passed he would show little mercy to his opponents in his Redis- tribution Bill. When he talked of giving the largest repre- sentation to the most remote districts, it seemed at first one of those fantastic theories which sometimes crossed the brain of men of genius, but, looked at closer, there was method ia the madness, beeause, while the circumference (Wales, Scotland, and Cornwall) was growing more Liberal, the heart (London) was turning more Conservative. He did not claim for the House of Lords the right to force a dissolution,, but they had the right to disapprove of any measure brought before them, and if the Government ob- jected to its rejection their remedy was to go to th.e people. He was sure that, in this as in many other cases, liberty bad to fear chiefly its professing friends. The peers had been maintaining the essential conditions on which popular gov- on neat reposed, and had been upholding the true and ancient principles of English liberty. The noble Marquis quoted more fully and fairly than he had done before from Mr. Bright's speech in 1859, and contended that Lord Hat- tington was against Mr. Bright on the necessity of redistri- bation. Sir STAFFORD NORTHOOTE said Conservatives must not be content simply to know that they were in the right, but should go forth among the people, teach them the truth, dissipate fallacies, and prepare for the not distant elections. A blow was being struck at the House of Lords.' If successful the caucus would next make it difficult to maintain the freedom of the House of Commons. The Gov- ernment wanted, by illegitimate means, to force the mea- sure upon the people. They said, "If we were now to put aside the Franchise Bill in favour of a Redistribution Bill, you would never pass the Redistribution Bill." On the other band, if once the Government obtained the enlarged measure, there would be great difficulty in getting them to give up their gain. It could not then be said to them, "Make your redistribution fair. or we won't pass the Fran- chise Bill," because they would say, "We have get the Franchise Bill, and as for a fair redistribution, that is a pretty thing to talk about," but—(the right hon. gentleman finished the sentence with a gesture which elicited much laughter and cheers)—but those before him had their own work to do. They bad that hall to look upon that day as a fresh beginning of the work of preparation for the election which must come, sooner or later. His hearers had to fight the battle of the metropolitan counties, and were fighting it in the best possible way, not through casual mass meetings or organised processions at Se. per head, but by calling together their chiefs, their working committees, and their representative associations, giving them the word which they were to pass on in turn to others who were not present. CONFERENCE OF LIBERAL DELEGATES IN
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 2, 1884

House of Lords as factious and unpatriotic.—Mr James Kin- ston moved another resolution expressing emphatic approval of the decision of the Government to hold an autumn session in order to pass the Franchise Bill during the present year.—The Rev J Guiness Rogers seconded, and Sir W Lawson supported the resolution, and caused great laughter by his references to Lord Salisbury, and was warmly cheered when he declared that a people which had put away the "divine right" of kings would not submit to the divine right of dukes.—Mr Bradlaugh said they did not want to abolish the House of Lords, but to abolish its veto on the people's demands.—Mr Jesse Collings, M.P., supported a resolution condetnning the habitual disregard of national will by the Lords.—All the resolutions were carried enthusiastically.

LETTER FROM M. BRIGHT.—A SA/ASHUR? " COR- RECTED.—A great demonstration in favour of the franchise was held in Sheffield, on Saturday.—Mr. MIINDELLA, M.P., said Lord Salisbury had made the audacious assertion that if the House of Lords was villified, it was villified by fol- lowing the counsels of Mr. Bright, and he went on to say that Mr. Bright bad made this remark—" Repudiate with- out mercy any hill of any Government, whatever its fran- chise, whatever its seeming concessions may be, if it does not redistribute the seata." But it did not suit the noble marquis to give Mr. Bright's words completely. Anyhow, he omitted the last part of Mr. Bright's expression, which was—" Repudiate without mercy any bill of any Govern- ment, whatever its franchise, whatever its seeming conces- sions may be, if it does not redistribute the seats that are obtained from the extinction of the small boroughs amongst the large towns." (Laughter.; Now, he had sent one of those statements to Mr. Bright, asking him what he thought about it, and the tight bon. gentleman replied in the following important letter :—" 132, Piccadilly, July 24, 1884.—My dear Mundella,—Soma years ago, the working-men, having no votes, demanded only the franchise. At the same time there was no Govern- ment zealous in favour of reform, and re-arrangement of seats was difficult and not liked at headquarters. I urged the people to keep their eyes on the seats, and not to con- sider reform secured when only an extended franchise was granted. But when Lord John Russell brought in one of his Reform Bills, I strongly urged him to deal with the fran- chise first, and in a separate bill. He stated this in the House, and quoted me as an authority for what he had done. As a matter of procedure, I have always held this opinion. I reoommended Mr. Trevelvan not to force the two questions on the House at the Came time, as I believed he would get a larger vote tbr tbe franchise if not connected with the ques- tion of seats. If the Franchise Bill has occupied almost a whole session, what could have been done with the two bills in one? Ignorant people may have no answer to this, hut Lord Salisbury and Sir Stafford Northcote know why they object to the courSa taken by the Government, although they give to the public explanations and answers which are deceptive and insincere. There Is, I believe, no mode of dealing successfully with the Reform question but that which the Government have adopted, and they will have the support of every man who is in the smallest degree earnest for an amendment of our representative system.— Believe me, always sincerely yours, JOHN BRIGHT." A. WELBECE ABBEY PICNIC.—A demonstration took place on Saturday, the Conservatives of Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire visiting Welbeck Abbey, the seat of the Duke of Portland, for the purpore of being addressed by Sir Stafford Northcote. Excursions were run from all parts of the two counties. In consequence a! the incessant rain the meeting, instead of being in the open air, was held in the famous riding school. The Duke of Portland presided. Sir S. Northcote, in his speech, said: It is not a question in which the House of Lords have an interest on one side and the people of this country on the other. It is not the House of Lords—it is the Conservative party throuehout the country who are taking up this position, and who are making this demand. It is the Conservative party in the House of Com- mons, in the House of Lords, and amongst the constituencies. (Cheers.) " COUITTER DEMONSTRATION" IN HYDE PARB.—An at- tempt was made in Hyde Park oa Saturday to hold a de- monstration eounter to the great reform demonstration of Monday. Bills addressed to working-men had been issued, setting forth that it would be a great mistake to regard the ravings of the 21st inst as the sober and mature view of the noble working-classes of old England. " The House of Lords," added these documente, is a house of English- men, but the House of Commons is 3 house consisting chiefly of foreigners." At five o'clock when Mr. W. Stokes and Mr. Cashen (the promoters of the meeting) drove up in the waggonette which was to serve as a platform, about 30 persons ware gathered together, and the number never grew to more than 300. Some of hose present immediately began bantering Mr. Stokes and his friends. Amid hearty laughter, one exclaimed, " test as hope the reporters will .report the tens of thousands that are here." An amendment (in favour of the Government) was declared carried by the Chairman, whereupon a Conservative brought forward a motion protesting agains "the misrepresentation of the Con- servative or any party by meetings called by an irresponsi- ble agitator ;" but before It could be put the Chairman de- clared the proceedings closed.

A CLERGYMAN ON TORY PICNICS.—The Rev. H. M. Kennedy, vicar of Plumpton, Cumberland, writes: It is well the Conservative peers are asked to lend their parks for one day for mass meeting demonstrations. By such meet- ings they shall demonstrate two things, their insincerity in condemning the vast gatherings of the people, and the costly splendour with which 200 years of class legislation has sur- rounded a privileged few. If the meetings come off, by all means let representatives of the wronged and heavily-taxed portion of the community, attend and take a note of what they shall see. SIR RICHARD CROSS, speaking at Cardiff in support of the action of the Peers, on Saturday, said it was untrue that the House of Llrds had rejected the Franchise Bill. The quarrel was not between the Government and the House of Lords, but between the Government and the great Con- servative party. The Government were alone responsible for the present position of the bill, for they had not given sufficient time to the question of reform. - . .

Lord Salisbury, in acknowledging the receipt of resolu- tions of the Bridgewater Conservative Association, expres- sed a hope that their support will be given to the •House of Lords in maintaining the constitutional position it has adopted against the attacks of the Government. Sir Staf- ford Northcote also wrote, saving be has full confidence that the country will recognise the justice of the principle for which Conservatives are contending. Replying to resolutions of the City of London Liberal Association protesting against the action of the House of Lords, Mr. Gladstone says it is gratifying to him to find from similar resolutions that the action of the Government has commended itself not enly to the Liberal party, but to the good sense of the public generally. On Monday afternoon a miner's demonstration took place at Queen's Ground, Barnsley, when addresses were delivered by Mr. Burt, M.P., and others. The resolution prayed for better inspection of mines, and thanked the Government for passing the Franchise Bill, condemned the action of the House of Lords respecting the same measure, and called npon working-men evervwhero to agitate until the House of Peers is either abolishea or reformed.
A mass meeting of miners and others, held at Rageley on Saturday, passed a resolution condemning the existence of an irresponsible and hereditary HOLISB of Peers, and de- manding its reform.

The Earl of Carnarvon addressed a large gathering of Conservatives on Saturday afternoon at Osterlev-park, near Hounslow. He asserted that there was no difference as to the Franchise Bill itself, but the Conservatives objected to the manipulation of the constituencies to their permasent disadvantage.

A ceetin—g attended by several thousand persons was held at Marble Rinks, Nottingham, on Saturday, in support of the Franchise Rill, Mr. A. Morley and Mr. Broadhurst, mem- bers of Parliament, being the principal speakers. Other meetings were held at Ipswich, when Mr. West and Mr. Jesse Collings, members of Parliament, spoke; at Middles- borough, addressed by Mr. George Howard, M.P.; and at Bangor, where Mr. Rathbone. M.P., spoke in support of the Franchise Bill and condemning the action of the House of Lords.
At Scarborough, on Saturday night. a meeting was ad- dressed by Messrs. Caine and Reid, M.P.'s, and passed a re- solution commending the Government policy and denounc- ing the action of the Lords.

Lord Northbrook. in opening the new premises of the Hull United Liberal Club on Wednesday afternoon, strongly condemned what he called the systematic misrepresentation by Lord Salisbury and Sir S Northcote as to the administra- tion of the present Government. He congratulated the Liberal party on its present unity, which he traced to the general agreement as to the justice of the Franchise Bill and the injudicious attempt of the Conservatives to defeat it.

Mn. GLADSTONE'S VISIT TO MIDLOTHIAN.—The arrancfe- ments in connection with Mr Gladstone's meetings in the Edinburgh Corn Exchange on Saturday, 30th August, and Monday, Ist September, are aoproaching completion. Tickets will be allocated C.l) to Midlothian electors and (2) to Midlothian uon-electors--the latter to the number of about 2,soo—but no one will be entitled to a ticket for more than one meeting. It is proposed to invite a limited number of delegates from Liberal associations throughout Scotland to the Monday meeting. Ihere will be a certain number of complimentary invitations, and, in addition, the Scottish Liberal Association is to have the distribution of several hundred tickets among its members. THE CONSERVATIVE DEMONSTRATION AT POMONA..—In addition to the Marquis of Salisbury, Sir R A Cross, and others who have been announced to speak at the Conserva- tive demonstration in Pomona Gardena, Sir Michael Hicka- Beach and Lord Rindolph Churchill have intimated their intention of taking part in the proceedings. At a Conservative meeting, addressed by Mr. Ashmead- Bartlett, M.P., at Eastbourne, on Wednesday night, consider- able disturbance was caused by the presence of a large Liberal element, and the row continued throughout the meeting. The show of hands for and against a resolution supporting the Houqe. of Lords was about equal. At a Liberal meeting at Anchtermuchty, on Wednesday evening, resolutions were poss.(' condemning the action of the Peers in rejecting the Franchise Bill, and demanding the abolition of the Housa of Lords.

div.head: LONDON.
div.p: LONDON.

On Wednesday, a Conference of Liberal delegates from the National Liberal Federation, the National Reform Union, the London and Counties Liberal Union, and the various Liberal associations and clubs throughout the king- dom, which was practically a continuation of the Confer- ence at Leeds in October last, was held in St James's Hall, which was crowded to excess. Some 2,500 delegates had been appointed to attend the Conference, and there Were delegates present from all parts of the country. Mr John I Morley. M P, occupied the chair, and amongst those on the platform were—Sir John Lubbock, M P. Mr A Arnold, M P, Mr Firth, M P, Mr Jesse Collings, M P, Sir Wilfrid Lawson, MP, Mr Samuel Morley, MP, Mr A Picton, M P, Mr Broadhurst, M P, Mr F Buxton, M P, Mr Lyulph Stanley,l MP, Mr Osborne Morgan, M P, Mr Bradlaugh, M P,•• Canon Bulstrode, Mr Carvell Williams, the Rev J Guinneiss 1 Rogers, the Hon F Strutt, Mr Chatfeild Clark, Mr Joseph I Arch, and Mr Noble; and amongst the representatives ap- pointed by the various Liberal Associations, there were besides those mentioned above—Lord John Hervey, Right Hon Sir A Hobhouse, K C S I, Sir Arthur Bass Bart, M P, Sir R A Cunt iffe, Bart, MP. Sir M Wilson, Bart, 11M P, Sir Thomas Brasaey, KC B, MP, Sir Edward Barnes, Sir Charles T Bright, Sir A Fairbairn, M P, Sir J J Jenkins, M P, Sir John B Phear, Messrs W Agnew, M.P., Benjamin Armitage, M.P., G Armitstead, M.P., W C Borlase, M.P., T Barran, M.P., Jacob Bright, W E Briggs, M.P., A 13rogden,M.P., Col. A H Brown, . M.P., J Bryce, M.P., Thomas Bert. M.P., S C Buxton, M P , E H Carbutt,M.P., W S Caine. M.P., R K Causton, M.P., S Clark, M.P., T Dickson, M.P., Joseph Dodds, M.P., L L Dillwyn, M.P., Thomas Earp, M.P., W Fowler M.P., Tneodore Fry. M.P., H J Gladstone, M.P., T Rowley Hill, M.P., Isaac Holden M.P., James Howard. M.P., F A Inder- wick, M.P., A J Illingworth, M.P., Henry Labouchere, M.P., R Leake. M.P., ..Eneas J Mclntyre, Q C., M.P., J G McMinnies, M.P., Frederick T Mappin, M.P., Hugh Mason, M.P., T T Paget, M.P., George Palmer, M.P., Arthur Pease, M.P., J Dick Peddle, M.P., F Ponnlngton, M.P., W Powell, M.P., J O'Connor Power, M.P.' Joseph Polley, M.P., J E Thorold Rogers, M.P., P Rylands, M.P., C 8 Roundel!, M.P., H B Samuelson, M.P., Thomas Shaw, M.P., EI Shield, Q.C., M.P., J Slagg, M.P., W Summers, M.P., J H Tillett, M.P., H W West, M.P., W Woodall, M.P., Henry Wiggin M.P. Isaac Wilson, M.P., drc., dm.

Mr John Morley, M.P., made a vigorous speech, in which he contended that events had justified the action of the Leeds conference. He spoke of the extraordinary unanimity, on the question of extending the franchise, and said the real reason why the bill was rejected was because the Lords hated it. The result was, however, that no power on earth could new separate the question of m 11117ng the House of Commons from that or mending or ending the House of Lords, a sentiment which was received with tremendous en- thusiasm. Sir J Lubbock moved, and the Rev Canon Bill- strode seconded the following resolution which was carried: —That inasmuch as the House of Lords has abused its legiti- mate functions by rejecting the Franchise Bill introduced by the Government in accordance with the expressed will of the nation, and passed through the House of Commons by great majorities, and has refused electoral rights to two millions of men, this meeting condemns the action of the

div.head: EARLES TOWN.
div.p: EARLES TOWN.

UNJUST SCALES AT EIELESTOWN.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, James Barr, grocer, Legh- street, Earlestowa, was summoned for having an unjust pair of scales in his possession on the 10th ult —The defen- dant pleaded guilty.—Superintendent Jackson stated that he visited the defendant's shop, and found his flour scales six drachms against the purchaser. He explained that the scales had been repaired some time ago, and a piece 6f lead on the inside of the scales had gradually worn away. That was how he (Supt. Jackson) accounted for the scales being light —The defendant was fined 5s and costs.

EARLESTOWN GOOD TEMPLIMS.—The members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars held a meet- ing on Monday evening, when there was a good attendance. Brother George E. Warburton, W.C.T., presided. After the transaction of the lodge business arrangements were com- pleted for taking port in the great united temperance de- monstration this (Saturday) afternoon. Brother George Clarke then gave an account of his visit to the Douglas (Isle of Man) Lifeboat Lodge of Good TomoJars, and stated that their brethren across the water sent their fraternal greetings. A " night of harmony," according to the pro- gramme, was afterwards spent. SavEnal selections of music were nicely given, and all present apparently enjoyed them- selves.

FRIDLY NIGHT TRAFFIC IT EARLE3TOWN. - Before Messrs R Houghton, T J Gillespie, C Pilkington, and A C McCorquodale, at the Newton Town Hall on Saturday, James Lawrenson was summoned for obstructing the foot- path in Market-street on the night of Friday, the 18± ult. —P C Lloyed explained that on Friday nights when the market was held at Earlestown the traffic was very great, and there was considerable difficulty in keeping the streets and footpaths clear. On the night of the day named the defendant drove a horse and trap on the footpath, and al- lowed it to stand thereon for some minutes. When the horse and trap were standing the foot-passengers could not walk down the footpath, but had to go into the middle of the street.—The Bench imposed a fine of 5s and costs.

FONNATION OF AN ODDFELLOWS' LODGE.—On Saturday evening a branch of the National Independent Order of Odd- fellows was formally inaugurated in Earlestown, the open- ing ceremony being performed by a deputation from the lodges forming the Warrington district of the Order. The provincial grand master, Mr. James Smith, past provincial grand master, Mr. J. J. Hands, and the district secretary, Mr. J. Newton represented the district, while many brethren acted as delegates from the lodges. The opening ceremony took place at half-past six o'clock in the evening in the Lodge-room at the Ram's Head Hotel, the proceedings be- ing conducted by the past provincial grand roaster, Mr. J. J. Hands. After 31 members had been initiated, making a total of 41 members, the office bearers of the newly con- stituted lodge were duly nominated, elected, and installed. The proceedings during the evening were enlivened with songs, and concluded with votes of thanks to the officers and brethren who had taken part. NON-PAYMENT OF RATES.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, Ann North, formerly a boot and shoe dealer in Bridge-street, Earlestown, was summoned at the instance of Mr. Henry Houghton (rate collector) for non- payment of Commissioners' rates, amounting to ti 17s.— Mr. Riley appeared for the defendant, and stated that she was altogether without means and unable to pay them.— The Clerk (Mr. Buckton): It is for the collector to show her means.—Mr. Houghton said she had means when the sum- mons was issued, and he (witness) had not seen her place of basiness for four months. He did not know in what posi- tion she was at present —Mr. Riley said she was absolutely without means, and she would be able to satisfy the Bench of that fact—Mrs. North was then sworn, and stated that the rates were laid in respect to the shop which she formerly occupied in Earlestown. She had since been sold up bath at Earlestown and St. Helens by the Sheriff of Lancashire. She was perfectly willing to pay the rates when she was able—The Bench dismissed the summons in accordance with the defendant's promise. EARLESTOWN FOOTBALLERS AT DIVENITAX—Ohe Of the principal events at the Davenham Athletic Festival (near Northwich), on Saturday afternoon, was a football contest for teams of five players; the let prize being, value £3, and 2nd £3. The following eight clubs competed : Crewe Alexandra, Northwich Victoria, Earlestown, Port Vale, Crewe Brittania, Goldenhill, Davenham, and Hartford St. John's; the Earlestown club being represented by James Whalley (captain), A. W. Dagnall,James Duxbury, Robert Green, and James Ellison. In the first round of the compe- tition Earlestown were drawn against Davenham, and the tie was played in a heavy shower of rain, the time allowed being five minutes each way. At the commencement the Earlestownians rushed down the field and had a ridiculously easychance of scoring, but the leather was sent outside the posts. Davenham then scorel an easy goal, immediately after which Duxbury secured an equalising point, and ends were changed. In this half Davenham scored, two goals owing to rnis-kicks and bad play on the part of the Earles- tonians, and the latter were thus defeated by. three goals to one.

THR BURGLARY AT ASHTON.—At the Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice Day, James Holland Glover (24), engine-tenter, and John Toner (34), sailor, were found guilty of burglary at Ashton-in-Makerfield, on the 20th April, and were sentenced—Glover to three months' and Toner to 18 months imprisonment with hard labour. i EARLESTOWN PRIMITIVE METHODIST CIIAPEL.—The Sunday Schoolanniversary in connection with the Primitive Methodist cause in Earlestown was commemorated with special services and a service of song on Sunday. The ser- mons, morning and evening, were preached by the Rev. T. Whittaker, of Leeds, secretary to the Connexioual Sunday School Union, and there was a fairly good attendance at each service. In the afternoon the choir, under the leader- ship of Mr. W. Banton, gave a service of song, entitled " Messiah, or the Story of the Redemption by Christ," arranged and composed by the Rev. W. Wilkinson. Mr. W. Austin accompanied the singing on the harmonium, and the Rev. F. N. Shimmin, resident minister, gave the con- nective readings. The service was impressively rendered, some of the pieces being given in an exceedingly creditable manner. A collection was made at each gathering in aid of the school funds, and the sum of £l7 23. was realised, an advance of £1 133. over last year's anniversary nonce- Lions.

WELSH CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.—In aid of the funds of the Welsh Congregational Church, Houghton. Street, Earlestown, a miscellaneous concert was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, Earlestown, on Wednesday evening. There was not as large an attendance as was ex- pected, but the concert itself was above the average in point of merit, and the efforts of the artistes were highly appreci- ated. ,The artistes were Miss Bothwell, Miss Owen, Mrs Harris (of Earlestown), Miss A E Jones (Tyldesley), Mr W Jones (Birkenhead), Mr S J Edwards (Sutton), Messrs E Jones and W Edwards (Tyldesley), and Mr P Hastie (Earlestown). The selections by Miss Owen, Miss Both- well, and Mr Hardie were given in a remarkably fine manner, and they were individually recalled—an evidence of the appreciation of their services by the audience., The other singers also creditably fulfilled their parts, and were warmly applauded, some of the pieces being redemanded. Several glees by Mr E Jones and party pleased the hearers. The accompanists were Miss Birks, Miss Cameron, and Mr B Davies.

THREATENING A STEPMOTHER AT EARLESTOWN. —At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, John Day and George Day, brothers, were summoned for using threatening language to their stepmother, Eliz tbeth Day.—The defen- dants pleaded not guilty.—Mr. H. L. Riley, of St. Helens, appeared for the complainant, and stated that she lived in Legh-street, Earlestown, apart from the defendants, who seemed to aspire to have control over their father and step- mother. On the date named one of the children played truant, whereupon the father chastised the child. The two defendants afterwards came to the house, burst open both the front and back doors, and used violent language to their father and complainant. They threatened to kill them, and so alarmed were they that they had since had to get the protection of the police. Mrs. Day was seized by the throat, and yet bore the marks of the violence she was subjected to. He (Mr. Riley) thought that was a case in which substantial sureties ought to be inflicted.—Mrs. Day (complainant) was then called, and supported Mr. Riley's statement.—The de- fendants alleged that their father and stepmother ill-treated the young children, and that they simply stopped them from continuing the ill-treatment.—The two defendants were each bound over to keep the peace for six months, them- selves in £lO each, and another surety of £5. THE SERVICES AT ST. JOHN'S CHURCIE.—There is no- thing of special moment to report in connection with the state of affairs at St. John the Baptist Church, Earlestown. On Saturday the apparitor (Mr. Stacey) received a note from the vicar (the Rev. T. R. Matthews) to the effect that his services would be dispensed with, and that if he attended church on the following day he was not to perform any duty. On Sunday, however, Mr. Stacey occupied his amts. tomed place near the door, and apparently the vicar's note had not made any alteration in his action. Both in the morning and evening the only clergyman present was the vicar, who abstained from making any allusion to the dis- pute. At the forenoon service there were 12 adults and 40 children, brought from the Sunday school, present, in addi- tion to the Vicar, Miss Matthews, Master John Matthews, Mr. Pemberton (organist), and the half dozen girls who serve as a "choir." There were only about 20 persons pre- sent at the evening service. The petition to the Bishop of Liverpool praying for the removal of the Vicar (the Rev. T. R. Matthews) has not yet been sent into the proper quarter. It was shown on the Earlestown Market-place, on Friday evening, and many hundred persons—adults—signed it willingly. Up to yesterday it was estimated that nearly 1,000 persons had attached their signatures to the memo- rial.

AN EiniESTowN MAN Drusto OF £lo.—Daring the present week, it is stated, an Earlestown man has been " bamboozled" out of the sum of MO in an extraordinary manner. It appears that the individual in question has an inclination for sports, pastimes, and gatherings where there is A chance of making a "good thing " by a careful "backing "of runners and competitors, and credit must be given to him in this respect that he has generally been suc- cessful. Perhaps this will account for the dishonest and contemptible trick which has been played upon him. The Earlestonian has obtained his information from a certain gentleman in Liverpool, whose "tips," it is understood, have given satisfaction to the local " backer." A telegram pur- porting to come from Liverpool was banded to the Earles- tonian one day this week, and the latter thinking he had a "sweet thing on "put down £5 at Earlestown and travelled to Manchester to lay down another .£5. The "sure thing," however, did not come off, the result being that the Earles- town man lost his £lO. On the following day he met his Liverpool friend, and informed him of what he had done, but to his surprise the latter was told that no such telegram as he had received had been despatched. It was evident that someone had played a trick upon the Earlestown man, and it is hoped that the offender will meet with the punish- ment he deserves.

SUBMISSION ON AN ANTI•TAOCINATOB.--B efore Messrs. 11. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkitigton, and A. C. McCorquodale; at the Newton Town Hall. on Saturday, Joseph Emmett, of Ear!Mown. was summoned for failing to comply with an order of the magistrates to have his child vaccinated within 21 days.—On the case being called, the Clerk (Mr. Buckton) remarked that it had been adjourned from the last court, because the order made upon the defen- dant was not then produced. He asked Mrs. Emmett (who appeared on her husband's behalf) if the child had since been vaccinated.—Mrs. Emmett: Yes.—The Clerk: When? —Mrs. Emmett: Last Wednesday.—Mr. Alfred Cooper (vaccination oflicer): I celled and asked the doctor this morning and he said it had been vaccinated, and that it is going on all right. Mr. Sutton has determined to leave the matter in the hands of the Fiench. He then handed a note from Mr. Sutton to the Bench. The letter stated that hi would not ask for the costs of the previous summons, as the defendant had promised to have his child vaccinated. He (Mr. Sutton) so acted in the hope that no further opposition would be made to what was required by the law. He could not adopt a similar course in futare.—The Bench made an order for the defendant tp pay the costs of the summons (lb 6d), and on Mrs. Emmett promising to pay the costs the summons was dismissed. GABBEN ROBBERY AT EABLESTOWN.—AI the New- ton Town Hall, on Saturday, William Warburton (14 years of age) and Joseph Lennon (16) were summoned for stealing a quantity, of apples and pears, value 3d., from the garden of George Tunstall, Cress-lane, Earlestown.— P.C. Lloyd stated that a little after three o'clock on the morning of the 22nd ult, he was going along Cross-lane, when he saw Len- non going away from the direction of Tunstall's garden. On seeing him (witness) Lennon ran away down Hotel-street, and witness thought something was wrong. Having hail previous complaints about gardens being rubbed in that neighbourhood he waited about for a short time, and then saw Warburton coming out of TunstalPs garden. Warburton immediatelyi ran down Hotel-street, and witness followed. In a short time he heard the defandants talking in the back- yard of a dwelling-house. He also heard them eating apples and pears, and saw them with a quantity of apples; and pears in their possession. They were in the closet, and the , lads on seeing him (witness) dropped the apples and pears down the closet and closed the door, fastening it in the in- side. It took witness twenty minutes to gain admission, and then the lads wanted to be let off, Saying they would not do such a thing again.—George Tunatall then gave evidence to the effect that his garden had been robbed on several occasions, and after his attention had been called by the last witness he missed several apples and pears from the garden on the date named.—Mrs. Warburton, on being asked what the lads were doing out so early, said they both worked at the glass works' and had to be at their work at 1 o'clock In the morning. There was no work for them to do on the morning in question, and they ought to have returned home.—The Bench cautioned the defendants, and fined each of them ss. and costs.

GREAT FRANCHISE DEMONSTRATION AT EARLESTowx. —The Liberals of Earlestown and Newton. and the sur- rounding districts generally, will be glad to learn that ar- rangements have been made for the holding of a great open air demonstration at Earlestown to protest against the action of the House of Lords in rejecting the Franchise Bill. The matter is in the hands of the Joint Committee of the County and Borough Liberal Associations of South-West Lancashire who have decided to arrange for the demonstration to be held on Saturday afternoon, August 16th. Arrangements will be made whereby the great population of the districts shall march to the ground in procession or travel by rail. This will be the opening meeting of a " Franchise campaign" to be conducted throughout South-West Lancashire, and to the meeting at Earlestown Liverpool will send a large con- tingent; and the operations will wind up just before the Autumn Session with a great borough meeting, to be held at Hengler's Circus, Liverpool. This is a programme the unity and vigour of which will commend it to the local Liberal party. In connection with this agitation a meeting will be held at Southport, and on Monday evening a meeting was held to consider what steps should be taken for rend ring such demonstration as influential and as successful as pos. ble. After some conversation as to the date on which the proposed meeting should be held, Mr. C. H. Croxden Powell, secretary of the County Liberal Association, said it had been decided to hold a meeting on Saturday, the 16th pros., at Newton Common or at Earlestown, at which Messrs. Broad- hurst, M.P., Samuel Smith, M.P., and, in all probability, Sir Wilfrid Lawson would take part, together with several of the Lancashire members. In September a large demon- stration would be held at Liverpool, and in October an im- mense county demonstration would take place either at Southport cr at St. Helene. He explained how difficult it would be at the present time to set down any Cabinet Minis- ters, although Mr. Chamberlain had promised at the earliest possible moment to keep his engagement to visit Soutbport.

CONSUMPTION Ow GAS AT ELELEsTOWN AND NEWTON. —From the annual report of the receipts and expenditure of the Newton Improvement Commissioners, recently issued, it appears that the total amount of gas made at the works for the year ending December 31st last was 23,177,300 cubic feet. Of this quantity the was consumed hy meters during the year was 17,794,500 cubic feet; the estimated consump- tion by public lamps and works was 2,505,000 cubic feet and leakages and unaccountable was were estimated at 2,877,800 cubic feet.

Bu E RIBBON ARMY.—A meeting in connection with the Earlestewn Gospel Mission and Blue Ribbon Army was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earleatown, on Tuesday evening, when Mr. John Clarke presided. There was a large attendance. A reading was given by the Chairman, Mr. A. Walker gave a recitation, and selections of music were given by Mrs. Walker and the choir. Several melodies were very nicely sung. Mr. Birk s presided at the harmonium. At the close of the meeting several persons signed the pledge and a goodly number of blue ribbons were donned. REMOVAL OF THE NEWTON POST OFFICE. —lt need scarcely be remarked that the building in which the postal, telegraph, money order, and other Governmental busi- ness has hitherto been conducted at Newton, was inconve- nient and thoroughly unsuitable for the purposes for which it was utilised. The authorities have obtained the house known as "Rose Cottage," at the corner of Golborne-road, and this week they have, been engaged in removing the fit- tings, telegraph machinery, ST.c., from the old office to the new premises. The latter were opened for the transaction of business for the first time on Thursday. The rooms are eminently adapted for the object for which they will in future be used. EARLESTOWN CONSERVATIVES AND THIS HOUSE OF LORDS- -At a special meeting of the Newton Polling Dis'rict Conser- vative Club, Earlestown, on Friday evening, the following re- solution was unanimously passed, and also that a copy be sent to the Right Honourable the Marquis of Salisbury:—" That this meeting while desirous that the Household Franchise should be extended to the counties cordially agrees with the House of Lords in desiring that any measure should be ac- companied by a just redistribution of political power, and that the opinion of the country should be taken on the com- plete scheme. It was further resolved that the thanks of all the Conservatives were due to the House of Lords for their action to defeat the designs of the Government which had far its object the permanent retention of political power by the Radical party." The Right Honourable the Marquis of Salisbury writes in answer to the above. "That he was very much pleased to be assured that the Conservatives of the Newton Polling District fully concur in the action re- cently taken by the Conservative peers in regard to the Franchise Bill and will support them in the present junc- ture of affairs.

ATHLETIC SPORTS AT NEWTON. A gathering of a singular character was held at Newton on Saturday afternoon, when the Liverpool employee of the London and North-Western Railway Company held their twentieth annual athletic festival. The affair par- took more of the nature of an immense picnic; as the sports were net locally advertised or pla- carded ; the competitors and spectators hailing from Liverpool and the immediate neighbourhood. A con- siderable nnmber of persons from Earlestown and Newton watched the proceedines, however, which took place in the " Castle Hill" field, which had been kindly placed at the disposal of the committee by Colonel McCorqusdale, JP. The committee could hardly have chosen a more suitable or lovely spot for the sports, and all that was requisite to make the gathering a complete success was a fine afternoon. This, however, was not the case, as rain descended heavily during the whole of the day, rendering the task of the competitors by no means an easy one, and placing the spectators in a most uncomfortable position. Nothing daunted by the un- propitious state of the weather a large company numbering about 1,500, left Lime-street station in two special trains, the arrangements in connection with which were, (in the hands of Mr Cook), all that could be desired. An admirable course had been prepared in the "Castle Hill " field, just overlooking Newton lake, and the sports, con- sidering the diffculties to be encountered, were excellently managed by the following officials : Chairman, Mr Size ; treasurer, Mr Oinks ; referee, Mr H Metcalf; clerks of the course, Messrs James and Bilton; starters, Messrs Eastwood and Lythgoe ; judges, Messrs Humphreys and Proudman ; handicapper, Mr Craike ; stew- ards, Messrs Barratt, Bowman Burchall, W D Burrows, Chesworth, Cook, Davison, D J Davies, Dykes, Ferrand, Fowler, Hall, J Jacques, Kirby, Lambert, Leigh, Lofthouse, Lowton, Marsden, Mather Milton, Podmore, Pres' on, Red- head, Richards, Ridehalgh, Rylance, Sumner, H B Taylor, Wade, and Walker; honorary secretary, Mr T Williams. Among those present on the ground were Messrs T W Edwards and Brooks (E H Wood and Co), Watt (Carver and Co), Rattray (Cheshire Lines), J W Emmett (wagon department, Earlestown), Stones (stores department. St. Helens Junction), Hales (manager of the Shropshire Union Canal), C B Walker, W Nixon, and Ahearn. Tea was afterwards partaken of in the "Pied Bull " and "Legh Arms" Hotels, Mr. Hail taking the chair at the former and Mr. Size at the latter. Dancing was then freely indulged in at the Town Hall, to the strains of the band of the locomotive department, Edgehill (conductor, Mr. O'Cal- laghan). A DUBLIN SCHOONER SUNK.—A Lloyd's telegram from Belfast on Thursday says that the steamer Thomas Dry. dale, of Fleetwood, reports having run into and sunk the schooner Mary Ann, from Dublin, in the river Lagan, on Thursday morning. The crew was s tved.

Mr. Oakley, general manager of the Great Northern Rail- way, one of the partners in the Cheshire Lines, said the proposed deviations would be an undoubted disadvantage to those lines, inasmuch as they would raise the gradients, and every adverse gradient added something to the cost of work- ing. Mr. James Grierson, general manager of the Great Western Railway, said his company and the North-Western Company were joint owners of the Birkenhad and Cheshire junction line, and the proposed deviation would be an in- jury to the line. He entirely agreed with Mr. Findlay's evidence.

ROBERT BURNS —The statue of Robert Burns, which has been given by Mr. J. G. Crawford and placed on the Thames Embankment, was unveiled on Saturday by Lord Rosebery, who claimed that Burns was not merely Scotland's greatest poet but was worthy to be ranked amongst the greatest poets of the world. The statue is said to be rather dis- appointing. SHOCKING DEATH OF & CHILD.—Mrs. IliggiTS, the wife of a pianoforte dealer, was walking along Oldham-street, Manchester, on Monday, carrying in her arms her infant daughter, aged seven weeks when a ladder which had been used by a painter fell and struck the infant on its head, knocking it out of its mothers arms. The child died within a tow minutes.

THE PENISTONE RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—ANOTHER DEATH. —Mr. James N. Poole, one of the persons injured in the dis- astrous accident on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln- shire Railway, near Penistone, died on Tuesday at the Man- chester Royal Infirmary. Mr. Poole, who was 55 years of age, received a compound dislocation of the ankle and a fractured leg, and from the first little hope was entertained of his recovery. Re was the only one of the dozen injured who were taken to Manchester who never made any pro- gress. The adjourned inquest upon the persons who Ried iss Manchester from injuries received in the Penistone railway accident was concluded on Thuraday. Technical evidence as to the fracture of the crank axle of the engine was given by Mr. John Hopkinson, consulting engineer. The jury found a verdict of Accidental death,' and exonerated the railway company and officials. They recommended. however, that railway companies should address themselves to discovering some means of detecting flaws in crank axles. DE. * ORIGIN OF TEA-MEETINGS. Originally started as a medium of raising funds, they were conducted in a very different style from that so Widely adopted at the present day. Our friends knew of no such thing as a contract for the supply of the viands at so much a head, and they had no experience to teach them how many square yards of bread a pound of butter could be made to cover. Our wives and sweethearts then undertook the purveying and management of our tea- parties. Each took a table accommodating from 16 to 20 Persons, and presided in person. And, oh! what hearty. Jolly, comfortable gatherings we used to have in the old music hall in Blackett-street, amidst the abundance of sinaing hinnies, hot wigs, and spice loaf, served up in tempting display, tea of the finest flavour served in the best china from the most elegant of teapots, accompanied with the brightest of spoons, the thickest of cream, and the blandest of smiles !—Tea and Tea-Drinking. Arthur Rea*.

div.head: ULUTING DEATH.
div.p: ULUTING DEATH.

Of the difficulties and dangers encountered by this gallant officer (Captain Butler), we know little, but th, following incident will show that they deserve the epithet Df hair-breadth. Early on the day following his arrival at a village beyond Kuchan' the Persians ordered a body of sixty soldiers into the fort, where they deprived Captain Butler and his companion of their arms and luggage; while on the morning following this, the governor of the place, with some forty men, took them to a spot in the glen, and, after separating them, ordered Captain Butler to dismount, as he was about to be shot. With this request he refused to comply, adding that, if he were to be shot, he would give the signal to fire by taking off his hat. The governor thereupon cocked and presented his gun, but he put it down in astonishment when the captain took off his hat, and in admiration of his courage asked him to be their chief. The governor was subsequently flogged and dismissed from his post. Reconnoitring Central Asia. By Charles Marvin.

div.head: LIFE OF THE PIKE.
div.p: LIFE OF THE PIKE.

Consider the conditions under which the jack exists. His limits are the brook, the ponds it feeds, and the ditches that enter it. He can only move a short distance up the stream because there is a high hatch; rspr can he go far down because of a mill; if he could, the conditions would be much the same; but, as a matter of fact,, the space he has at his command is not much. The running water, the green flags, the lesser fishes, the water-rats, the horses and cattle on the bank, these are about all the things he is likely to be interested in. Of the one only the water, the lesser fishes, the flags, and the bottom or sides of the brook, are actually in his touch and complete understand- ing. As he is unable to live out of the water, the horse on the bank in whose very shadow he sometimes lies might be a mile away for aught it concerns him. Night and day he knows, the cool night and the sunbeams in which he basks; but he has no way of ascertaining the nature of anything outside the water. Centuries spent in such conditions could add but little to his experience.— The Life of the Fields. By Richard Jeferies.

div.head: HOW STEEL WAS FIRST MADE.
div.p: HOW STEEL WAS FIRST MADE.

The primitive apparatus (used in the first experiment which ended in the production of steel) being ready, the engine was made to force streams of air under high pressure through the bottom of the vessel, which was lined with fire-clay, and the stoker was told to pour the metal, when it was sufficiently melted, in at the top of it. A cast-iron plate—one of those lids which commonly cover the coal-holes in the pavement—was hung over the con- verter; and all being got ready, the stoker in some be- wilderment poured in the metal. Instantly out came a volcanic eruption of such dazzling coruscations as had never been seen before. The dangling potlid dissolved in the gleaming volume of flame, and the chain by which it hung grew red and then white, as the various stages of the process were unfolded to the wondering spectators. The air-cock to regulate the blast was beside the con- verting vessel, and no one dared to go near it, much less to deliberately shut it. In this dilemma, however, they were soon relieved by finding that the process of decar- bonisation, or combustion, had expended all its fury ; and, most wonderful of all, the result was steel.— 2/se Creators of the Age of Iron. By W. 2'. Jeans.

div.head: CREMATION BY MK VIKINGS.
div.p: CREMATION BY MK VIKINGS.

The only literary evidence we possess in regard to them is the strange narrative by Ahmed Ibn-Fozlan, an eye. witness of the ceremonies attending the incremation oz the dead body of a Northern chief: The scene is on the banks of the Volga, and the date is towards the close of the Viking time. The narrator tells us that there was a temporary interment till all the preparations were made, and that a female slave who had elected to die with her master was given in charge of an old hag, who, as mistress of the ceremonies, was significantly styled the "angel of the dead," and the dead man's ship was hauled up on the strand and prepared to be his funeral pile; that when all was ready the corpse was taken out of its temporary grave, arranged in fur-mounted and gold-embroidered garments, and laid in state on the deck, where a banquet was spread for him; that his weapons were placed refitly to his hand, and two horses, two oxen, his dog, and two fowls were hewn in pieces with swords and cast into the ship; that the woman who was to die, after taking leave of her friends, was first drugged with strong drink, and then brutally slaughtered with a big knife by the "angel of the dead," while two men pulled the ends of a cord round her neck and the crowd beat upon their shields to drown her shrieks; that she was then laid beside her dead lord and the pile fired by his nearest relative, and after it had burned out a great mound was raised over the ashes.— Scotland in Pagan Times—The Iron Age. By J. Anderson.

div.head: FIELD OF THE .CLOTH OF GOLD.
div.p: THE FIELD OF THE .CLOTH OF GOLD.

The palace was an exact square of 328 feet. It was Pierced on every side with oriel windows and clerestories curiously glazed, the mullions and posts of which were overlaid with gold. An embattled gate ornamented on both sides with statues representing men in various atti- tudes of war, and flanked by an embattled tower, guarded the entrance. From this gate to the entrance of the Palace arose in long ascent a sloping dais or hall-pace, along which were grouped "images of sore and terrible countenances," in armour of argentine or bright metal. Outside the palace gate, on the green sward, stood a gilt fountain, of antique workmanship, with a statue of Bacchus " birlyng the wine." Three runlets, fed by secret conduits hid beneath the earth, spouted claret, by-pocras, and water, into as many silver cups, to quench the thirst of all corners. On the opposite side was a pillar wreathed with gold, and supported by four gilt lions; and on the top stood an image of blind ' Cupid, armed with bow and arrows. The gate itself, built in massive style, was pierced with loop-holes. Its windows and recesses were filled with images of Hercules, Alex- ander, and other ancient worthies, richly gilt and painted, In long array in the plain beyond, 2,800 tents stretched their white canvas before the eyes of the spectator, gay with the pennons, badges, and devices of the various oc- cupants; whilst miscellaneous followers, in tents of thousands, attracted by profit or the novelty of the scene, camped on the grass and filled the surrounding slopes, in spite of the severity of provost marshal and reiterated threats of mutilation and chastisement. Multitudes from the French frontiers, or the populous cities of Flanders, indifferent to the political significance of the scene, swarmed from their dingy homes to gaze on kings, queens, knights, and ladies dressed in their utmost splendour. Beggars, itinerant minstrels, vendors of provisions and small luxuries, mixed with waggoners, ploughmen, labourers, and the motley troop of camp followers, crowded around, or stretched themselves beneath the summer's sun on bundles of straw and grass, in drunken idleness. No better lodging awaited many a gay knight and lady who had travelled far to be present at the spectacle, and were obliged to content themselves With such open-air accommodation. Backwards and fm, wards surged the excited and unwieldy crowd as (ilia) hour brought its fresh contigent of curiosity or criticism, in the shape of some new-comer conspicuous for his fan% tastic bearing or the quaint fashion of his armour. Each new candidate for the love and honour of the ladies, for popular applause, or less noble objects, was greeted with ehouts and acclamations as he succeeded in distinguishing himself from the throng by the strangeness or splendour of his appointments. Christendom had never witnessed such a scene.—The Reign of Henry VIII. from his Acces- sion to the Death of Wolsey. Reviewed and Illustrated from Original Documents. By the late J. S. Brewer, M.A.
