I " Does your baby kick when you try to put it to sleep ? " asked one young married man of another. "No " was the reply ; " but I do when I am asked to put it to sleep." In a Minnesota breach of promise suit a broken-down ; front gate was brought into court, and when the contending parties saw it they looked at each other and both blushed painfully. AN ADVERTISEMENT.—A young widow, in erecting a monument to the " dear departed,' cleverly availed herself of the opportunity to inscribe upon the tomb, "Sacred to the memory of Mathasin Beznchet, who departed this life aged sixty-eight years, regretting the necessity of parting from the most charming and best of women "—herself. Wendell Phillips was waiting once or the train at Essex Junction, Vermont, where passengers at times have to exer- cise great patience. He saw a graveyard not far from the village, near the depot, and very fall. He inquired the reason, and a Green Mountaineer calmly informed him that it was used to bury passengers in who died while waiting for the train! Ile THE MIDST OF DANGER, SAFETY.—" Above] all, sir," said a worldly father to his son, who was about to enter society, "avoid flirtations; but, if you must flirt or fall in love, sir, be sure that it is with a pretty woman. It is always safer." " Why ?" asked the son. "Because some other fellow will be sure to be attracted, and cut you out before any harm has been done." MANAGERIAL OVERSIGHT.—SOMe years ago, at one of the Dublin theatres, one of the tragedies of Sophocles was put on the stage. At the close of the performance the " gods" called loudly for the author, whereupon the manager explained that, as the author had been dead more than two thousand years, he could not very well appear. Nothing disconcerted, a very small gallery-boy called out, "Then let's have his mummy !" RESULT OF A LEARNED JUDGE'S HAVING CHILDREN.— "Eat your bread, Charles—do not fling it away," said a learned and good judge to one of his family the other day, adding, " for who knows, in the vicissitudes of this life, if you may not some day want it ? " The old gentleman had to cough, look learned, and go away when his youngest an- swered, more logically than his parent, "If I eat it, how can I have it when I want it? " WANTED A HAT.—" I want a Henry Two Eyes hat," said she. The assistant, altogether at fault, replied: "If you will excuse me a moment I will see if we have it in stock," and went away to see if anybody could tell her the shape nearest to a Henry Two Eyes hat. It was as good as a Christmas riddle, and wanted as much puzzling over as a society paper acrostic, but at last they made it out that what was wanted was a Henri IL Looxisea AHEAD. —First Chicago lady: "Speaking of wedding-cake reminds me that an aunt of mine has a piece of hers. It is forty years old." Second Chicago lady. " Only a piece How careless! I have the whole of mine I did not allow it to be cut." First Chicago lady: " But what are you saving it for ?" Second Chicago lady: "You know, wedding-cakes are a good deal of trouble to make, and I thought I might need mine again some time. One never can tell what may happen." The bullying manner of the German students is prover- bial, as is also their mania for duelling. It was at Heidel- berg that a quietcitizen leaving the cars said to a swaggering student, "Sir, you are crowding me! Keep back, sir !" The student turned fiercely, and said, in a loud tone, "Do you not like it? Well, sir, lam at your service whenever you please !" "Oh, thank you!" said the traveller. "Your offer is very kind, and you may carry my valise to the hotel for me." The student fled amidst shouts of laughter. A SACRIFICING HACEMAN.—A hackman yesterday walked into a hotel and up to a guest who was reading a paper, and holding out a silver dollar on his palm he said: "When I drove you up here this morning you made a mistake, and gave me half a dollar too much. Here is your dollar. I want only my regular fee" The man took the coin and handed out a fiftrcent piece without speaking a word. His conduct nettled another guest, who followed the hackman out and remarked: "My man, that was an honest action on your part." " Well. yes, but you see the dollar he gave me was a base counterfeit!" Two yonng ladies of literary tastes were discussing their reading, when one of them remarked: "I have been engaged with a delightful work for a week past." " Indeed ! 51 hat is it ?" "Anthony Trollope's Autobiography." "Who is the author ?" "Really, I don't know! I have looked over the title-page and through the preface; but I can't find any re- ference to the author at all. Whoever it is is a charming writer, and seems to have known the novelist very intima- tely." "I'll get it and read it; but it is too provoking, isn't it, that so many delightful authors of late are writing anonymously ?" PARTING—Turner, Prout, and Varley were on a sketching tour in Devonshire. They had to cross a ferry, the passage charge for which was twopence. Varley did not happen to have any change, and borrowed the money from Turner— advanced reluctantly. The next morning Varley and Prout took the Exeter coach for London, leaving Turner behind. ' But, to their surprised gratification, although the hour was daybreak and the morning bleak and dark, they saw Turner at the coach-office waiting to see them off. Varley acknow- ledged the compliment and thanked him. "No," said Turner, "it isn't that; hut you forgot to give me back the twopente I lent you yesterday." How IT CAME ABOUT.—Mrs Blank: nere is a funny paragraph which says that a married man can be distin- guished by the way in which he carries an umbrella over his wife, carefully shielding himself and leaving her ex- posed to the drippings.—Mr. Blank: It is not true, though. —Mrs. Blank: No, it is not. You never do it. You were a good deal more awkward at carrying an umbrella over me before we were married than you have been since.—Mr Blank: Ah !—Mrs. Blank: Yes; I had several bonnets and two dresses ruined by the drippings in those days. But you have become ever so much more careful—oh ever so much more careful !—Mr. Blank: Yes, indeed. I have to pay for your things now. A good story is told in Forest and Stream of a man in Kansas who found an Indian skull while out hunting one day. There had been a war between the Indians and the whites, and he thought it would be a pity merely to say in a prosaic manner that he had found the skull. His atten- dant too considered that, if he told the truth about the skull when questioned, the " tenderfeet," as they call new-corners, would seem disappointed ; so he used to romance a little. One morning be related to a lone-land seeker a most blood- chilling account of how he shot the Indian in the stomach and cut off his gory scalp with his own bowie knife. The next day another man questioned him, and he forgot that Number One, who was present, had ever heard anything about the skull; so he killed the Indian over again in quite a different fashion for Number Two, and afterwards cut off his head with an axe. "Hold on!" said Number One. "You told me yesterday that you shot him in the stomach with a rifle and scalped him." " Yes ; but that was when I killed him another time !" remarked Jim, looking Number One mildly in the face. A CROP.—An old Londoner was some years ago a visitor in Oxfordshire at a time of terrible drought, when the gravest of agricultural distress was imminent. At length the welcome rain came—a regular deluge of it—on market. day too. He had been all that day talking with farmers and dining with farmers, wining with farmers and whiskey- tag with farmers, till he ontfarmered any farmer of them all in his joy at the change in the weather. Almost fiercely he refused the loan of an umbrella to shelter him in his transit from the "White Horse," where the last drink had taken place, to the "Red Lion," where his trap was put up. While going over this course he caught sight of a man crouching in a doorway. " VVh'ar' you doing there ?" thundered the citizen, in a voice of authority. "Trying to keep out of the rain. What d'you suppose ?" answered the man. "What !" shouted the Threadneedle citizen, "Have you so little patriotism? Don't you know this rain is worth a thou- sand guineas a second to the country? Come out and let it beat upon you, as I do. Come out and try to grow above yourself. Come out and be a crop !" In a certain European country that it is not necessary to name, where military glory is regarded by the sovereign as the noblest of all regal ambitions, there took place a series of army manoeuvres culminating in a simulated battle, in which his majesty was of course to command the victorious forces. The battle was fought, the day was lost and won ; but the conquering general galloped, pale and trembling, from the dreadful field, and never drew bridle till he reached his home, where his agonised looks struck terror into the mind of sympathetic wife. 'ln Heaven's name," she cried, "what is the matter ?" "I am a lost man !" he groaned, flinging himself into a chair and hiding his face in despair. "What has happened ?" "We were in the midst of the sham fight." he gasped rather than replied. "The king was —" his by failed hi, wife

div.p: THE EXAMINER. bA U RDAY, AUGUST 2, 1884.

AMERICAN FREE TRADERS AND PROTECTIONISTS. Four years have wrought a change in American tastes, and made an impression on its institutions. These changes may not have been perceptible to frequent visitors, but they are not the less striking to those whose visits, like angels, are " few and far between." The Amercan industries have been gradually sinking. Wages have fallen, and are still falling; and those of the operative classes who were earning wages that in England would be dignified by the name of salaries, now find it a difficulty to make both ends meet. Strikes have been rife,i but with the result they almost invariably have and what is, or has been, the cause of these changes? The political weather-cock, moving gratingly on its work-worn centre, is beginning to point to a quarter hitherto indicated by itstail, and while this change is going on working people continue to drop out of employment. In one of the mills I have visited two-thirds of the hands are at rest, not in conse- quence of a striae, but through the depression of trade. A large iron works employs only about a fourth of its usual complement of hands. Is protection the cause of all this? is being asked. The people—l mean the working people— are beginning to think so. A little more grating of the weather-cock and we may hope to see it pointing towards the horizon of Free Trade. Will other countries follow the lead of England? In a discussion I heard last evening be- twixt a Free Trader and a Protectionist, the former a Tory and the latter a Radical—most incongruous to me—this was the way in which one of the disputants pat his case :—" I have got something to sell; so has Mr. Brierley. I am an American, on my own sod. Mr. Brierley is a Britisher, coming all the way from a small patch of country, and hav- ing to pay his freight. He offers for sale a piece of cloth that would shame mine into fits. But I've got to beat him. You come between us and say, 'Here, Britisher, it's all very well for you to take our corn free, because you want it. But we ain't going to take your manufactures free, because we can manufacture for ourselves." "Just my argument," said the other. "Is it, is it ?" said the Free Trader. "What I have always stood by." "Oh, and the tax is to pay off the war debt, is it ?'; "Put on for the very purpose." "Glad to hear you say so. Then how was it you went to England last fall, to buy three suits of clothes, and said it paid you to do it, you patriotic old cuss? You merchants can buy goods from the foreigners, and have them invoiced at half the price, that you can evade the pay- ment of half the duty. It is the working man who has to suffer. He has to pay a big price for a pair of pants that a monkey would be ashamed to wear. We've got to pay through the nose for most everything. Only sech as you get the benefit of protection." If this be true it is no wonder that people are beginning to clamour for Free Trade. I enclose a circular I received this morning, which in a measure endorsed what I have stated. The matter will speak for itself. Until to-day I had no idea that such society as the circular represents had an existence : ADDRESS OF THE MASSACHUSETTS TARIFF REFORM LEAGUE. To the People of Massachusetts More than twenty years ago, to meet the exigencies of the great civil war, Congress imposed a tariff of duties on im- ports higher than this country had ever before known, and higher than any civilised nation now maintains. The pro- tective features of the war tariff have been kept in force without essential changes up to the present time. The act of last year, framed by the representatives of protected in- dustries, and enacted by Congress for the purpose of evading the demand for tariff reform has given no relief. So far from materially reducing duties, it has in some cases in- creased them. The tariff has diverted labour and capital from those industries in which they produce the greatest results. In many branches of manufacture we lead the world; in agri- culture we have an incomparably rich field. The industries which can be carried on to the best advantage in this coun- try are checked, and are in many cases shut out from foreign markets, in order that others less profitable may be artifically stimulated. The war tariff, no longer required for purposes of revenue, has laid heavy burdens on the consumers by raising the prices not only of the important articles taxed, but also of a great mass of similar articles which are made at home. The higher prices of the latter give no revenue to the Govern- ment. They simply add permanently or temporarily to the profits of the producers. Where this profits have been per- manent, as they have been in many cases of monopoly, they merely represent a contribution taken by the Government out of the pockets of one class and put into the pockets of another class. More often the high profits are only tempo- rary. They give an unhealthy stimulus to the industries assisted, and finally result in over-production, stagnation of trade, failures among employers, distress among the employed. They burden consumers, and evendually benefit nobody. The defenders of our present extravagant system of pro- tection assert that it brings about the general high rate of wages in this country. But it is absurd to suppose that taxes on the necessaries of life and on the instruments of production cause high wages. As a fact, wages are higher in this country in the industries not affected by Protection, in agriculture, the mechanic trades, and in the self-supporting ' manufactures. They are lowest in the protected industries, and wretchedly low in many of these. As consumers, the labouring classes are the chief sufferers from the existing , taxes. It is they who bear the heavy burdens on articles of universal consumption. The high tariff has kept down the international commerce of the country. It is avowedly intended to check imports and obstruct foreign trade. Exports and imports being de- pendent of each other, in checking the latter we necessarily cut down the former. We cannot sell unless we buy. The result of our present policy is seen in the fact that our inter- ' national commerce cannot now compare with that of other nations. For ten years ending in 1880, the combined im- ports and exports of England were annually for each inhabi- tant, 95 dollars; of France, 39 dollars; of Germany, 34 dollars, 40c.: of the United States, 22 dollars 80c. The com- merce of Germany, with a smaller population than the United States, was, during this decade, almost 50 per cent. greater than our own. That of France, also with a smaller population, was nearly 40 per cent. greater. Although unable to prevent entirely the growth of our commerce, the tariff has clearly deprived us of the great expansion which more liberal laws would have secured. Not content with giving protection to the finished pro- ducts of manufacture, the tariff raises the prices of most of the raw materials upon which manufactures depend. In order to maintain our artificial policy, its supporters are obliged to bring all classes of producers within its scope. Wool-growers and the producers of iron mines are brought within the protective system. Every other industrial nation, whatever its general policy may be, pecognises the expediency of allowing free trade in raw materials. We, however, tax iron ore, pig-iron, lead, copper, wool, coal, lumber, hemp, flax, jute, dye-stuffs, and many other raw materials, we tax many finished products which are essen- tial to any success in domestic industry. These taxes fetter the very industries which the protective policy is chiefly intended to benefit. Growing whenever a profit is made at any stage of manufacture, they finally fall on the consumer with increased force. They serve no possible useful purpose, and should be entirely abolished at the earliest practicable moment. Our duties on imports, arranged" not for the purpose of raising revenue, but solely with reference to protection, pour annually into the treasury at least 100,000,000 dols, more than is needed for any legitimate public purpose. This im- mense surplus is a temptation to a wasteful and extrava- gant spending of the public money. It 'is demoralizing alike to legislators and to those who believe themselves to have any title to Government aid. It should be cut down shortly and sharply. It has been proposed in the interests of protection to reduce the revenue by abolishing the inter- nal taxes on spirits, beer, and tobacco. These taxes are re- cognised rued imposed as fit and proper by every civilised Government. They have the advantage of taking nothing from taxpayers over and above what they yield to the pub- lic treasury. It would be monstrous to abolish or reduce any of these while retaining the protective taxes which affect the necessaries of life, impose a useless burden on consumers, and fetter the trade and industry of the country. The League is not formed for the purpose of abolishing at once all protective duties without giving time for indus- tries which have been artifically stimulated to adjust them- selves to new and better conditions. But protection should no longer be maintained at the extravagant point where it now stands. The present extreme tariff, with duties rang- ing from forty to one hundred per cent. and more, is inde- fensible, and the sooner it is reduced to a reasonable basis the better. A great reduction of duties, if wisely made, can be borne by the industries which are now protected. The League believes that it is time that the great abuses of our tariff system should be put an end to; that war taxes' after twenty years of profound peace, should be reduced ; that the revenue should be brought down to the sum required for the legimate expenses of the Government; that the profits of individuals at the expense of the public should be cut off; and that this country should be enabled, to take its proper share of the trade and commerce of the world. The special industries which have combined together for the purpose of resisting any substantial charges in the tariff have succeeded, by perfect organisation and constant pres- sure, in creating a false impression at Washington as to the opinions of the people upon this question. This impression can only be corrected by organised and well-directed action on the part of those who believe that the present policy is unsound, and are willing to enforce their opinions, if need be, at the polls. The League invites all persons who sym- pathise with its objects to become members, and to aid actively in the work of local organisation. The secretary can be seen at his office, 40, State-street, Room 52, Boston, and letters addressed to him will receive prompt attention. —By order of the Executive Committee JOSIAH Committee, &MOAT. Putting tariffs away as old-fashioned things only fit to gather dust in a political lumber-room, let us look at the fresher life of America. "You have grown powerful under tariffs." says my Yankee friend. "We have grown more powerful without them," I reply. "We were bound to be a powerful nation under any circumstances ; and so are you. Bat it is much more pleasant to work with your limbs free than it is when shackled. We have thrown away the irons; and you will follow the example. Then won't the stupid , worn-out old country knock the stuffing out of you ?" This bit of bunkum so tickled my friend that I believe he was in a mind just then to "club " all protective ditties on the head; ; and clear for a fair race with other countres. The idea that a ; young man,With energies unimpaired, should seek an advan- P tage over his father, and handicap the old man so as to keep him I in the rear, was not flattering to his abilities; and he " squir- I t med" under the infliction. "You are right, stranger," he ; I admitted, when he had swallowed the pill. "And it reminds me of a young feller who could make holes into the best man

of his own age and weight. But he got on to a wiry old gineral old enough to be his dad, and he was bound to lick him. He didn't want to; but the ancient piece of hickory wouldn't have his nay; so they fought—not much. The man that was handicapped with years just got his swing, and young America had to take a mouthful of dust. It git out that the old one was the young one's father; and he was just proud that no one could taae him out of his boots only the man that married his mother. If ever America loses the belt and cups' the old country's bound to git them. Let us wash our necks, stranger. If you're not going home with the tourists you'll think better of this country before you leave. But I know you think well of the people,—just some of them, the gold. You'll find the nickel in all countries." This ended controversial matters, and we got upon plea- santer things, in which I knew I would have no chance of being foremost, and could draw out the Yankee "right through his pants." "I read so much about American storms that I would like to see one," I remarked. " Yaas, through a fifteen inch telescope, I guess, one that you could shove yer head into," he replied. "You wouldn't like to be within fishing distance of it. Why, siree I have known a cyclone pass over a town of some five hundred in- habitants, and just take every building under the stoop, and cut it like a paper-knife, then carry the shingles right out for miles, and fix 'em thar, like a deserted city, with nothing left in it only an old parrot in its cage; and when the bird got settled, and looked around, it shouted—' Oh, •Nurse of Mose 3 aint this a big move ? " "What became of the inhabitants ?" "No one left alive to make a newspaper paragraph."

" How did you escape?" "By a near shave. The wind just swept in front of me, and took away a button from my vest. I haven't got another fixed in its place, you gee. If I'd been another inch to the fore, I guess the tripe business would have flourished."
I had got my friend "on his ear," and I justly expected quite a length of extravagant bounce. To plant the spurs in his flanks I hinted that I would like to see an American blizzard.

"You take a blizzard to be a kinder animal, I guess," he said, with a smile that said he had got me. "You git cro- codiles, and 'gators down in Florida; but they aint got any blizzards thar. The blizzard, yer see, is a winged bird; and you just get to feel the flap of them wings, and if you don't lose every ounce of your flesh, and leave your bones for antiquarians to speculate on, I'm a coon of rare parts." "I was not aware that it was a bird," I confessed. "Just what it is, siree. It don't crawl nor swim ; but it sweeps around for miles; and by the tree that choked Absa- lom, nothing's bound to live. It's just a snow that's got to the depth of a corn stick ; and a cyclone comes, tosses the whole mass within half a mile of where it came from, till it's like a sea of frozen milk. Then the stars have to look out. If they were to be caught in one of them blizzards, the firmament would be swept as clean of light as Barnum's show would be by the howl of a nor' wester. It would, stranger. For three or four days after the country is dange- rous from the showers of cart-wheels, ploughs, and the skeletons of cattle. You aint anything like that in the old country, I guess."—From " Great Britain over the Sea," by BEN BRUMLEY.

ANTI-VACCINATION. Sir,—l am somewhat at a loss to understand what Mr. .J. C. Sdtton, the Warrington Board of Guardians clerk, means wnen he uses the word "moderation." He is reported as saying at the Guardians' meeting, held on the 23r4 ultimo, "that in endeavouring to enforce the law in the Board's be- half in that district be wished to move with moderation and do the duty in as fair and as moderate a spirit as possible" in dealing with the defaulters under the Vaccination Acts. Perhaps the word " moderation " means something differ- ent now to what it did when I west to school. If no, I should be glad if (fort am rather fond of etymology) if he would kindly conde.scend to throw a little light on the word at the neat Board's meeting, and give us the interpre- tation of same as it stands in his own vocabulary. Mr. Sutton's moderation reminds me very much of the moderation of the dark ages, when priestcraft reigned supreme, when the latter gentleman's commodity was exerciaed in the shape of "either you most believe as / do or else go to the stake." Perhaps, Mr. Editor, some of your -readers will feel a little startled and think that I am going to an extreme; but I will endeavour to explain the parellel- ism of the metaphor. We as anti-vaccinators can by bowing to the "goddess Vaccinia " and obeying the dogmas of medical priestcraftiam, escspe the Nine and penalties im- posed by the law en defaulters, whicn are tines that may be anything according to the discretion of the magistrates, from a farthing without costs to 20s with costs. Well, to get to the point. Mr. Sutton had a number of us up before the magistrates. With see part the most that could he done was to Make an order for us to have the children vaccinated within a certain time, and on the other part impose a penalty of 203 and costs. At this stage of the proceedings Mr. J. C. Sutton step 3 in with his moderation and asks the magistrates sot to be lenient but to impose the full penalty in each case. If any of your readers can reconcile this kind of be- haviour with the above quotation I will alter my opinion of the word rantioned.—Y ours, .tc PRO BONO PUBLICO.

MR. HOWES V. MR. BOTTOMLEY. Sir —t have just had brought under my notice Mr Bottomley's letter of the Bth of July, in which he says:— "The acceptance of the challenge to debate the question, 'ls the policy of the Beaconsfield or Gladstone Government most likely to strengthen our position at home or abroad?' I have never beard of until now, and certainly it has not yet appeared in The Teesdale Mercury." And then in a foot note he says :—•• Your readers will see the character of Mr Howes in writing to a paper that I should never have seen I had it net been for the kindness of Mr .Westbrook." Now, sir, this letter of Mr Bottomley's is dated July Bth. On July 3rd I sent the enclosed letter to The Teesdale Mercury, and I have since received no reply from the Conservatives there. What will Mr Bottomley's party think of him after thie 2—Yours, Sec., J. HOWES. rThe letter referred to as enclose I is of considerable length, and deals for the most part with what has taken place in other towns. We give the portion teaching on the distinct challenge which Mr Bottomley so impudently shirks. It is as fellows :—En. Ex.] It le a good thing to have got Mr Rottomley, at last, to screw his courage up to a defence of Toryism. Your readers Will remember that all the delay has been caused by Mr B's backwardness in reference to this one point. He now, for the first time, says that he is willing to discuss the question of Whether the Beaconsfield or Gladstone Administration I is the one best calculated to strengthen the position of Eng- land at home and abroad.' This challenge lat once accept. 1 All I want is an opportunity of comparing the past Govern- ment with the present, and I hive no fear of the result. I shall new leave the local committees to make the neeessary arrangements. As to the number of nights Over which the debate shall extend, that I shall love to my opponents. They may also decide whether Mr 13. or I shall lead off each evening. All: ask is that they will inform me of the dates they prefer as soon as possible, 80 that I may accommodate them if possible. In reply to my statement in my last letter about Mr B's failing to find an association to put him forwsrd, he says, 'ln accepting a challenge Jam exactly in the same position as my opponent, and we both rely on our party accepting us as their representative.' I reply, with this difference, via., that my party is at all times welling to put me forward to represent them, while Mr B.'s party is not willing to do the same in his case. Mr B. re- fers to Littleborough and Oldham as places where he was put forward by his party. I reply, yes; and at those places I met him in debate, and I again repeat that he cannot men- tion a single place where either he or any other Tory lec- turer has been put forward by the local Conservative Asmo- elation, without my being willing and ready to meet such Tory champion on the platform."

div.head: PENKETH PECULIARITIES.
div.p: PENKETH PECULIARITIES.

Sir,—As you are aware we had a meeting here on Monday night in support of the Government, and to protest against the recent action of the House of Lords. At that meeting we were favoured by the presence of a real live Tory working-man, who proposed an amendment to the resolu- tion condemnatory of the Lords. This might have been an idiosyncrasy; but this person actually found another odd-minded man to second him in his attempt to restrict the liberties of his fellows. New, Sir, these good folk, and the few sympathisers they found in the audience, can surely not have seen the logical consequences of their contentions These people were householders without votes, using the second-hand arguments which bard filtered down to them from from my lord Salisbury and his folleving in the House of Lords. Now their lordships' opposition to any extension of the Franchise is natural and consist- ent enough, as also is their seizing at the redistribution straw to prevent their being swamped by the flood of new electors. The lords aversion to thie measure is, I re- peat, natural and consistent. They see the all-but despotic power so long hell by them, gradually, but surely, fading away before the advancing ferns of a solid and substantial democracy? They are sufficiently far-toeing to forges their doom. Be the change for good or evil, our present here- ditary, irresponsible House of Lords has surely out-run its lease. The principle of patrician government is quite dead in England, and the feeble remnant of the practise will fade before the younger and more life-like principle and praetise of popular eelf-government. This the lords see and fully appreciate. They are concerned to see the power they have "Told so long, and latterly so badly used, surely, if slowly, slipping from their grasp. This was -natural, and might have been foreseen and fore- told ; but that an unenf7anchised householder—one of the very class sought to be benefited by this measure of political jus,Lice—should deliberately attempt to frustrate the boon thug offered to his class by the Ile' of stale arguments bor- rowed from his contemners and would-be oppressors is indeed strange. This anomaly is only explicable upan the assumption that the extreme modesty of the in- dividual led him to douot the fitness of himself and his class tr, receive and to exercise that right and privilege of citizenship—the franchise; a diffidence perhaps rightly felt by the individual, but utterly unwarranted when applied by him to his ease. In other words, it is open to any man to proclaim himself satiefied with the degrading position of being, politically-, a willing slave ; of being denied (by an arrogant and privileged class, who are themselves in the en- joyment of a double representation. in the Lords by them- selves and in the Commons by their relatives and connec- tions) the fall privilege of citizenship. But let this man speak for himself; he has no right to assume that his fel- lows have the same political apathy, nor ought he to attempt to rivet upon them the chains of politicl bondage. If this man revels in the Slough of Disfranchisement he cannot be taken as a type of his Close, who show no scorn of the boon held out to them, nor want of appreciation of those who are -striving to obtain it for them. But the strain of our aacient vassalage most surely still run in our blood, and manifests itself occaeionally in such freaks of self-abasernent.—l ant, Sir, yours, dv!, Penketh, July 29, 1884.

div.head: SUNDAY CLOING.
div.p: SUNDAY CLOING.

Sir,—Will you kindly allow mo a last word with "Social Reformer ?" I wish in the first place to disclaim being an opponent If it is possible for the ingenuity of man to pro- pound a scheme which will make us a sober people it shall have my hearty support. Sunday closing will not do this. It merely proposes to treat the people as if they were a lot Of children. I know, perhaps better than my reforming friend, the evils the working classes suffer through their proneness to drink. Having dozens of times seen the bane- ful irflsence it has over men's minds at times when their brains should be clear, and when questions involving their very existence had to be discusse,S, I can assure "Social Reformer" that I at least speak not from theory but from real practical experience, and I have no wish to hide or burk the knowledge that has come within my ken. Children of tender years may be seen on Saturday nights haunting the ale house bars, and, as it gets close on eleven, struggling for Precedence, all to secure the tilling of a bottle or can with beer, that will of a certainty make their parents at home forget all decency, that will let loose the obscene tongne, and that will display to these children's wondering gaze their parents turned into demeniacs. More than this, I must say that the experience so gained by these children bears fruit, Ind we see it in the streets in the form of drunken girls ant our young lads we meet strutting with pale tams and short pipes, and this I grant has its root in the great drink question. No problem I to-day so loudly calls for solving as this drink question. No our" to-day hangs so heavily on the working-man, and DO Class to-day are so intensely selfish as the publicans. There are exceptions, and I am pleased to :icknowledge such, but. take the political publican, and, as a rule, he is Tory. Why? Because be imagines the Liberals harrass " toe trade ;" all 1 impend politics he puts on one side; mhisfirstobject grantisself. I think, after having said so much, y friend wilt that I know something of the drink question, and, as one in the mighty crowd of workers, I have a- large experience of their likes and dislikes. Work' ine,nsen will not put bp 'with legislation of the kind advanced by teetotallers. There is a growing desire amongst the thinking portion of them that sober principles should be more common than they are at present ; that the alehouse and the publican should be servants, not masters ; but there is no desire whatever that their privileges should be filched from them. Why Is Sunday closing advanced so persistently now-adays? Is it becinse the other fads have failed in robbing us of our glass of beer? and now an attempt must be , made to stay the desecration of the Sabbath day. Why not ask for Satur- day closing ? Tell working-men plainly that their wives bad better meet them on wage days. take their money, and Send them home to bed until Monday morning. My friend says I resort to " banter and chaff of a poor quality." Well, in one sense I think the Sunday Closing idea deserves little else but chaff. But I recognise that there Is quite a heap of views to be taken of this question. In
CATHOLIC PITILANTHROPIC SOCIETY.

On Monday evening the annual dinner in connection with the above society, took place in the Clubroom, Bulerrnarket- street, Warrington, when about 60 members and guests sat down to an excellent dinner, the catering for which had seen entrusted to Mr and Mrs Maskell, who proved quite equal to the task, and to whom great praise is dae for the ad- mirable style in which it was provided. The room had bees tastefully decorated for the occasion by members of the committee and presented a striking appearance. The invi- ted guests present were as follow : The Right Rev T A Bury (Preston), Rev F Sumner (chaplain), Rev F Scannell, and Rev F Thompson Messrs R Hind, T Wallington, Fleming, J Moore, T Miller, W Houghton, Dr Geary, Major McCarthy, J G Civanagh. After dinner Mr. H. ECCLE3, the secretary of the society, rose and pro- posed a vote of thanks to Father Bury for having travelled from Preston to be amongst them that evening. He might be a little ou.: of place in proposing this vote of thanks, but , Father Bury was about to leave to catch his train.

Mr. T. MATHER, in seconding the proposition, said that he felt sure that they all appreciated Father Bury's kindness in attending. He had done great work in Warrington whilst he was amongst them, and had left behind him many things which were a credit to him, and which were standing memorials of his energy. (Applause.) The Right Rev. T. A. BI7RY, ia responding, said that he had been their pastor, and h 3 thought that there was one standing memorial which they all gave him credit for, and that was he was noted for his short sermons. He sold that he had only a very few maments to say how extremely pleased he was at what had been said, and he could assure them that he was only cony that railway time obliged him to leave, but he hoped at some future time to be able to spend a much longer evening with them. (Applause.) The Rev. F. SUMNER proposed the toast of " His Holi- ness Pape Leo XIII.," and in doing so said that there Was little cause for him to sly much in regard to the Pope, as he was speaking to a Catholic assembly, but as he hid been called upon to propose it, he did so with much pleasure, and wished his Holiness long life and happiness. (Ap• planes.) Mr. WILLIAM ALLEN, president of the society, proposed the toast of Her Majesty the Queen and Royal Family, and slid it required very few words on his part. He thought that if they were to turn over the pages of history there could tmt be found any king or queen that cauld in any way excel our present Queen, and he was sure they could sym- pathise with her in the sorrow which had befallen her of late. (Applause.) The Bishops and Clergy of the Dioceses of Liverpool and Shrewsbury respectively were proposed, and duly responded to by Fathers Scannell and Thompson. F. Sumner pro. posed the toasts of the President, Vice-President. Officers, and other officials, and responded to by Mr. Allen, Mr. .1. Moore gave the Army and Navy, which was responded to by Major McCa, thy. Mr. WILLIAM STIRRUP proposed "Our Society," and in doing so said it was a pleasure to him to see the present assembly. The Society's registration had, been in abeyance for two or three years, but it was no fault of theirs. The Government wanted to put restrictions on them which they as Catholics could not accept. The Government officials had struck out nearly every line of Catholicity in their rules and they were determined, rather than sacrifice their one great object, namely, that of keeping it strictly a Catholic Society, not to have the Society registered. At one time the club had nearly ceased to exist, and a sugges- tion Was thrown out to divide what funds existed to enable its members to join some other society, but they strenuously opposed it, for they were determined that the Catholic Club should not cease in Warrington. He hoped that all would endeavour to get more to join the Society, for he could not see why they should only number about ea Out of the many Catholic young men in Warrington they ought to number MOO. He hoped the club would succeed in gaining more members and in extending its benefits far beyond its present imits, (Applause.) Mr. Ilminv ECCLIII9, in responding, said he wished to thank Mr. Stirrup for the kind manner in which he bad spoken of the society and the members in general for the manner in which they had received the toast. He went on to say that there were many other societies in the town, and he did not wish to say one word against any of them, for ' they were all established for a good purpose, and it was pretty generally admitted that they were a aource of great benefit to the working-classes ; but he claimed for that society far greater benefits to its members than these societies. The contribution each member had to pay was less than in any other society, and he could mention mary ether benefits which they as Catholics well knew. After giving a short history of the society ten or twelve years back, he added that this year the society had been most successful. He would like it to extend its usefulness still further. Other societies had what was termed a widows and orphans' fund, and also a children's burial society, and he wonld like to see the same established in that society. It could be done by a very small contribution, and it would be a great boon to all who joined. (Applaul2.) Other toasts followed, which were ably responded to, the rest of the evening being spent in singing and other amuse- ments ; and after a vote of thanks had been accorded to the retiring president, Mr. Wm. Allen, a very' pleasant evening was brought to a close.

DISGRACEFUL ATTACH UPON A HANTICER. —At the County Police Court, Strangeways, Manchester, on Samuel Clarke and James Arstall, of Hollins Green, reported labourers, were placed in the dock charged with assaulting and otherwise injuring James Hall, a fish hawker, of Colly- hurst-road, Manchester. According to the evidence of the complainant, who was hawking fish in Cadishead, on Satar• day afternoon, the two prisoners came up to him, took some fish from his basket, and refused to pay for them: He fol- lowed them, when they seized his basket, amd threw his stock of fish in the roadway. On his asking again for the money they assaulted hirn, threw him down, and kicked him, and the second-named prisoner threw a brick at him which struck him on the temple. The complainant appeared in court with his head bandaged, and '-claimed 35., the value of the fish wasted, besides 61. for those taken from his. basket.—Thomas Morgan, of Glaze.. brook, spote of the way in which the complainant had been Mused, and Catherine Frier, a married wsiran, cf Cello- head, saw both the prisoners kick Hall when he was on the ground, and when she tried to separato them from him, Arstall threatened to assault her.—Mr. Dickens, who pre- sided. spoke of their conduct as disgraceful, and sent t'aem to prison for two months with bard labour.

the first place Sunday is the working-rnan's holiday. On this day he takes his ride or walk into the country, and he wMes to enjoy himself during the day and have his glass of hoer ; " No," say our reformers, "-you must not have this beer on Sundays, because we wish to put a stop to Sunday drinking. Your poorer brethren, who, screwed down in I their wages by beneficient employers).know not how tc.001.. duct themselves, so we shall shut the public houses up al- together." Now I protest against this view altogether- Acts of Parliament will not make men sober, any more than a, good education leads judzes to live moral lives, or noen in high nositioaa to lead lives that would make "Dublin, scandals" impossible. I as a moderate drinker of beer refuse to abstain because a dmwta. other men know not how to _conduct themselves.

I also refuse to allow my representative in Parliarnent to vote for Sunday closing, because I wish "the trade "'to-be controlled entirely by public opinion, unfettered by any Parliamentary tastics whatever, even to the abolishing of the licensing system. The public-house b not bad in itself, it is what the people make it, and if those who are now uttericg. pharisaical sentiments would only mix mare with the people it would soon become as great a &grata,: to a man or woman to be known as a fit ankard as it is to be known as a thief. The rich man has his wine cellars, During the week days he is driving Out with his wife and family, spending three or four months out of the twelve at the seaside, while he who earns the means for all this is cooped up. in mill or factory, denied the right of a " St. Monday." Poor beggar! we know he cannot afford. to lose this day or spend his bit of wage on drink. Barely aver- aging a pound per week as labourer, he finds it impossible to keep a wife and family, and so gi yes up the task in des- pair. Shenstone's words find an echo in his breast. Who'er has travelled life's dull round, Whate'er his fortunes may have been. Must sigh to think how oft is found Life's warmest welcome at an inn.

I ask "Social Reformer" to put himself in the place of some of those who live on School-brow, Tanners-lane, or the Old-road, and tell us what he would do. I have no doubt he will answer. "Why, keep my wages from the publican, and live in a better neighbourhood." This is no answer ; man is the creature of circumstances, and, although he is also their creator, as an individual he is their victim. Life's path is a thorny one to the poorer wage earners. Taught by Christianity to rest satisfied in the position in which it has pleased Goa to place him, he bee, until recently, been look- ing forward to a future life for rest, its ignorin4 the f lot that the unscrupulous and selfish around him were quietly• gathering the money and the power to make and to keep his life one perpetual round of toil. Thanks to a real and not a sham education, his eyes are gradually being opened. In conclusion, I beg your readers to vote for Mr Crosfield, not because he is a Sunday closer, but because he is a mem- ber of that political party which is gradually, though un• consciously, leading us up to the point when the people will not only throw off all saintly Sundayism, but that base and vicious system that gives all the toil to one man, and all the spoil to another. If abstainers wish to benefit the work- people of Warrington, let them take up the question of the supply of clean water to workmen during working hours. Not only the workers of our largest fu-3tian cutting shop., hut those of large wire mills, are denied a drop to drink ; and yet these employers are called Liberals. CAPTAIN CUTTLE,

IRE EXAMINER. SATURDAY. AUGUST 2, 1884.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. REJECTION OP THE BILL. There was something like consternation in Warrington last evening when it became known that the House of Com- mons Committee haebrejected the Ship Canal M. Mr. Pember began his closin4 speech for the promoters yesterday afternoon. In summing up the case, be said that was the ninth speech he had made in behalf of the Bill, and if the promoters had been foolish enough to aceept the suggestion of the petitioners that they should conotenct an inland canal from Puncorn to Cerston a new vista, would have been opened which would have been as tiresome to him as it would be to the committees. In consequence of the short time left for the consideration of this Bill several im- portant elements had been late almost unproved: This grand commercial case in all its ramifications had not been pat before the committee in so complete a way as was the case in the other House. The learned counsel then pro- ceeded at great length to criticise the evidence. Mr. Pernber concluded his address at 20 minutea to four, and, the room having been cleared, the committals procee- ded to consider their decision. Re-admission was granted in about three-quarters of an hour, when The Chairman said: The ccoarnittee have come to the conclusion—and I may say unanimously—that the PRE.- AM3LE was7slo:7 3EEN PROVED• to their satisfaction; and I should like to, say to you, Mr Pember, that your clients have lost nothing by your fcebearing to pureue the com- mercial case so far as you might otherwise haw thought it necessary to de. The decision of the committee caused the greatest surprise in Maneheeter. The news was conveyed to the head offices in Marketseereet by.a private telegram, and many merchants and otb.ees who have interested themselves in, the promotion of the sehome also received the same information by tele- graph. The intelligence soon became generally known, and the keenest disappointment was expressed on every band. Toe Central News save :—The rejection, of the Bill has caused general surprise, nothing which hat taken place since the measure came before the Coaamons' Committee having prepared ite promoters to expect its rejection in so summary and complete a manner.. The Bill has been before Parliament two sessions. Curiously enough it was passed unanimously by the Commons' Conanaittee and rejected by the Lents' Committee last year—a procedure which has been exactly reversed this session. It is estimated that up to the present time from one hundred and fifty to two hundred thousand pounds have been spent by the promoters and opponents of the Bill, a sum which is equivalent to a little over one thousand pounds for each day upon which it has been before the Parliamentary Committees. The Central News representative, in conversation last evening with a member whose name appears on the back of the Bill, learns that they had regarded the Committee which threw out their scheme as a thoroughly sound and judici- ouelv selected body. The Committee, however, in their wsiciorn, had unanirnonsly decided that the scheme was a wild and impracticable Otto; bat, added the gentleman referred to, a canal to Manchester most be made at some time or other. It is, however, douhtful whether another guarantee of £BO,OOO will be forthcoming by next year to promote the Bill a third time. Such was the confidence in London that the Bill would pass that the correspondent of the Vanchoter Evening writing on Friday mot ning, said This afternoon the country will know the decision of the Select Committee of the House of Commons on the Man- chester Ship Canal Bill. This committee meet at one o'clock to hear Mr. Pember reply on behalf of the promoters, and the result may be expected in Manchester between four and five o'cl.ck. It is not generally known perhaps that Mr. Pember has beau piloting at the same time the Manchester Ship Canal Bill in the House of Commons arid the Barry Dock Bill in the House of Lords. Success has crowned his efforts in the case of the latter, and the same result. I ven- ture to predict, awaits him in respect to the for- mer. He has really a very easy task before him, tu-d ty. By the promoters the decision of the committee is awaited with perfect confidence, and the opponents are just as much dejected. They blame themselves now for having at first misjudged the character of the scheme which they had to oppose, and the opinion has' been very generally expressed among them that had they concentrated their energy on the ques,lon of injury and ruin to the estuary they might have made a greater impression upon Parliament. The country, of course, has no concern in such matters, and the fact that the Bill has received the sanction of the committee will. I do not hesitate t say, be received with feelings of unfeigned satisfaction from one end of the country to the other.

They decided to convey the sewage in ventilated drains to three or four tanks placed along the bank of the stream, and there treat it by precipi- tation with, lime in properly construlted tanks before it was turned iato the brook. He complained strongly that the noxious vapours emanating from neighbouring places were carried by the wind to irbarrington, and did great damage to vegetation. SUICIDE AND AriVIPTED SUICIDE. A most distressing case of suicide occurred at Warring- ton yesterday morning, when Mr Thomas Saxer, landlord of the Fox Inn, an hostelry of very ancient appearance, situated in Buttermarket-street, and in close proximity to Market-gate, took his life by cutting his throat with a razor. At about severs o'clock in the morning P C Singleton, who was on duty in Bridge-street, received information that Saxon bad cut his throat, and he at once proceeded to the Fox Inn, when he found that the information was correct, Saxon being in bed with his throat very severely cut. A razor covered with blood was found lying near and is no doubt the Instrument with which the deed was committed. Medical aid was also promptly sent for and Dr Joseph was soon in attendance on the injured man, who lingered until shortly after one o'clock yesterday afternoon, when he died. The wound that he had inflicted was found to be nn- usually severe, the cut being a deep one, touching the jugu- lar vein and also the windpipe, but not being sufficiently deep as to cauee immediate death. From what can be ' cleaned of the sad affair, the act seems to have Seen a premeditated one, as Mrs Margaret Saxon, the wife of the deceased, who rose between six and seven o'clock in the morning and went downstairs, leaving her husband in bed, received by post about 6-55 a letter !: that hail been. posted at Market-gate and which was from ; her husband. On her reading it she immediately ran up- stairs and, although she had not been long out of bed, she was too late to prevent her husband carrying out the inten- tion he had evidently expressed an the letter. The police authorities were reticent regarding the contents of the letter, but from what could be ascertained there was a state- ment in it to the effect that his body would be found at an hotel near Newton Bridge Station. From that it appears as though hie original intention had been to destroy himself there. No definite cause can yet be assigned as the reason of the rash deed, though it is said that the deceased load appeared to be in a despondent state for some time. It is also stated that he had received a dunning letter from a London firm and a further statement is to the effect that he had beet money in betting, bat these allegations must be accepted with reserve until the coroner's inquest that wilt be held takes place, when no doubt the affair will be tho- roughly investigated. The deceased was 46 years ol are, was an old resident of Warrington, and was very well known. THE ATTEMPTED SLUMP.. On Tuesday evening Peter Millar, 60 years of age, who re- sides at the Five Houses, Winwick-road, made what appears to have been a determined attempt to commit suicide. In the morning he went for a walk in the direction of Rowley. lane, and in the afternoon a woman, who was attracted to the spot by hearing the ceies of some children, found him struggling in a ditch of water. As soon as possible he was got out of his dangerous predicament and conveyed to his home. The assistance of Dr. Adams was procured, and it was found that Millar had cut his throat in two places, the wounds having been inflicted by a penknife. One was a severe one, and touched the windpipe; it required seven stitches to sew it up. For some time the injured man Was conaidered to be in a dangerous condition, but he afterwarde rallied, and, at the time of writing, strong hopes are enter- tained of his recovery. Millar is a cripple and walked by the aid of crutches. It is supposed that he was in a despon- dent state of mind.

div.head: RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

A meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhousq, Warrington, yesterday morning, under the presidency of Mr. W. D trbyshire, the other members present being Mes3rs. Cooper (vic3-chairman), Long. Forster, Humphreys, Grange, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, C. Broadbent, Swinton, Sutton tclerk), Owen (surveyor), Rawlings (inspector of nuisances), and Dr. S 3 phton (medical officer.)

IHE I,ONDITION Or SANKEY CANAL—The CLERIC read a letter received from the Local Government Board, trans- mitting a copy of correspondence that had passed between the Board and Mr. G. H. Bolton, of Peuketh House, near Warrington, together with a copy of a letter received from Mr. Johnson, Ferry Hotel, Penketb, relative to the state of Sankey Canal, and requesting the observations of the Authority thereon. The first letter was dated from Penketh House by Mr. Bolton, and called the attention of the Local Government Board to the offensive and dangerous state of Sankey Canal, extending through the district of the War- rington Rural Sanitary Authority, and also of the Widnes Local Board. The sickening effluvia from the canal per- vaded the district throughout its course, but the local authorities were either powerless or indifferent. A second letter front 'Mr. Bolton, in substantiation of the first, In- formed the Board that he believed the nuisance did not come from Widnes works, but from St. Helens and Enloe- town districts, polluting the entire district in the course of the canal. In reply the Local Government Board asked Mr. Bolton if he had addressed any communications to the local authorities on the subject, to which be wrote that he had addressed the chairman of the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority respecting the state •of the canal, and had also brought the matter under the notice of the Widnes Local Board; who had inspected the canal, but he was not aware of any action havim been taken. The letter of Mr. Johnson stated that he was advised by several gentlemen to write to the Local Government Board regarding the nuisance. Hts house was about three miles from Warrington, and people came to it to enjoy the country, .but owing to the abomin- able smell that rose from the canal they had determined not to go there again. He had written to the Local and Sani- tary Authorities, bat they seemed' to take little or no notice: he begged the Board to take action in the matter, as the nuisance was injurious to health and to his business.—The CnAtArettaN said that he did not take upon himself indi- vidually to answer the letters he had received; he simply brought such letters that were addressed to him before the Authority to be dealt with.—The CLERK said he had written to the hendon and North-Western. Company in reference to the matter, and had received a reply to the effect that the nuisance was caused at St. Helens, partly by the Corpora- tion, sad- that the mattirhad been referred to the divisional engineer of the comoany.—The CHAIRMAN said that far from being neglectful or indifferent, the Au, bority had paid great attention to the eomplaints—Mr. BROADBENT asked if the Authority had jurisdiction over the canal.—The CLERK said that they had power over that part that was in the Board'odistrict.—Mr. BBOADRBIPB said that the canal be- longed to the Railway Company, and therefore if it was a nuisance it would be for the company to insist that the Cor- poration of St. Helens did net pollute the canal.—After con- siderable discussion as to what would be the best course to pursue, it was decided to await the result of the correspond- ence between the company and the St. Helens Corporation, the company in the meantime to be requested to clear eut the caral within two months.

ewerAtax PRECALITIONS, —The CLERK said that he had received several documents containing, regulations as to cholera, which were directed to be banded over to the medi- cal of3cer and inspector.—Mr COOPER remarked that the cholera epidemic was causing a terrible panic in Toulon and Marseilles, and they should not lose sight of the matter.— Mr. BnoanelEtcr remarked that it was just such things as the Sankey canal that were liable to cause cholera.—The sublect then dropped. PENILETH PAROCI-ZIAL COMMITTEE.—A meeting of this committee was held en the 30th July. A discussion arose respecting the position of drains and cesspools, and it was proposed by Mr GARNETT, and seconded by Mr RERFOOT, and unanimously resolved that four uncovered settling tanks be erected according to the plans approved by the commit- tee and Dr Sephten, to be placed as defined upon the copy of the Ordnance map, and that sewage in each tank be treated with lime before being turned into the brook. It was reported to the cemmittee by the chairman that two men had been engaged to clear out the brook, and it was re- solved that the Authority be asked to sanction the expendi- ture.—The minutes of the committee were passed without discuseion. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—The MEDICAL OFFICER reported that the births for July were, males 11. females 16, and the deaths, male. 8, females 4. The excess of births over deaths was 15 The death rate from all causes was equal to 114 per 1,000, against 17 the average of the last three month., and against 13.3 the corresponding month of last year. The death rate from aymotic diseases was equal to 28 per 1,000, against 21, the average rate of the last three :months, and against 1.9 the corresponding month of last year. DiirDIELANSI INCAPABLE.—At the Sale Petty Sessicns, on Monday, a man named Edward M.,:rphy was charged with being drunk and incapable at Lymm on Saturday evening. As he had been is gaol two nights tiro. Bench dismissed him with a cantina.

Excurtsrozsr ed, JUVENILES TO LTiliVs.—On Monday next, which is Bank Holiday, the children and teachers connec- ted with Mr Allsopp's missions. ic Manchester, will have an outing to Lymm. On arriving at Lvmm they will be takenito the Park at Lymm Hall,,and will' be there regaled with pies, butts, &c. The cost of this excursion will he de- frayed by public subscriptions, about £4O having been raised in Lymm for that purpose. The Primitive Methodist Brass Band will be engaged for the day. ATTB:IIIerED STJICIDE.—Oa Thursday, Mrs Drinkwater, the wife of Samuel Drinkwater, labourer, Lymm, was brought on before Mr Collins., at Lvmm Police Court,. charged with having attempted to commit suicide. It appeared from the evidence given that both the defendant and her husband have recently been drinking heavily; and 'some time last week defendant took a large dose of laud- ATIIIIM evidently with the intention of committing suicide. She was discharged on her twoisons becoming sureties for her future good behaviour. AN IMPOSTER.—A man named Michael Lewin, of Man- chester, was on Thursday charged on remand at the Lynam Police Court, with having obtained by means of falsa pre- tences' 4s, the property of Mr Thomas IVinstanley, of the Nag's Head, Lymm. The prisoner, it appeared, had repre- sented himself to be a "gas engineer and illuminator" and by means of fraudulent pretences and representations, man- aged to sell a number of gas burners to the defendant and other gentlemen in the neighbourhood of Lymm, for sums greatly exceeding their value. He was committed for trial to the Knutsford Quarter Sossions.—On Thursday two lads named William Middleton and John Evans, aged 16 and 14 respectively, of Liverpool, were charged on suspicion at the same Court, with having stolen a quantity of boots and goloshes. On Tuesday evening P C Chatterton found the lads rambling about the lanes near Thelwall, having in their possession some new shoes and goloshes. Ile apprehended them, and subsequently inquiries were made of the Liver- pool police, and it was ascortaised that the articles in the lads' possession bad been stolen from Wilson's boot and shoe shop, Park-lane, Liverpool. The lads were accordingly handed over to the Liverpool police.

div.head: ANNUAL FLOWER SROW.
div.p: ANNUAL FLOWER SROW.

The second annual Fk,wer 'ShOW-for Lymin and district was opened in the Park at Lymm Hall (by the kind permis- sion of Mr. Bettersbn yesterday afternoon under, as far as the weather was concerned, very favourable conditions. The Park in which the glow was held is also in every way suit- able, having a fine velvety sward and being pleasantly wooded. The exhibits which were more various than what era generally seen at flower shows were displayed in three tent& The largest of these contained the bulk of the flowers, vegetables, and fruits, and there was also in its centre S beautiful arrangement of splendid flowering and foliage plants, including paliee, ferne, celide, and begonias, lent by Mrs Battersby, Mr G C Dewhurst, the Rev U W Guest, Mrs Crosfield, Mr J D Dewhurst, Mr Stanton, Mr Stubs, and Mr Grundy. Mrs Bettersby had a further ex- hibit, though not for competition, of a very fine collection of fruit which were highly commended; a collection of seed potatoes Bent by Mr E Gibbon were also highly commanded; as were likewise a similar collec- tion beloeging to Mr Shakeshaft. Of the general body of exhibits it may be fairly said that they did credit to the horticultural skill of the cottagers of Lymrn and its neigh- bourhood. If any distinction were to be made it would, perhaps, be in favour of the fruit and vegetables, as some of the flowers appeared in some cases to be somewhat over- blown and faded. The second tent was devoted to the "arts and manufactures," and was tilled with interesting exhibits. To the left on entering, a stall was filled by Mr. J. B. Tay- lor, ironmonger, Lymm, with a large assortment of the finer sorts of ironmongery ; and a little turther down a fustian frame was erected at which a workman practically xemplified the mysteries of fustian cutting, which is one of the staple industries of Lymm. :On a central stall and frame was a fine and varied assortment of pictures and fancy and useful articles. An antique-looking silk hat,ouce belonging to the Duke of Wellington, and exhibited by Mr. Bettersby, Came in for a good deal of curious attention, as did also a plate of porcelain, also exhibited by Mr. Battersby, which had formed part of a present to the "Iron Duke by the King of Prussia. A relic of Nelson in the shape of a plate of Worcester porcelain, decorated Cy Mr. Baxter, was like• wise exhibited by Mr. Battersby. A fine 'l.l Sevres choco- late service and a quantity of other rare kinds of ware toge- ther with an ivory Chinese pagoda and other specimens of the skill of the Celestials " had been contributed by Mrs. Guest. The third tent was in some respects the most in- teresting of all, an important portion of its con- tents being a nnnaber of bees under the care of an expert from the Cheshire Beekeepers' Associa- tion. The bees were in hives of various construction and their workings could be seen through glass partitions. Some lessons as to the management of this useful insect were also given during the afternoon by the expert in a bee tent erected on the ground. A small refreshment tent was under the care of Mrs Ardern. Miss Knight, and Miss Gosling. Three bands were in attendance, viz, the Lymm Tradesmen's Braes Bend, Larrum String Band, and the Church Temperance Band, and these discoursed selections of music during the afternoon.
