div.p: RATNIULL.

CIIIJRCU SuNDAY SCTIOOL.—TtiI annual sum- mer treat of the above schools was held on Wednesday, July 30th, when the elder scholars, to the number of 150, accompanlA by a large party of teachers and friends, were taken to New Brighton. An excellent tea was provided for them at the rooms of the New Brighton Cocoa-rooms Com- pany, The return journey commenced soon after 7 p.m., and all arrived home safely, after a most enjoyable day, about 9 o'clock. RAINHILL WESLETAN SUNDAY Scoot.—The children of this school, attended by teachers and friends, had their an- nual outing on Wednesday, the place selected being the pleasant village of Hale. The visitors put up at the Ctedde of Hale Hotel, having been conveyed there in vehicles kindly lent by Messrs. H. Baxter, W. Longton, W. A. Meadows, T. Welsley, R. Naylor, J. Lowe, J. Thomas,- Mrs. Duxberry, and Mrs. Wigglesworth. A spacious field near the hotel was thrown open to them, and several hours were spent there most pleasantly. Tea was supplied at the Childe of Hale Hotel.

WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT—A sitting of this court was held on Thursday, before the judge, Mr W Wynne Ffoulkes. The only case of any importance was one in which a man named Richard Birehall, a plasterer living in Cborley-street, sued his eon-in-law' a person named Barnes, for the sum of 103 odd, alleged to be due for the payment of a gaB bill under an agreement arrived at between the parties.—Mr Moore appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr Browne defended.—Mr Moore said that the parties to the action had lived in two houses that adjoined each other, and about Christmas last the plaintiff let one house to the defen- dant on the terms that he should pay 3s a week and half the gas bill—because the meter that supplied both houses was in that one occupied by the plaintiff —The plaintiff deposed that the meter was in his house, and that he had paid the gas hill. The agreement was as Mr Moore had stated.— Mr Brcwne, for the defence, submitted that the parties really lived in one house, catntnunication being effected by a door, and that Barnes and his wife.were lodgers, and not separate tenants. The agreement was that the 31 a week was to in- clude everything except coals.—His Honour, in giving judgment for the plaintiff, said that it was unreasonable to suppose that be would let the house at 35 a week and supply gas as well. . .

'2 CRUELTY TO Ammats.—The Warrington borough magis- trates were on Monday engaged in bearing a number of pro- secutions instituted at the instance of the Royal Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, which Was represen- ted by Inspector Harper. The first case heard was one in which Patrick Harden, a labourer, of Winwick-street, was' charged with workbag a horse in an unfit state, two men named John Hamblett and Peter Robinson, being charged with causing the animal to be worked.-Mr Moore defended.- Inspector Harper said that ,the defendant Harablett bought the horse at Bold and directed H mien to take it thence to Warringten, when it was found that the animal was suffer- ing from an injury to the spine, and that it could scarcely walk. Its legs knocked together SO much that the tops of the hoofs were bleeding. Harnblett tied some seeking round them, and with difficulty the horse was got to Sankey Brid- ges, where it fell down. It was ultimately get to Warring- ton and put into a stible. It Was not in a condition to be taken into the fair and the defendant Robinson agreed to purchase it to kill. Hamblett Suggested that it should be killed on the spot, but Robinson directed Hanlan to take it to his (Robinson's) place. On the way the horse was noticed by a constable. The Bench, without calling upon Mr Moore for his defence, dismissed the case on payment of costs, being of opinion that the cruelty had not been inten- tional under the circumstances of the case --The follow- ing were also charged with similar offences, viz : Peter Rocker, fined 101 and costs, Mathew Bate, dismissed; Stephen Heesom and Thomas Curley, dismissed on payment of costs; Henry Barber, fined 5a and costs, James Chester, dismissed; William Harding, fined 103 and costs. COMMITTAL OF A BANK-RV-PT FOR CONTEMPT OF COURT. —The adjourned application for the committal for contempt of John Taylor Taylor, a bankrupt brewer's traveller, late of Heatley, and now of Altriacham, came before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, at the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, when the bankrupt was represented by Mr. Hill, of Manchester.—The official receiver (Mr. Ridgway) said that at the last hearing, on the 7th July, his Honour ordered that the hearing of the application should be adjourned until that day, and that before that day the bankrupt should file the accounts ordered by the court, and also should pay him (Mr. Ridgway) the payments out of pocket and court fees incurred in respect to the application. The bankrupt had been served with a copy of the order, and his Honour would see that he had filed an affidavit in which he stated that he had not paid the payments out of pocket. He did not think it was his duty to call attention to what had been filed, except to the eighth paragraph of the affidavit, which read to the effect that he (the bankrupt) Was absolutely un- able to file any further or better accounts than those filed by him on the 30th June, and he called the attention of the court to the fact that be had not kept books of account, except two items which appeared !n the deficiency account in his statement of affairs. He submitted to the court that in tiling the accounts he had done he had complied with the 24th section of the Bankruptcy Act of 1863 to the best of his power, and that if any further statement was required by the official receiver it should be prepared by some person appointed and paid by the receiver, as provided by the 10th section of the Act.—Alr Hill asked his Honour to allow him to call a gentleman who had pre- pared the bankrupt's statement of affairs, who would ex- plain how it Was impossible to prepare anything better.— His Honour said that the affidavit that had been filed was anything but a proper roe in some respects. It made ob- jection to the order of the court and set out the bankrupt's view. That was not the part a bankrupt ought to play when he came there. The :affidavit was argumentative and irrelevant. He did not see how it would forward the matter to call the gentleman as the order was upon the bankrupt and not upon a professional gentleman.—Mr Hill said the bankrupt was totally unable to do it himself.—His Honour said that he had managed to file what he called a deficiency account. What the court had ordered was a statement of _accounts to show how the bankrupt came into the position he was in, whether there were any assets, how ha had incur- red his debts, and to file an account of his business for the last six years. That Was ggite a different thing to what had been done. his affidavit the bankrupt made important assertions, and one paragraph might be called perfectly scandalous and irrelevant.—Mr rani : The bankrupt says he ' cannot do any more.—His Honour: Has he got the £1 3s 2d 'to pay the amount out of pocket. —Mr Hill : He has not yet. Mr Hill further mentioned that the professional gentle- man who bad assisted the bankrupt would pay the money. —His Honour said that he was afraid he must take the only course pointed out by the Act, and should commit the bank- rupt to prison until such a statement as was required Should be fortbcoming.—Netice of appeal was given.

TRIP' TO NEW BRIGHTON.-- Mt W H Rigbey advertises a popular picnic to New Rtighton, to take place next Saturday, the 9th inst. The fares are very low, and the combined attractions offered cannot but prove tempting to holiday makers.

• A IltzY PasExr.—T homes Spencer, of Kinder's.yard, was charged before the Warrington Bench, on Friday, with having neglected his family whereby they had become chargeable to the Warrington Union.—Mr Shearer, relieving officer, stated that on the 15th tilt the defendant's wife and six children were admitted into the workhouse, and the Guardians directed that a warrant Should be issued for the defendant. Both the defendant and his family, Mr. Shearer added, had spent most of their time in tile workhoase, and this year alone they had cost the ratepayers £35. Defend- ant said he was in bad health, but on his making a similar plea about 12 months ago, he was examined by the doctor, who said he was not ill, but merely shamming. When he was in the workhouse there was great difficulty in getting him to work, and laziness in fact seemed to be his greatest weakness.—Defendant was sent to gaol for it days. EXCURSION TO BLacirPsot. —T he annual excursion of the employee of Messrs. William Smith and Son, Dallam- lane Wire Works, Warrington, took place on Saturday, Blackpool being selected as one of the most appropriate of places within reasonable distance. Every arrangement pos- sible was made by the committee to ensure the comfort and enjoyment of the passengers, at least se far as the railway journey was concerned, and the railway officials also did their best to make things as pleasant as they could be. The train, well-filled with excursionists, left Bank Quay Station (high level) shortly after seven o'clock in the morning, arriving soon after nine, when the excursionists dispersed, and, following the bent of their own inclination, proceeded to visit the scenes of interest and enjoyment with which Blackpool is so favoured. Unfortunately the weather was anything but propitious, as a steady rain fell with a most depressing influence nearly the whole of the day. This somewhat marred the wajoymont of outside pleasure seekers. but the attractions of the Winter Gardens, Raikes /fall Gar- done, and the various places, of in-door amusements, fully atoned in mast instances foe the loss of the usual bath, sail, or stroll on the beach, so pleasant under a genial sun and so unpleasant to roost peori:e in a downpour of rain. On the whole the Warringtonians at Blackpool, on Saturday, may be said to have madra the best of circumstances and to have enjoyed themselves in the face of considerable opposition from the weather. The homeward, start was made about 7-30,, Warrington being reached by the very respoc,allit h.Scr ol ktia o'clock,

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Ws now stated that the prorogation will take place on Tuesday, the 12th of August. A meeting of the financial advisers attached to the Con- ference was held at the Foreign Office yesterday. Under threat of a mandamus the Dewsbury guardians have at length appointed a medical officer under the Vac- cination Acts.

The Press Association states that authentic news of General Gordon is expected by the Government from Major Kitchener early next week. The roadway in Hamilton-street, Birkenhead, above the Mersey tunnel now ia course of construction, collapsed yes- terday. Nobody was injured. Mr. John Delaware Lewis, formerly member of Parlia- ment for Devonport, died on Thursday night at his country residence Westbury, near Peterstield, from rheumatic fever. Two young men named Thomas llDGuinness and John Murray, aged respectively 16 and 16, were drowned whilst bathing in the mill lodge of the Dacca Twist Company, Bolton, on Thursday night. Yesterday the Australians won the match by nine wickets against the Players of England. There was some distur- bance through the Players returning to luncheon when the Australians had only 11 runs to vet. A FATAL Fnesr.—On Friday morning an inquest was held at Rawtenstall ou the body of a girl 13 years of age, who died on Wednesday from the effect of eating 53 worth of fruit and confectionery. The money had been given to her to pay a rate.

. - DEATH SENTENCE COMMUTEII.—The Governor of Durham Gaol on Friday morning received an intimation from the Home Office that the sentence of death passed on George Soulsby at last Durham Assizes had been commuted to penal servitude,for life.

THE PECr.:MAR PEOPLE.—At Chelmsford Assizes, on Friday, William Dedmau, a labourer, and member of the so-called Peculiar People, was sentenced to a month's im- prisonment for causing the death of his infant daughter by neirlecting to afford medical treatment when the child be- came ill.

THE ANTI-SLAVERY Juikutka.—The Prince of Wales pre- sided yesterday at a jubilee celebration of the British and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society, in the Guildhall, and in open- ing the proceedings reviewed the work accomplished by the society in all parts of the world. Earls Granville and Derby, Sir Stafford Northcote, Mr Forster, Mr Hy Richard, the Primate, and Cardinal Manning were among the subsequent speakers.

LEGAL APPOINTMENT.—Mr. Justice Grove, while on cir- cuit at Chester, appointed Mr. Fre,lerick Marshall, of liar- court Buildings, Temple, of the North and South Witl.9 circuits, revising barrister for the counties of Montgomery- shire and Merionethshire. Mr. Marshall, who was until re- cently a well-known resident of Chester, enjoys an extensive practice on circuit, and is regarded by the profession and public as a rising man.

THE BRITISH—MEDICAL ASSOCIATION.—OB Friday morn• ing the members of the British Medical Association were en- tertained at breakfast on board the Dominion liner Van- couver in Belfast Lough. On resuming the deliberations in Queen's College, an address on obstetric medicine was de- livered by Dr. Kidd, Dublin, and the Medical Reform Corn- mittea's report, moved by Dr. Watters, Chester, and seconded by Dr. Cameron, M.P., was adopted. ROBBEEty OF' DYNAMITE. The Press Association's Glasgow correspondent telegraphs that a few nights ago a building in which dynamite is stored by miners working at the Carfin Collieries of Messrs. Dixon' near Airdrie, was broken open by a portion of the brickwork being dug out with pickaxes, and the whole stock of dyne- Mite, about 6511)3., was carried off. The robb3ry was dis- covered by the pit officials early next morning, and informa- tion given to the police. but no apprehensions have yet been made. THE SHOOTING OF CONSTABLES NT BURGLARS.—AI the Worship-street Police Court, London, on Friday, James Wright and William Wheatley, under remand, charged with shooting Constables Snell and Garner at Roston. were again brought up, and, as the injured men were unable to appear, Mr. Poland, for the Treasury, went into a second charge against the prisoners of shooting Police-constable Chamberlain, at Islington, on the 24th June last.—Police- constable William Chamberlain was examined, and positively identified Wright as the man who shot him in Park-street. IMPORTANT APPEAL CASE.—Judgment was given in the case of Cunliffe Brook and Co. v. Blackburn and District Benefit Building Society, on Friday, in the House of Lords. Their lordships held that the bankers had no lien upon the securities of the society, that an overdraft was borrowing, and that the society had no power to borrow. They accor- dingly sustained the judgment of the Court of Appeal, holding that that judgment did not decide the rights of parties, except as to the particular action, nor did the judg- ment in any way prejudice the rights of parties. The ap- peal was dismissed with costs. THE FENiAN TRIAL AT WARWICK.—The trial of Daley, Egan, and M`Donnell, the alleged Liverpool and Birming- ham dvn miters, was resumed on Friday morning before Mr Justice Hawkins, the same counsel appearing as on the previous day. Daly, in the course of a long address, in which he showed remarkable ability, thanked judge, jury, and counsel for the forbearing manner in which they had dealt with him during the trial. He contended that the bulk of the eeidence given against him had been simply got up by a well-organised scheme. At two o'clock the judge commenced his summing up to the jury.

div.head: CHOLERA.
div.p: THE CHOLERA.

TOCLON, FRIDIY, 10 A.m.—There were two deatha from cholera here last night, one occurring in the Bon Rencontre Hospital and one in the town. The city, however, now presents a more animated appearance, several shops having been re-opened. The mortality from June 20th to July 31st was 98, including 728 deaths from cholera.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF 'LORDS. The House met at 4-0.

MISCELLANEOUS.—Eari NORTHEROOX, replying to Earl Ashournim, explained the circumstances under which three Victorian war ships joined Admiral Hewitt at Suakin), but as their services were not wanted under the Queen's regula- tions, they could not fly the white ensign.—Tne Contagious Diseases Animals Act (Districts) Bill was read a third time. —The Prisons Hill passed through Committee; and the Expiring, Laws Continuance Bill was read a second time. The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four p'clocic.

QUESTIONS, &c.—Mr. M-lINDELLA, replying to Mr. Talbot, said the New Code would do all that council of education was empowered to do as regarded over pressure —Lord FlTumAuttrcE, replying to Mr. Alexander McArthur, said the Foreign Office had no sdefinite information as to the in- tentions of France at Madagascar, A British war vessel had proceeded to the Malagasy Coast to protest British pro- perty.—Mr. GnansToNE made a motion that the standing- order relative to Supply on Monday and Thursday apply to Saturday's sitting. Next day, he said, would be devoted en- tirely to Supifiy.—A long discussion ensued, Irish members insisting that Irish votes could not be concluded on Satur- day night —On a division there was—for the motion 123, against 23. limn Scepor. TRACHERS.—'VIr. H. MCCARTHY called at- tention to the grievances of Irish national school teachers. He moved a resolution stating it to ba the opinion of the House that a bill for tempolarily improving the incomes of teachers should be introdnced by the Government next ses- sion.—. Colonel NOLAN seconded the resolotion.-4r. THE- VELYAN did not think a teacher's position in Ireland was as bad as it was sought to make out. If Irish ratepayers acted as Scotch ratepayers had done, the salaries of the teachers could at once be improved.—After much debate, Mr. H. McCarthy's resolution was rejected by 63 against 61. The announcement of the numbers was received with cheers from the Irish members.
Sum.Y.—The House then went inTommittee of Supply OR the Civil Service Estimates. The vote for the salaries and expenses of county courts in Ireland was agreed t,o. [LEFT SITTING.]

FITZMAURICE, who was questioned about the Congo,stated that it appeared from the newspape s that an agreement had been made between the French Prime Minister and the President of the Belgian As- sociation giving to the French Government a right of pre-emption of certain territory on the Congo, though Her Majesty's Government had not received official notification of the fact, nor had the right been previously offered to Her Majesty's Government.—The PRIME MINISTER announced with much regret and disappointment that the Conference had been informed by the French Ambassador that he was not in possession of sufficient instructions, and that he had to re- quest a further adjournment until Saturday. Mr. Gladstone declined to state whether it was probable or not that he should have a proposal to submit for the judgment of the House, because such a statement might cause further dis- appointment.—The LORD ADVOCATE announced that it was not the intention of the Government to proceed with the Scotch Burghs Bill.—Upon the motion to go into Committee of Supply Mr. SEXTON raised a debate upon the death-bed confession of a man named Gandy, who stated that he was guilty of a crime for which Bryant Kilmartin had been con- victed and was now under sentence of penal servitude.— The CHIEF SECRETARY promised that the case should be thoroughly examined.—Several votes of Supply were then agreed to after considerable discussion. MISCELLANEOUS —The House went into Cemmitte on the Revenue Bill. The bill passed through Committee. The Public Health (Ireland) Districts Bill and the Criminal Lunatics Bill were read a third time. The Crown Land Bill was withdrawn. The East India Unclaimed Stocks Bill was read a second time. The Royal Courts of Justice Bill was withdrawn. The Burgh Police and Health (Scotland) Bill was withdrawn. The Cholera, ckc. Protection Bill passed through Committee. The consideration of the Infants Bill was resumed. The bill was read a third time. The House adjourned at five minutes past three.

RELIGIOUS RIOTS IN RUSSIA. BERLIN, MONDAY.—An outbreak of Russian peasants and workmen has occurred at Klimoff, in the government of Tschernigoff, against tradespeople belonging to the sect of Old Believers. Several shops were sacked, and in the fight- ing that ensued one man was killed and two wounded. The rioters, in reviling their victims, declared them to be worse than the Jews. NOVA SCOTIA. HALIFAX, SUNDAY.—Nir. Fielding, who undertook the re-constitution of the Ministry on the recent resigna- tion of the Hon. W. T. Pipes, has succeeded in forming a new Liberal Cabinet, in which he holds the position of Premier. TERRIBLE SCENE AT AN EXECUTION. VIENNA. TUESDAY.—At the execution to-day, at Krems, of a man sentenced to death for murdering a gaolor, the cul- prit offered violent resistance, struggling for five minutes on the scaffold with the executioner and his assistant. The noose was finally adjusted by the hangman. THE CAPTIVE CREW. SINGAPORE, TUESDAY.—The agent of tha Governor of Singapore, sent to treat with the Rajah of Tenom for the liberation of the crew of the Nisero, sailed yesterday.

DRUIDS' DINNER AT LATCHFCRD.—The“ Pride of Latch- ford" Lodge of the Order of Druids held their annual din- ner at the Brook Inn, Latchford, on Saturday afternoon, when the chair was occupied by Bro. Dunbobin. About 50' sat down. The usual loyal toasts were given from the chair. —Bro. Starkey, in responding for the " Army- and Navy," said that he bad belonged to lthe army for sixtasn years, and should no doubt have remained in it still, but for the short service system that had now come into oneration.—Re- spouding to the toast of "The Clergy and Ministers of all Denominations," the Rev. B. B. Prescott evinced hie sympathy with the work of the society, and urged upon the gathering the necessity. of unity. In sickness it was some- thing to know that there was money due to them, and that they would not therefore have to appeal to charity. The • society also provided funds for a decent and becoming funeral. He believ,d that such societies were a benefit to • health, because its members, to pay regularly to the funds, must'be hard-workers, careful, and abstain f-om excess.— Bro. Pointon, P.D.M , acknowledging the toast of the "Order eftDruids," stated that they had in the district 12 lodges, with 1,280 members and a capital of £1,700. He re- ferred to the subjects ef graduation and equalizatien, re- marking that in his opinion the former was a scheme really requisite in all friendly societies Ia connection with • equalization, he rem trked that it had been said at a late Lodge dinner that something like XGO had been spent in supporting "indolent lodges." He had rather that had not been said, as it was caused by the heas v sick list, there being no indolent lodges in Warrington.—Other toasts were given, and the evening was spent in a pleasant manner, songs being given at intervals.
